# Catervas Specification

Version 0.2 (draft for review). Owner: project founder. Status: not yet implemented; this document is the contract the first milestone is built against. Revision 0.3 also carries the rules the phase 1 reviews pinned down as the harness was built, each marked where it appears. Revision 0.2 (2026-09-14) adds sections 5.11 to 5.15, requirements F14 to F17, the `locked` and `references` contract fields, and the amendments marked "added in 0.2", all from the planning review recorded in `docs/plans/project-plan.md`. Revision 0.3 (2026-09-15) records the founder's decisions of that day and the move of the backend to Rust (section 8, ADR 0005). Revision 0.4 (2026-09-17) names in section 8.5 the six event kinds phase 2 emits that earlier revisions left unlisted, and records in 8.4 where task ids come from and where they stop. Revision 0.5 (2026-09-17) says in 5.14 what the repository's default branch is when there is no remote to record one, and that one task integrates at a time, both from the phase 2 step 04 reviews. Revision 0.6 (2026-09-17) names in 5.5 and 8.3 the two files phase 2 step 06 gave a place -- the price override and this machine's sandbox choice -- neither of which earlier revisions put anywhere. Revision 0.7 (2026-09-18) says in section 3 what `catervas init` writes, the starter team included, which phase 2 step 08 had to decide because no team editor exists until phase 5. It also says what the reading commands of step 09 show, and adds `lock_mismatch` and `contract_unreadable` to the `drift.detected` event in 8.5, which step 07 had added to the store and left the event unable to report. Revision 0.8 (2026-09-22) corrects 8.3, which put git operations inside the container while ADR 0004 runs them on the host through `catervas_git`, and says in 5.5 that a day is a UTC day, that a cost is priced when it is recorded, and that a model no price table knows is refused rather than costed at zero. It also says in 8.4 that a task id is never one a contract file in the repository already holds, and that a new contract is refused rather than written over a file already there, from the phase 2 landing review, which found a fresh clone filing its first request over a committed contract. It also names in 8.5 the two event kinds phase 3 step 04 emits that earlier revisions left unlisted: `transition.refused`, which records a move the governor refused with every reason, and `contract.evaluated`, which records each Definition of Ready or Done evaluation. It also says in 8.3 that no-sandbox mode leaves the user's credential files readable, and a push through a wrapped git possible, from any command, and that its warning says so. It also says in section 6 what a role's `role.yaml` holds, and that a role's permission tiers and session limits are not in it but are the governor's defaults, overridden per agent in the team file. It also names in 8.5 the two event kinds phase 3 step 05 emits that earlier revisions left unlisted: `criterion.recorded`, an exit criterion's result as the agent that ran it recorded it, and `note.written`, an assignee's or reviewer's note about the work. It also says in 5.6 that Catervas's coordination tools need only `read` and are governed by the rule each names, and in 5.6, 8.2, and 8.3 that git is four tools, one per tier-checked action, rather than one `catervas_git`. It also says in 8.2 the order of the sections of a session's system prompt, which of them are marked as untrusted, and how much of each is kept (ADR 0011). It also says in 8.2 what the daemon's `PreToolUse` hook denies, a path outside the session's worktree among it, and that the hook commands fail closed, in 5.6 that no MCP server but Catervas's own reaches a session in this release and what the hook cannot keep a search from reading, and in 8.5 what the three `tool.` events record, which phase 3 step 07 emits. It also says in 5.5 how much of the budget table this release enforces, which phase 3 step 11's orchestrator does: costs recorded, a session a budget ran out for aborted, and no session started for a task or a day with no room, while the table's blocks and escalations wait for phase 4. It also says in 5.4 how phase 3 step 12's orchestrator verifies a task: Catervas runs the mechanical criteria as the reviewer, the reviewer may neither record them nor commit, no agent records a `human` criterion, Catervas files a failed review's rejection with the review note, a task with a `human` criterion or of risk `high` waits for the human, and the reviewer's session has the read-only built-in tools alone. It also says in 5.4 that Catervas runs those criteria in a sandbox made afresh for them, what becomes of one it could not run, and that a refused request from a verification's own sessions also waits for the human, and in 5.2 that the governor escalates a task over such a criterion. It also renames the integration policy `local_merge` to `auto_merge`, which a new project now gets and which pushes to `origin`, says in 5.14 how each of the three policies integrates, that a failed integration escalates a task that stays `accepted`, and that one lock serialises integration across processes, and says in 5.15 what recovery records and removes (ADR 0012). It also names in 8.5 `agent.updated`, which phase 3 step 14 emits, and what `question.answered`, `human.accepted`, and `escalation.resolved` carry. It also says in 5.7 that a resolution moves the task to the status the user names with a message, that approving a contract is not a resolution, that the user moves a task with a reason, and how answers and messages reach the next session. It also says in 5.2 that the user's stop aborts the session, and in F1 how a pause blocks an agent's tasks and a return unblocks them. It also says in 5.1 and 5.4 that Catervas runs an epic's mechanical criteria for the human who reviews it (ADR 0013), and in 5.16 the triage model, the move from draft to refining, the judgement of a written contract, and how an epic is assigned, broken down, closed out, and accepted. It also says in section 3 which commands drive the team and which reach a process driving it, in 5.7 that the user answers from any terminal and what a driving process says waits on the user when it ends, in 5.13 what `catervas contract new` files and how it asks its questions, in F3 what `catervas task show` says of a task and that the human files a task under an epic, in 8.2 how `catervas run` and `catervas plan` start, name their credential, hold the run lock, take commands on the daemon, and stop on Ctrl-C (ADR 0014), and in 8.3 the warning's words. It also defines in F17 each of the five harness metrics exactly, and names `catervas metrics` among the reading commands of section 3. Revision 0.9 (2026-09-23) makes every dollar limit optional, with no default (ADR 0015), in sections 3, 4.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.5, 5.12, and 10: the daily budget, a sprint's budget, and the team's cap on a task's budget are each the user's to set, and one left out is no limit of that kind. A team file that never wrote `max_task_budget_usd` no longer has the five-dollar cap it used to get by default; a team that wants it writes `max_task_budget_usd: 5`. It also says in 5.5 that a usage report for a model no price table prices is recorded at no cost and marked `unpriced`, rather than refused as 0.8 said, and in sections 3 and 5.5 that `catervas doctor` and every start of `catervas run` name such a model. It also says, from phase 3 step 15's landing review, in 5.13 that `catervas contract new` starts driving before it files anything and takes a contract with `--lock` only once the Product Manager has written one, in 8.2 that Ctrl-C does not cut short a tick busy outside a session, in 8.3 that the no-sandbox warning names `daemon.json`, whose token lets an agent's command act as the user, and in 8.6 that the command line escapes the control characters agents write. It also corrects 5.5, from phase 3's final review, which said a session that exhausts a budget is aborted: token and dollar budgets are checked when a session reports its usage, which Claude Code does at the session's end, so a live session is bounded by its wall clock and its tool-call limit, and a budget crossed during a session stops the next one from starting. It also says in 5.6, from the same review, that `catervas_git_commit` reads each path it names as a path and refuses a directory. It also says in 5.4 and 5.6 that the Definition of Done refuses a diff that changes a protected path, even one inside the allowed paths. It also says in 5.4 that the fresh sandbox of Catervas's criterion runs mounts the task's worktree, gitignored build output and all. It also raises in 5.5 the default of a contract's `max_sessions` from 5 to 12, from phase 3's live testing, in which a small request's triage, refinement, plan, implementation, and review took the five sessions and left none for its acceptance: 12 is the most a task needs before its iteration limit escalates it (triage, refinement, plan, and acceptance, and an implementation and a review for each of `max_iterations` 3 passes and the one after them), so that `max_sessions` bounds only the loops the iteration limit cannot see, such as implement sessions that keep ending early. It also says in 5.4, from the same testing, in which a reviewer called `catervas_exec` and was told its session had no sandbox, that a `verify` session is not offered `catervas_exec` or the git writes. Revision 0.10 (2026-09-24) records what phase 4 step 01 built, which gives a team the Scrum Master, the Architect, and the Marketing Specialist. It says in 5.3 that the Scrum Master's judgment is recorded as `contract.judged` by `catervas_record_judgment` in a Scrum Master session of its own, that the governor asks for it only once every other rule of the Definition of Ready passes, that a contract written after its judgment needs a new one, and that a failed judgment goes back to the Product Manager as a failed Definition of Ready. It also specifies in 5.3, on the founder's decision of that day, the configurable judgment, a team policy `judgment` with `required`, `questions`, and `judge`, which the team editor builds (phase 5) and whose defaults are what this release does, and adds to section 10 that configuring the harness is user-friendly and foolproof, which F1 and F15 say the team editor meets. It also says in 5.1 and 5.4 that Catervas runs an epic's mechanical criteria for whichever reviewer it has, that the human accepts any epic's result only once those runs passed, not only one the human reviews, and how the Product Manager reviews an epic the Scrum Master broke down, asked again for any criterion its review left unanswered; and in 5.16 that an epic's reviewer, once assigned, is read from its row rather than from the team as it is now. It also gives in 5.6, 6.3, and 6.5 the Architect `git_local` and the Marketing Specialist `write_workspace` and `git_local`, because a task reaches `verifying` only with a commit on its branch. It also says in 5.16 and 6.2 that triage is the triager's session, the Scrum Master's when the team has one, on the cheaper model whatever the triager's own, and in 5.16 that an approved epic is assigned to the Scrum Master when the team has one, with the Product Manager as its reviewer, and that a rejected epic's close-out carries the rejection until the tasks that fix it are filed. It also drops the Architect's spikes from 6.3, since an Architect's task is a document and only the Developer writes application code (the founder, 2026-09-24), says in 8.2 which Catervas tools a session is registered with, the judgment session's `catervas_record_judgment` alone among them, and names `contract.judged` in 8.5. Revision 0.11 (2026-09-24) records what phase 4 step 02 built, on the founder's decision of that day that only the Software Developer changes code and that a task's branch says what it changes. It adds to 5.3 the rule that holds a task for any role but the Software Developer to the team's document paths, and says when an allowed path counts as inside them; to 5.12 the team rule `document_paths`, its default, and what an empty list means; and to section 3 that `catervas init` writes that default into the starter team. It names in 5.11 the contract's new `change` field, `feature` or `fix`, among the content, and says in 5.14 that a task works on `feature/CTV-<n>`, `fix/CTV-<n>`, or `docs/CTV-<n>` where it worked on `catervas/CTV-<n>`, with no migration of a branch made before, and that git refuses the worktree where the repository has a branch named `feature`, `fix`, or `docs`. It also says in 6.1 to 6.5 that only the Software Developer writes application code and that every other role's tasks are documents under `document_paths`. Revision 0.12 (2026-09-24) records what phase 4 step 03 built, on the founder's decision of that day that sprints are optional. It says in section 3 that the human starts a sprint, with a budget or none, that the assigner plans it from the ready backlog, and that it ends by itself once every task in it is accepted or cancelled or when the human ends it, and names `catervas sprint start`, `end`, and `show` and `catervas metrics --sprint` among the commands. It adds to 5.2 that while a sprint is open the governor assigns only its tasks, and those within what is left of its budget; to 5.3 that the remaining sprint budget a contract is held to is its own sprint's, and none for a contract in no sprint; to 5.5 that the sprint budget is read from the sprint, that spending it stops new assignments into the sprint and aborts no session, and that a cost stays with the sprint it was spent in; and to 5.11 that the governor writes `sprint` when a task is planned into a sprint and clears it when the task leaves one. It says in 6.2 that the Scrum Master plans the sprint, the Product Manager when the team has none; names `.catervas/sprints/` in 8.4 and `sprint.started`, `sprint.planned`, and `sprint.ended` in 8.5; and computes F17's metrics per sprint. From the step's landing review, it says in section 3 that no task is left in an ended sprint, and that `catervas doctor` reports a contract whose `sprint` disagrees with the log, recorded as a `drift.detected` of `sprint_mismatch`. Revision 0.13 (2026-09-24) records what phase 4 step 04 built. It changes 5.5's first row, so that a session that runs out of its tokens, its wall clock, or its tool calls leaves a note from Catervas for the next session rather than blocking its task, and gives `budget.exhausted` the consequence `end_session_with_note`, which reads `end_session_and_block_task` in logs recorded before it as the same consequence; rewrites 5.5's account of what this release enforces: the note, the escalation of a task whose dollars or sessions are spent, the daily budget unchanged, and the sprint budget as 0.12 left it; and adds to 5.5 how Catervas reads a model provider's usage limit from a session and the residual of that reading, that the session's agent then sleeps until the limit resets, and that a run waits for it. It says in 5.2 that Catervas asks for the `any -> escalated` row for a task whose budget is spent, and in 5.7 that such an escalation resolved without more room is raised again; names in 8.2 the session end `provider_limit`, what the stream parser reads to find it, and that a driving process waits for a sleeping agent and says so, and that a command of the user's ends the wait; names `agent.slept` in 8.5; and says in F1 that a sleeping agent stays active and is not paused. Revision 0.14 (2026-09-24) records what phase 4 step 05 built: the team channel. It says in 5.9 what a message is and who writes each of its six kinds; that an agent's reaction to a move comes from the session that made it, on that session's model, which replaces "ambient and reaction messages use a cheaper model"; that Catervas posts a system line, with no model, for a move by the governor or the human, for a rejection it files in a reviewer's name, for a spent daily or sprint budget, and for an agent asleep at its provider's limit; the ambient allowance, counted per sprint or, with no sprint open, per UTC day; that a mention gets its agent one short conversation session on Claude Sonnet 5 at low effort, and that replies are one deep; and how the channel summary is made. It says in 5.1 that chat reaches work only through `catervas_create_task` without a parent; names `catervas say` and `catervas channel` in section 3; says in 8.2 which tools a conversation session has and on which model it runs; describes `message.posted` in 8.5; says in F7 what the command line gives of the channel; and adds the channel's message counts to F17. It also corrects 8.4, which listed a channel projection this release does not build. Revision 0.15 (2026-09-24) records what phase 4 step 06 built: the ceremonies and escalation hygiene. It says in 5.9 that planning, standup, review, and retro are each one session of the Scrum Master, the Product Manager's when the team has none, on Claude Sonnet 5 at `medium` effort, posting at most three messages in the ceremony's thread; when each runs and what each is given; and that a ceremony's messages start no conversation. It says in 5.7 that the planning ceremony posts a digest of every open escalation and every budget spent since the previous planning, which replaces the digest "at the start of each sprint", and that an escalation left waiting past the team policy `escalation_age_hours` is recorded as `escalation.aged` and said in the channel as a system line, while something ticks, which replaces the ping through the app's notification channel until phase 6. It says in 5.8 that the retro ceremony appends to `team/retro.md` with `catervas_append_retro` and that the planning ceremony is given its end; in 6.2 that the Scrum Master runs the four ceremonies, the Product Manager when the team has none, and plans the sprint in the planning ceremony rather than a `plan` session; in section 3 that a sprint is planned in that ceremony; names `retro.appended` and `escalation.aged` in 8.5 and `session.started`'s `thread`; and says in F7 that the command line shows a ceremony's messages with their thread. Revision 0.16 (2026-09-24) records what phase 4 step 07 built: memory and decisions. It says in 5.8 that an agent writes its notebook only through `catervas_write_memory`, which replaces it whole and is recorded as `memory.written`, within the team policy `memory_cap_tokens` (500 to 16,000, default 8,000), a text's tokens being a quarter of its characters rounded up; that every session's prompt says how full the notebook is and, past 80 percent of the cap, asks the agent to prune it; that a decision is immutable once written, not once accepted, written only by the Architect and the Product Manager through `catervas_write_decision`, numbered, in a fixed format, never half-written or written over, recorded as `decision.written`, and read by every agent through `catervas_read_decisions`; and that the project scan is refreshed after an integration when what it reads has changed, which replaces "whenever the tree changes materially". The team policies are not listed in 5.12, so `memory_cap_tokens` is described in 5.8 alone. It says in 5.9 and 8.2 that ceremony and conversation sessions are also given `catervas_write_memory` and `catervas_read_decisions`; in 6.1 and 6.3 that the Product Manager and the Architect write decisions with `catervas_write_decision`; in 8.2 that the memory section opens with a line saying how full the notebook is and that the notebook is cut at its cap rather than at 32 KiB; and names the bodies of `memory.written` and `decision.written` in 8.5. Revision 0.17 (2026-09-24) records the fixes of phase 4's final review. It raises in 5.5 the default of a contract's `max_sessions` from 12 to 14, because a task's normal path now holds the Scrum Master's judgment and a spent session budget escalates whatever the status, so that under 12 a task that passed its last allowed review was escalated before its acceptance. It says in 5.9 that `catervas_plan_sprint` is refused outside the planning ceremony. It says in 5.3, 5.4, and 5.8 that files under `.catervas/` change only through Catervas's tools: the Definition of Ready refuses a contract whose allowed paths reach under `.catervas/`, and the Definition of Done a diff that changes a path there, whatever the role. It says in 5.12 that a path with a `..` segment anywhere, before or after a wildcard, is within no ceiling, and in 5.8 that the retro is appended by whoever runs the retro ceremony. Revision 0.18 (2026-09-24) records the founder's decisions of that day (ADR 0016): Catervas is for non-technical users, ships as a web app and a desktop app with native iOS and Android apps after launch, and has a brand the founder supplies before implementation goes further. It says in the opening paragraphs that Catervas is a web and desktop application with phone apps to follow, and that the pixel office is the desktop app's; adds to section 1 the goal that a non-technical user sets up and runs a team with no terminal, and phone apps at the first launch to the non-goals; and adds to section 2 the non-technical founder or creator as the primary persona. It says in section 3 that the web and desktop apps drive the team with the command line's commands, and in 4.1 that the first run is a wizard, one question per screen, in the browser or the desktop app. It adds to 5.4 what a human gate shows, a contract's approval, a `high` risk task's acceptance, and an epic's acceptance: a plain-language summary written by the agent that asks, the Product Manager in its contract and the assignee and the reviewer at the opening of their notes, the diff, and Catervas's check results, required from the web UI on (phase 6), and says so in 5.7 and 5.16 item 2; it changes no other rule of section 5. It says in 8.1 that `apps/web` is served by the local daemon on 127.0.0.1 and later by the hosted tier, that `apps/desktop` wraps it, and adds `apps/ios`, `apps/android`, and `packages/brand`; in 8.6 how the web UI gets its token and that the daemon refuses a foreign `Origin`; in section 10 WCAG 2.2 AA, a web app responsive from 360 px wide, and clients built from the brand's tokens; in section 11 that Milestone 1's test runs in the browser first with at least three non-technical users, that Milestone 2 launches the web and desktop apps, and a mobile milestone before premium; in section 12 the brand and how a phone reaches a running Catervas as questions 7 and 8; and a new section 14, the brand, which is not yet supplied. It also moves the forward pointers to the new phases in 5.3, 5.6, 5.7, 8.4, F7, and F12: the team editor to phase 6 step 04, MCP and the apps' notifications to phase 8, and the channel's view to the web app in phase 6. Revision 0.19 (2026-09-26) records the founder's choice of AWS for everything Catervas hosts (ADR 0017): it says in 8.1 that the public website on the project's domain runs on AWS from phase 8, and the hosted tier from phase 10, while the working web app stays served by the local daemon; and it adds `apps/site` and `infra` to the tree. Revision 0.20 (2026-09-27) ships Catervas on the web first (ADR 0018), in sections 1, 5.6, 5.7, 8.1, 11 and 12: the launch releases the web app alone; the desktop app becomes Milestone 3 and starts only after the web release has been tested with real users; mobile becomes Milestone 4 and premium Milestone 5. Revision 0.21 (the same day) adds a sixth role, the Finance Specialist (6.6; ADR 0019): optional, with private spreadsheet books in `.catervas/local/finance/`, the team's AI spending and Stripe read-only before the web launch, and receipts from a dedicated mailbox over IMAP after it; 1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, 5.6, 5.8, 5.14, 8.2, 8.4, 8.6, 9, F17 and 11 each take what a role with no branch and no worktree needs. Revision 0.22 (2026-09-28) adds role kits (6.7; ADR 0020), in 5.4, 5.6, 6.7, 8.1, 8.2, 9 and 11: each role's skills and connectors, pre-tagged and pinned, with allowances for connectors that spend the user's credits; the launch becomes phase 9 and the phases after it renumber. Revision 0.23 (2026-09-28) records the founder's decisions for the web UI (ADR 0021), in sections 3, 4.1, 5.4, 5.9, 8.1, 8.2, 8.5, and 8.6: `catervas serve` is the always-on driver, started in any folder, with `catervas pause` and `catervas resume` (`team.paused`, `team.resumed`); the first run picks or creates the project in a folder browser, checks the computer, and connects the user's AI account, whose credential is kept in the OS keychain; and the browser holds a session it traded a one-time code for, not the daemon's token, how the built web app is served and how a browser disconnects, in 8.1 and 8.6 (the page headers, `GET /session`, `POST /disconnect`, and the event stream's close on failed reads), and in 14 that the brand is recorded, its tokens have no elevation, and no two jobs share a colour. Revision 0.23 is extended (2026-09-29) by phase 6 step 05, with the founder's approval of the first-run order, computer, then AI account, then project: sections 4.1, 8.3 and 8.6 describe the setup screens as built, and the credential falls back to a private file where the computer has no keychain (ADR 0022). Revision 0.24 (2026-09-29) records the founder's decision of that day (ADR 0023), in sections 1, 5.6, 5.7, 6.6, 8.1, 8.2, 11, and 12: a user can connect an AI account from any provider and choose any agent engine, open-source ones included, with the same tools, skills, connectors and governor enforcement; this comes in a new phase 7, Engines and providers, after the web UI and before the ecosystem, so the phases from the ecosystem on renumber by one. Revision 0.25 (2026-09-29) records the runtime phase 6 step 07 built for the web UI's gates (ADR 0024), in sections 5.1, 5.2, 5.4, 5.5, 5.7, 5.11, and 8.5: the human's send-back, which waits for the review; more tries, granted on an `iterations` escalation; the summary a human gate leads with, required in a contract the human decides on and at the head of a completion or review note. Revision 0.25 is extended (2026-09-29) by step 07's landing review, in sections 5.1, 5.7 and 5.11: the criteria a human's send-back names are checked as a reviewer's are, more tries come only with a move back to `in_progress`, a task's result is listed as waiting on the human once its review has passed, and a save from the web UI never changes `locked` nor a frozen contract the team is working to. Revision 0.26 (2026-09-29) records the founder's rule of that day for who judges a plan, and what phase 6 step 06 built for team setup: the plan check is the team's own policy, built (5.3, 8.5); its judge is the Architect, else the Scrum Master, else the Product Manager (5.1, 5.3); the wizard's steps 4 to 8 and its Start the team are described (4.1); a change to what an agent may do waits for its next session by the session's own record (4.4); and every change shows its effects before it is saved (10). Revision 0.26 is extended (2026-09-29) by step 06's landing review, in F1: a retired agent is not one of the seven; in 5.6: the team's permission answers; in 4.1: where the user's words are kept, the marker's name, and only setup's start resumes the team; in 8.6: the AI account's row and Disconnect; in 10: refusals by code, the defaults a setting is put back to, and the daemon, not the page, works out each agent's model, tiers and who checks plans; in 4.4: a replacement is one change, and the last agent of a needed role is not paused or retired; and in 8.2: an agent's effort may be set without its model. Revision 0.27 (2026-09-30) says in 4.4 and 10 that the answers setup asks for are changed from Settings after setup, each change shown before it is saved, from phase 6 step 09's Task 4b. Revision 0.28 (2026-09-30) says in F3 what the web app's board, task page and sprint page show, and in F17 what its Costs page shows, from phase 6 step 09; its landing fixes keep the last sprint's figures on the Costs page once it ends, and leave a session's tool calls out of a task's history. Revision 0.29 (2026-09-30) says in F7 what the web app's channel shows, from phase 6 step 10. Revision 0.30 (2026-09-30) records the founder's ruling of that day on a key the model provider refuses, found by testing the web UI with a key that did not work: in 5.5 such a session is not its task's, and the team pauses at once; in 5.7 Today's one row for it; in 8.5 `credential_refused` and a `team.paused` by `catervas`; and in 8.6 the account row says so and connecting the account again resumes the team. It also records, from the same test, that the web app words a move's channel line in plain words (8.6). Revision 0.31 (2026-09-30) records the UI/UX Designer, from phase 6 step 11 (ADR 0026): in 1, 3, 4.1 and F1 the suggested team of six, which it joins; in 3, 5.3, 5.12, 5.14 and 6.1 to 6.5 that only the Developer and the UI/UX Designer change code; in 5.1 and 5.4 its reviewer; in 5.2 and 5.6 its plan gate and its tiers; a new 6.8 for the role, its explore, plan, approval and implement flow, and what the web app shows of it; in 8.2 the `explore` session and the Designer's model; in 8.5 the three `design_plan.*` events; in F17 the `explore` purpose; and in section 10 the first-day figure, now an estimate for the suggested six. From the step's landing review, it also says in 4.1 that a take-on that fails goes back to the wizard on the same port, and in 6.8 what a Designer's activity line says while it explores and while its plan waits, and that each Team card shows its agent's line; in 6.8 the plan card's words, as the approved mockup has them; in 4.1 that each setup row says its role's job; in 6.8 that an explore session's calls are held to the read tier; and in 10 that the first-day figure is "about" twenty-five dollars, an estimate, not a bound. It also says in 8.2 that the shipped defaults are the newest priced model of each family, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5, at the efforts they had. Catervas is a production-grade harness system for multi-agent systems, whose agents are its own team rather than other agent systems run under it. It is a web application, with a desktop app to follow once the web release has been tested and native iOS and Android apps after that (changed in 0.20), that lets a person, technical or not, assemble a small team of AI agents, each with a named role, a face, its own tools, and its own skills, and put that team to work on a software product. The team runs a lightweight Scrum process: a product manager writes task contracts with explicit exit criteria, a scrum master keeps the board moving, and specialists do the work. A deterministic governor enforces the rules the agents cannot be trusted to enforce on themselves. The web app shows the team's work on a board, where the user can open any task and any agent and talk to them one-on-one or in the team channel; the desktop app wraps the same interface and adds a pixel-art office where the user can watch the team and open any agent's desk (changed in 0.18).

The governance layer is the product. The pixel office is how people fall in love with it. The roles are the first content shipped on top of both.

## 1. Goals and non-goals

Goals for the initial launch:

1. A user can create a team of two to seven agents (at least one Product Manager, changed in 0.103; the team builder suggests six, changed in 0.31, and offers three ready-made teams, added in 0.103), name them, pick avatars, and assign each one of seven launch roles: Product Manager, Scrum Master, Architect, Software Developer, UI/UX Designer (added in 0.31), Marketing Specialist, and Finance Specialist, which the team builder offers but does not suggest (added in 0.21; on the Team page from 0.54, and in setup, under "More roles", from 0.70); the Procurement Specialist is offered the same way, in both places (6.10; added in 0.49, built in 0.70), and the DevOps Engineer when its step lands (6.9; added in 0.32). A team needs an active Product Manager and no Software Developer, whether or not it builds software (ADR 0040, ADR 0055; changed in 0.103, when this came forward from phase 17).
2. A user can point the team at an existing git repository or start a new project from a one-paragraph brief. From phase 17, a project is a business workspace, a folder of its own on the user's computer, which a software business's repository already is (ADR 0040; changed in 0.50).
3. Work flows through a task lifecycle that the user can inspect at every step, where every task has a written contract with exit criteria before anyone starts on it, and where nobody accepts their own work.
4. Every agent action is logged to an append-only event stream, and every expense (tokens, wall clock, tool calls) is attributable to a task and an agent.
5. The user can talk to any agent directly and can read and join the team's group channel, where the agents talk to each other in plain, conversational language.
6. Each agent can be given its own MCP servers and its own skills, independent of the others.
7. The core is open source and runnable with the user's own API key. A hosted premium tier exists in the design but is not required for the first release.
8. A non-technical user can set up and run a team with no terminal, in the web app (changed in 0.20): the first run is a wizard that asks one question per screen (4.1), and every human gate explains itself in plain language, with the diff there for whoever reads code (5.4) (added in 0.18).

Non-goals for the initial launch:

- The desktop app and the phone apps. The first launch ships the web app alone. The desktop app follows once the web release has been tested with real users, and native iOS and Android apps follow the desktop app (section 11; added in 0.18, changed in 0.20).
- Non-software businesses in the first launch (changed in 0.50). Catervas is for every business, software or not (ADR 0040, the founder's decision of 2026-10-05), but the first launch is built and measured around shipping software; business workspaces, where a team with no repository and no Software Developer runs any business, are phase 17, after the launch, though a team with no Software Developer already runs (ADR 0055; changed in 0.103), with no workspace without a repository yet, and cloud-hosted workspaces for paying customers are phase 20. The Procurement Specialist (6.10) ships at the launch and already serves any business.
- Teams larger than seven. The coordination cost grows faster than the output. Seven is a hard cap in the first release.
- Multi-user collaboration on one team. One human, several teams (changed in 0.144; ADR 0059): each team on its own project, all driven by the one `catervas serve` (4.1, 8.1). Team templates are reuse, not several live teams: a saved team is copied into a project's team, and the project's team is what runs (3, 4.4; added in 0.35).
- Fully autonomous operation with no human at all. The harness assumes a human is reachable for escalations, even if hours pass before they answer.
- A model-agnostic runtime before the web UI's Milestone 1 test, which runs on Claude alone (changed in 0.24, from "on day one"). See section 8.2 for the provider decision. Other providers and agent engines come in phase 13, after the role kits, which are built on Claude first, Catervas Cloud, and the kit check and the milestone runs, and before the rest of the ecosystem and the launch (renumbered by ADR 0029, ADR 0048, ADR 0049, ADR 0051 and ADR 0057), with the same tools, skills, connectors and governor enforcement on every engine (8.2; added in 0.24, ADR 0023).

## 2. Who it is for

Three people matter for the first release, and the first of them most (changed in 0.18).

The non-technical founder or creator (added in 0.18). Someone with a product in mind who can say what they want but cannot read code. Catervas is built for them first. They must be able to set up a team, follow its contracts, and accept what still needs them through plain-language summaries alone, with the diff there for whoever can read it (5.4), and never be asked for a glob, a regular expression, or a file format unless they open a setting's advanced view (section 10).

The solo builder. Someone with an idea and a repository, technical enough to read a diff, who wants a product to keep moving while they are at their day job. They are price sensitive and will run on their own key. They care that the agents do not wreck the repository while unsupervised.

The small-team lead. A founder or engineering lead with a two-to-five person company who wants an always-on "extra squad" that takes the backlog grooming, the boring implementation tickets, and the release notes. They will pay for hosted execution if it saves them an afternoon a week and if the audit trail is good enough to trust.

The small-business owner (added in 0.50; ADR 0040). Someone who runs a business that is not software, flipping cars, reselling goods online, renting cars, and wants a team that researches, buys through purchase orders they approve, keeps the books and markets the business. Served from phase 17; until then, the Procurement Specialist works for them inside a software team's workspace.

A third persona, the enterprise platform team, is deliberately deferred. Their asks (SSO, SOC 2, private model endpoints) are real but would bend the first release out of shape.

## 3. Core concepts

**Team.** A named group of two to seven agents attached to exactly one project at a time. A team has a shared channel, a one-to-one chat between the user and each agent (4.3; added in 0.34), a board, optional spending limits, and a memory (ADR 0015).

**Team template (added in 0.35).** A team the user saved to start other projects from, kept on this computer outside every project (8.4) and held to `docs/schemas/team-template.schema.json`. It has a name of 1 to 60 characters with no space at either end, when it was saved, two to seven agents, and the four answers setup asks. Each agent keeps its id, name, role, persona, picture and model with its effort; the answers are what agents may do (`run_commands` and `push`), how finished work is added, which is always a pull request, and the daily spending limit, none when there is none (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: the plan check is gone, and a template saved before that carries one, which is read and ignored). A template saved before 0.116 may hold a policy key that the team no longer has; it is read and ignored (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062). It leaves out everything that belongs to one project: the team's rules, the criterion library, how to open the app, the integration branch, the team's name, and each agent's status, grants, revokes, preauthorized tools and connectors; a retired agent is not saved, a paused one is, and an uploaded picture is left out, the agent taking its role's shipped picture where the template is used, since nothing copies a picture between projects yet. A template is held to the team's own rules (F1): a team made of its agents, all active, must be one `validate_team` accepts, and a hand-edited file that is not gets the team's sentences at the template's own paths. Its file is named by its slug: the name's ASCII letters and digits lower-cased, every run of anything else one `-`, trimmed, at most 64 characters; a name that leaves nothing is refused. A template is never a second live team: using one changes the project's one team (4.4). Catervas ships three ready-made teams as built-in templates (added in 0.103; ADR 0055): Software product, a Product Manager, an Architect, a Software Developer and a Marketing Specialist; Online store, a Product Manager, a Procurement Specialist, a Finance Specialist and a Marketing Specialist; and Financial analysis, a Product Manager and three Finance Specialists, whose desks are the portfolio, its risks and its opportunities. The three Finance Specialists share one books folder and work one task at a time, told apart by their desk personas, which the Product Manager reads when it gives out a task. The built-in teams are embedded in the binary, listed as `builtin`, and have reserved names: a saved team cannot take one (`template_builtin`, 4.4). They are there without a state folder, and are never renamed or deleted.

**Agent.** A persistent identity: name, avatar, role, persona, model configuration, tool permissions, MCP servers, skills, and a private memory. An agent is not a running process. When work is assigned, the runtime starts a session for that agent, seeded with its identity and the task. Sessions end; the agent persists.

**Role.** A template that an agent is instantiated from. A role defines a mandate (what this agent is for), the artifacts it produces, the gates it owns, its default tools, and, importantly, what it is forbidden from doing. Roles are shipped as files and are editable. Two roles change code, the Software Developer and the UI/UX Designer; every other role's work is documents (6; added in 0.31).

**Claude Code history (added in 0.139; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 02).** What `catervas discover` reads of the owner's Claude Code use on this computer: the transcripts under `projects/` in `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, else `~/.claude`, and nothing else. Running the command is the owner's consent, and it says so in its first line; nothing leaves the computer. Only metadata is kept: a session's folder, branch, Claude Code version, how it started, a title of at most 200 characters, its first and last time, and the tokens of its replies by model, never a conversation's text. A session is placed in a project in this order: home and the temporary folders (`/`, `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `TMPDIR`) are never a project, and a git root that holds one is ignored as if there were no git; else the repository's main worktree, so every worktree, Claude Code's own among them, folds into its repository; else the longest known root that contains the folder (only roots with git for a folder that still exists, any known root for a deleted worktree); else a deleted folder is listed as no longer on this computer; else a folder with no git folds into the outermost session folder with no git that contains it. A session is Catervas's own, counted as its team's agent activity and never as a project, when its folder is under `.catervas/local/` or its project's log names its id; any other is the owner's. A repository is explored, not the owner's, when it has a commit, git knows the owner's email, and no commit on any ref was authored by it; otherwise it is the owner's. `catervas discover --forget` deletes the index and reads nothing. Out of this step: claude.ai's export, every screen, a daily rescan and prices.

Jobs (added in 0.140; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 03). `catervas discover` also finds the owner's recurring jobs and prints each under its project, or under "this computer". Kinds: GitHub Actions, Vercel, Kubernetes, Render and Terraform, read from the schedules committed in the owner's repositories (files git tracks: `.github/workflows/*.yml|yaml`, `vercel.json`, `render.yaml`, `*.tf` and any other YAML file that holds `CronJob`; a Terraform file is scanned for literal `schedule_expression` values, not parsed); crontab, systemd timers (user and system, those a package installed under `/usr/lib` or `/lib` skipped), launchd agents and Windows Task Scheduler under WSL, read from the schedulers' own answers, only Task Scheduler tasks tied to a project kept; and session crons (`CronCreate` calls, expiring seven days after the call, whether the session still runs unknown), saved session crons (`.claude/scheduled_tasks.json`, expiring seven days after creation when recurring and not permanent) and Claude Code's background jobs (`~/.claude/jobs/<id>/state.json`, undocumented, read fail-soft). A job's key is `(origin, file, name)`. A job is tied to the deepest present project root that contains any path it names, else it is under "this computer"; explored repositories are not scanned for schedules, and a worktree outside its repository's folder ties to nothing. A job keeps its schedules as written, its name and its project; transcript tool calls are kept as id and name only.

**Services used through Claude (added in 0.142; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 03b).** `catervas discover` also says which services the owner reaches through Claude's connectors. They are found in Claude Code's MCP settings (the user's, each project's, a found project's `.mcp.json` minus the servers the user turned off, enabled plugins with a user-scope install), the connectors claude.ai has connected as Claude Code knows them, Claude Desktop's settings and extensions, and above all the tool calls of transcripts (`mcp__<server>__<tool>`). A catalog in `catervas-core` (a table the compiler checks, matched by host, then name, then program) sorts a service into bookkeeping, spreadsheets, payments, selling, marketing, code or other (an unknown server, shown by its name). A service is one record however many sources name it (keyed by its catalog id, else by its normalised name and host) and is attached to every project whose sessions called it, with its calls and when last used; the owner's sessions count and Catervas's agents' do not. Catervas's own servers, Claude Code's session, remote-control and IDE servers, the Claude app's browser, preview, device and Chrome surfaces and Claude Docs are not services. Sessions at home or in a temporary folder form a project named "<Work> (<service>)" when at least three of a session's calls are of one kind of work (bookkeeping and spreadsheets are bookkeeping; payments; selling; marketing; code and other form nothing) and those are more than half of its calls to services; a Microsoft 365 call is spreadsheets work only when its tool's name contains excel, workbook, worksheet or sheet. A present folder with no git whose sessions called a file tool on a spreadsheet (`.xlsx`, `.xls`, `.csv`) at least three times is marked bookkeeping. The command ends with one line of every service, and `--json` gains each project's `work` and `services`, the top-level `services` and `desktop`.

**claude.ai's export and one record across sources (added in 0.143; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 04).** `catervas discover --claude-export <file>` reads the data export the owner downloaded from claude.ai, the `.zip` it emails, on this computer; nothing leaves it. Only metadata is kept: each conversation's id, title (at most 200 characters), start and last change and its number of messages, each Project's id, name, description (at most 2000 characters) and the file names of its documents, and the account's id; never a message, a document's content, or a person's name or email. A later export updates an earlier one by id, and an item is marked "not in the latest export" only when its account has an export with later content that lacks it, whatever order the exports were imported in; nothing is deleted except by `catervas discover --forget`. The report prints the conversations per month over the twelve months ending with the newest start, the undated ones and the Projects. Across sources each thing is kept once: a session is keyed by its id and a reply by its message id; a session copied from another computer (teleported) keeps its replies with new ids, so two sessions are linked only when they share at least three replies, told by their time to the second, model and token counts and never by their text, and the shared ones cover every reply of one of them from its start; a linked pair in which neither is in another link counts once (the later is the copy, and the project says it was teleported), any other linked pair is reported as "may be copies" and both are counted, their shared replies once; a repository is keyed by its normalised remote (host and path in lower case, without a user, a password, a port or a final `.git`, so SSH and HTTPS forms are one and a token in a remote is never kept), a folder by its real path. A project says where it was found, derived each time and never stored: `local` when a scan found it, `teleported`, `export` for a claude.ai item and `by_hand`. `catervas discover --add-project <name>` with `--folder <path>` or `--repo <address>` adds a project by hand: it joins the found project with the longest root that holds its folder, else the first with its repository, and then shows under the owner's name; one that matches none is listed as added by hand. A claude.ai Project and a found project are never merged.

**Finding projects from the web app (added in 0.146; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 06).** What `catervas discover` finds is asked for from the browser too, by the hub (4.4): the same scan, the same index, and nothing in any team's log. The owner chooses for each found project Team, Watch or Ignore, and Catervas suggests one: a folder or repository of the owner's own, and a project formed from connector work, is suggested Team when it was last worked in within 30 days and Watch when older; a repository the owner is only looking at is suggested Ignore; a claude.ai Project, and a job on this computer with no project, Watch; a project added by hand, Team; a folder that is gone is suggested nothing and is only located. The owner's choice is kept by the project's key (its normalised repository address, else its real path, the connector project's name or the claude.ai uuid) and replaces the suggestion; it is never acted on in this step, since making a team of a project is a later one's. "These are different" keeps two folders of one repository as two projects, and Locate says where a gone folder is now.

**Which projects work together (added in 0.149; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 06b).** Two found projects are one team only when the owner says Yes to a proof that they work together, and a proof is checked again whenever it is shown and whenever a team is made from it. The proof is one of eight kinds, the first found in the owner's Claude Code sessions (added in 0.154; ADR 0085) and the others in the projects' committed files: at least two sessions each changed a file under both projects' folders (a `Write`, `Edit` or `MultiEdit` call; reading does not count, a resumed session counts once, and a session placed with Catervas's agents never counts), and the sentence is "You worked on a and b together in N sessions."; one project uses the other's code through a local path (a `package.json` dependency `file:` or `link:`, a Cargo `path` dependency or workspace member, a `go.mod` `replace`) that resolves into the other's folder; includes it as a submodule whose address is the other's remote; depends on a package the other's own manifest names and whose `repository` is the other's remote; deploys it (a compose `build` or `context` path into it, a Terraform module whose source is its remote, or a Kubernetes or compose `image` that its workflows publish); runs a workflow on it (`actions/checkout` of its `owner/name`, or a `repository_dispatch` or `workflow_dispatch` call naming it); names the domain it deploys to (its `CNAME`, `vercel.json` `alias`, `netlify.toml` custom domain or `package.json` `homepage` host, with the whole name matched, and a host such as github.com never counting); or a claude.ai Project's description or file name holds its address. These are never a proof: two projects depending on the same public package that neither owns, the same remote owner, the same days, similar names, a session that read both, and the same service used through Claude. Pairs with only those are hints: the same owner, at least three shared days of sessions within 30 days, a shared word of four letters in the names, and exactly one session that changed a file under both folders (two or more are a proof). A hint is listed under "Maybe related", counts as separate unless the owner opens it and says otherwise, and joins nothing. A folder that is not a git repository has no proof and only hints. A fixture corpus of invented projects holds nine related pairs, one for each kind and a second `deploys`, and twelve unrelated pairs that look related (a session that wrote in both, and sessions that read both and wrote in one, among them), and a test holds that every related pair gives its proof and no unrelated pair gives any.

**Project.** A git repository plus a `.catervas/` directory inside it that holds the backlog, contracts, decisions, and memories as plain files. Everything the team knows about the project lives in the repository, so it can be diffed, reviewed, and version controlled like any other code. A project also holds `docs/catervas/` (added in 0.91; 5.17), where each role keeps the documents it owns.

**Project folder (added in 0.110; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 01).** A project is one repository, as above, or a project folder: a git repository of its own that Catervas makes, with no remote and never pushed, which holds `.catervas/` and `docs/catervas/` and whose `.catervas/repos.yaml` lists two to sixteen member repositories, each a git repository elsewhere on the computer that stays its own repository on GitHub. No member is primary. Having a `repos.yaml` is what makes a folder a project folder; a one-repo project has none and is unchanged. This revision makes the folder and its members; the tasks that work in a member, the documents' `repos/<name>/` folders and the rest of the design come in the steps that follow it. Its criterion library is its members' (added in 0.112): each member is scanned on its own and the folder itself never is (4.1, 5.13).

`catervas init` makes a repository a project: it writes `.catervas/`, the event log under `.catervas/local/`, `project.md` holding the scan's read-back, and a criterion library seeded from what the scan found. When there is no team file it writes a starter team of two agents — a Product Manager and a Software Developer, the software default (changed in 0.103; a team needs only the Product Manager, F1) — named after their roles for the user to rename in the team editor, on the models 8.2 ships, with no dollar limit (5.5), with one unfinished task per agent (`wip_limit_per_agent: 1`), writing none of the older policy keys that 8.4 lists (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062), and the rest of the policy as sections 5.2, 5.5 and 5.14 give it, and with the team rules empty but for the three default document paths of 5.12, which it writes out so the user sees them (changed in 0.11). A second `catervas init` is a rescan: it keeps the team and the criteria a person wrote and replaces the ones the last scan found, and it refuses rather than writing past a team file or a criterion library that is there and cannot be read. The team and the project are identified in every event by the slug of the team's name and of the repository's own directory name, both fixed by the first `catervas init` and read from the log thereafter (added in 0.7); each slug is at most 64 characters, as a team's agent id is, by the rule a template's slug follows (changed in 0.35), and a project already identified keeps its slug from the log. Everything the project knows is then readable from the command line: `catervas board` shows the lifecycle, `catervas task show` one contract with its events, `catervas log` the event log with filters and a JSON-lines export (F11), `catervas rules show` and `catervas criteria list` the two team files a person hand-edits (F15, F16), `catervas metrics` the harness metrics of F17 (added in 0.8), and `catervas doctor` every way the files and the log disagree — each recorded as a `drift.detected` event — plus a team rule that does not compile, a setting Catervas does not know, a criterion whose verification matches no branch of its `oneOf`, and an active agent's model that no price table prices (5.5). `catervas doctor` exits 1 when it found something (added in 0.7). In a project folder (a `.catervas/repos.yaml` is there) `catervas init` writes the same files but scans the members instead of the folder, as 5.13 says, and records a `team.updated` when it wrote the team, then one `project.scanned` and one `criteria.updated` by the human (added in 0.112).

The team is driven from the command line (added in 0.8). `catervas run` starts the daemon and the orchestrator and works the board until nothing on it needs doing, the user stops it, or Ctrl-C (since 0.137, ADR 0081, an idle tick with no session to start says what waits on the owner instead of "nothing on the board needs doing": "CTV-21 waits for you to accept it" for each task held by the owner's answer to a `human` criterion, and "CTV-23 waits for CTV-21" for each ready task held only by an unaccepted dependency, the lines joined with "; "; a spent day or a sleeping agent still comes first; Today's waiting list already shows the first as an acceptance row); `catervas plan` does the same with the planning rules alone, triaging, contracting, breaking down, and assigning without starting any work, a breakdown with an Architect stopping at the Architect's plan task, which only a run writes (8.2; changed in 0.98). The user's own commands are `catervas approve <task>` (a contract awaiting approval, which only an older log holds since 0.115; ADR 0061), `catervas accept <task> [--message <text>]` (a result that waits for the user), `catervas answer <question> <answer>`, `catervas integrate <task>` (or `catervas integrate folder-<n>`, a folder change, 5.14; added in 0.94), `catervas resolve <task> <status> [--extra-tries <n> | --extra-room] <message>` (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062: `--extra-tries` and `--extra-room` give a task that used its tries or its room more of them, 5.7), `catervas cancel <task> <reason>`, `catervas stop` (the run, after its running sessions; changed in 0.118; ADR 0064) and `catervas stop <session or task>` (one session, now), with `catervas triage` and `catervas contract lock` and `unlock`. Each works from any terminal: while a process drives the project the command is sent to it, and otherwise it is handled where it was typed (ADR 0014). `catervas stop` needs a driving process. `catervas pause` stops the team starting sessions, letting the running ones finish, until `catervas resume`; the pause is kept in the log, so it holds across a restart (added in 0.23). While the team is paused no rule runs but the chat rule (5.9), which still answers the user's one-to-one chats unless the team is paused because the provider refused the key (5.5; changed in 0.34): no other session starts, no criterion is run, nothing integrates by itself, a finished delivery does not close, and no aged escalation is posted. The human's own commands are all still handled, `catervas integrate` among them, since the human is not the team, and `catervas run` on a paused team ticks once, says the team is paused, and exits as it does on an idle board (added in 0.23). `catervas serve` drives the team as `catervas run` does but never exits when the board is idle, waiting instead for something to do; it can be started in any folder, and opens the project there, else the last project it served, else the first-run wizard (added in 0.23). A tick that fails because this computer's sandbox is not ready, Docker not answering or the sandbox image missing, does not end `catervas serve`: it prints the error, goes back to the wizard on the same port, waiting on the project ("the sandbox is not ready: prepare it in the browser"), and the wizard's computer check, once the sandbox image is ready, takes the project on again and answers `taking_on: true`, on which the page opens the project as it does after `account.connect` (added in 0.153). On WSL the link opens in Windows' browser (`cmd.exe /c start`), Linux there having none of its own (added in 0.153). The web and desktop apps (8.1) drive the team through the same daemon and give the user the same commands, so a user who never opens a terminal has everything the command line has: in the web app, once `catervas serve` is started, and in the desktop app with nothing started at all. There the first run, `catervas init` among it, is the apps' wizard (4.1; added in 0.18).

**Task.** The unit of work. A task is not ready until it has a contract. A task belongs to an epic, or stands alone when it came from a small request.

**Epic.** The translation of one large request from the user into a contract, written by the Product Manager after asking the user its questions, and, since 0.115 (ADR 0061), not approved by the user before anyone plans it: the Architect then writes its implementation plan, in lanes no wider than the team's builders, and the Product Manager writes its tasks from the plan (5.16; changed in 0.98). A small request becomes a single task instead; the Scrum Master or the Product Manager decides which (5.16; added in 0.3).

**Contract.** A structured document attached to an epic or a task: intent, scope, requirements, exit criteria with a verification method for each, constraints, budget, and a named reviewer who is not the assignee. The schema is in `docs/schemas/task-contract.schema.json`; the `kind` field says which of the two it is. Every exit criterion's `id` names one criterion, and every requirement's `id` names one requirement: a recorded result, a note, and an event all refer to a criterion by its id, and a criterion names the requirements it satisfies by theirs, so a contract that gives one id to two of either is refused when it is read, which JSON Schema cannot express and the validator therefore does. No array in a contract holds more than a hundred entries, so that a refusal naming what is wrong stays readable and an untrusted contract cannot make the governor walk a list without end (added in 0.3). A contract may also carry `plan`, the implementation plan the task writes or is built from, a path of the shape `docs/catervas/architecture/plans/<epic-id>` followed by the team's extension (`.html` or `.md`), and `lane`, an integer from 1 to 16 saying which lane of its epic's plan a task belongs to: the tasks one builder does in order, tasks in different lanes being built side by side. Both are content, written by the Product Manager while refining and frozen from `ready` (5.11), and a lane is read only on a task with a parent (added in 0.98; 5.3, 5.16; ADR 0051). In a project folder (added in 0.111; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 02) a task's contract also carries `repo`, the name of the member repository the task changes, a name `repos.yaml` gives (the shape of a member's name, 3 and 8.4); the contract's `allowed_paths`, and the paths of its `command` and `artifact` criteria, are relative to the task's repository, the member `repo` names, else the project root. `repo` is content, written by the Product Manager while refining and frozen from `ready` as `plan` and `lane` are, and fixed once set (5.11).

**Delivery (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062).** The unit the team's ceremonies run over, (ADR 0062, which supersedes ADR 0028): the work accepted since the previous delivery. The governor closes one, recorded as `delivery.closed` (8.5), the first time since the previous one that an epic was accepted, `TASKS_PER_DELIVERY` (5, a constant in `catervas-core` and not a setting) tasks with no parent were accepted, or the team has no work left (something was accepted, and no task is `ready`, `assigned`, `in_progress`, `verifying` or `rejected`). A changelog task, which the governor files at the close (6.1), never counts towards a delivery. Nothing is held for one and nothing is started or planned by the user: a ready task is assigned to the first free agent of its role as soon as that agent is under its work limit (5.2), and a team that has not closed one has just no review yet. Each closed delivery gets once a review, the Product Manager's and the Architect's refreshes of their documents, and a retro (5.9), run by the Scrum Master, or by the Product Manager when the team has no active one; the review is told the digest of the escalations still open (5.7). A new delivery closes only once the previous one's retro is held, unless the team has no one to run it, and what is accepted meanwhile counts towards the next. A project made before 0.116 keeps working: the older keys and events that 8.4 and 8.5 list are read and ignored, and a task an older version held back is assigned like any other ready task.



**Goal (added in 0.130; ADR 0075).** The one aim the owner gives the team, such as "Reach 10 paying customers" or "Create a mobile application and reach 10k downloads": the owner's words, optionally a number to reach with what it counts, and, for a goal with a number, how it is counted (read from a service an active agent has connected, or told by the owner). One goal stands at a time. While it does, the team plans its next steps whenever the board is quiet and keeps working within the daily budget, until the owner marks it reached or ends it; no reading marks it reached (5.18).

**Governor.** Deterministic code, not an agent, that sits between every agent and every tool. It checks permissions, budgets, iteration limits, and path allowlists, and it is the only component that can move a task between certain states. Agents propose; the governor disposes.

**Channel.** The team's group chat. Agents post there in a human register when events happen and when they want to coordinate. A message in the channel is never an instruction to do work. Work comes only from tasks. On the command line (added in 0.14), `catervas say <text>` posts the human's message, sent to a process driving the project as the user's other commands are, and says "posted in the channel"; `catervas channel [--last <n>]` prints the channel from the log, oldest first, the last 50 messages unless `--last` says otherwise, one line each as `<time> <author> [<thread>] <text>` with the thread only when there is one, every message escaped as agent-written text is (8.6), and `--json` gives one object per message: its fields and its `seq`, `recorded_at`, and `task_id`.

**Chat (added in 0.34).** The user's private conversation with one agent (4.3), one per agent, kept in the log apart from the channel and never read by another agent (5.9). On the command line, `catervas chat <agent> <text>` sends the user's message, as the user's other commands are sent, and says "sent to <Name>"; an agent not on the team is not found, and a retired agent's chat is refused, being read-only. `catervas chat <agent>` prints the chat from the log, oldest first, one block per message, blocks apart by a blank line: `<time> <author>`, the text with its line breaks, and a proposed request's title and text after "Proposed request:", every message escaped as agent-written text is (8.6); `--json` gives one object per message, its fields and its `seq` and `recorded_at`.

**Skill.** A folder containing a `SKILL.md` and supporting files, following the Agent Skills format, that teaches an agent a procedure. Skills can be assigned to one agent, to a role, or to the whole team.

**MCP connection.** A configured Model Context Protocol server (stdio or remote) that gives an agent tools. Connections are configured per agent, with credentials stored in the operating system keychain locally or in a vault when hosted.

**Catervafication (added in 0.101; ADR 0051; phase 8 step 07).** The first work of a project, in which the team documents it before building anything. It is an epic, "Catervafy the repository" for an existing repository and "Catervafy the new project" for a new one, with one docs task for each role that has a folder, an active agent and a reviewer, each written from a fixed template and held to the role's folder (5.17). It is filed like any epic and opens nothing of its own (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062). For an existing repository the team also hunts for bugs and starts the marketing plan beside the documentation (changed in 0.117; ADR 0063; 5.16). The Scrum Master takes no task, since it holds no writing tier; it writes the team's cadence at the retro of the delivery that documented the project (5.9).

## 4. User journeys

### 4.1 First run

The user opens Catervas, in the browser or in the desktop app, and a wizard starts. It asks one question per screen, each with a safe default and a one-line explanation in plain language (section 10), and nothing in it needs a terminal (changed in 0.18). In the desktop app it opens on an empty pixel office with a door. The wizard's order is the computer, the AI account, the project, and then the rest (changed in 0.23; approved by the founder 2026-09-29): the first two need no project, and taking a project on starts the team's driver, which needs Claude Code signed in (changed in 0.141; ADR 0084). In the browser, Catervas is started with `catervas serve`, which opens the page itself (added in 0.23). Run outside a project, `catervas serve` serves setup and reopens the last project it served, when that is still a project (added in 0.23). A project found while Claude Code is not signed in, under the Claude engine, opens on the account screen with the project already chosen (added in 0.23); a working sign-in or check there takes that project on at once, and the page follows Catervas to it (added in 0.23; changed in 0.141).

First, Catervas checks the computer: the Claude Code program at its oldest supported version, git, and Docker, and whether the sandbox image is built (for this Catervas, its tag carrying the Dockerfile's digest, 8.3; changed in 0.110), saying in plain words how to fix what is missing; it builds the sandbox image when Docker is ready and the image is not (added in 0.23; changed in 0.124: the build runs in the background, `computer.check` reads `preparing` with the build's step count, `done` of `of`, while it runs, and the page asks again each second and shows Ready by itself when it ends; ADR 0070), and offers no-sandbox mode with its warning (8.3) when Docker is missing. When the team has a UI/UX Designer, which setup's suggested six always do, the check has a row "Browser for the UI/UX Designer", ready when the pinned Playwright image (8.3) is on the computer and missing otherwise, with a button that fetches it (added in 0.33). Then the user connects their AI account, which Claude Code holds, so that Catervas never sees the key (changed in 0.141; ADR 0084, which supersedes ADR 0022). The screen checks the sign-in first with `claude auth status`: signed in already, it says so, runs the connection check with no press, and shows "It works." with Continue, or, when the check fails, why ("Your key was refused.", "Your plan's limit is reached for now.", or "It didn't work: <detail>") with the sign-in choices and "Check again"; not signed in, it offers "Sign in with Claude (Pro or Max)" and "Sign in with an Anthropic Console account". The one pressed starts `claude auth login` with no terminal and opens the page it names in a new tab, and the screen asks for the code that page shows, "Your sign-in code", which goes to Claude Code and is kept, logged and echoed nowhere; "Open the page again" and, for a user who prefers the Terminal, `claude auth login` then "Check again" are beside it. A sign-in that passes the check goes on to the project step. Where a key is set in the user's own environment, the screen names the variable and checks the connection (8.6).

Then the first question about the work: existing project or new one? For an existing project they pick a folder, in the browser from a folder browser limited to their home directory (added in 0.23); Catervas checks it is the root of a git repository and not the home folder itself, where Catervas's own settings folder would be part of the project (added in 0.38 after review), that no other Catervas is running it, and that the account is connected, scans the tree, and produces a short read-back ("TypeScript monorepo, pnpm, 3 packages, tests in vitest, last commit 4 days ago") (a project on cargo or go names no other test runner, since that toolchain runs its tests, whatever runner a web app inside it configures; changed in 0.37). For a new project they write a paragraph and pick where its folder goes; Catervas makes it, runs `git init` and makes a first commit, and files the paragraph as the project's first request (added in 0.23). It also records `project.started { name, description }` for the project, before the request is filed (added in 0.99; ADR 0051): `name` is the folder's name and `description` the paragraph, trimmed, and a project is new when its log holds the event. `project.scanned` stays the scan's, new project or not; a repository taken on records no `project.started`. The first request is still filed, and waits in `refining` until the product plan's task is accepted (5.3; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061), when it is refined against the spec. Catervas takes the project on in the same process, on the same port, without a restart, and the page carries on (added in 0.23). A take-on that fails goes back to the wizard, which says why, on that same port: `catervas serve` holds its port from start to end, so nothing else can take it between the wizard and the team, and a page that connects in between waits rather than being refused (added in 0.31; changed in 0.37). Until setup ends the team is kept paused, marked by `.catervas/local/setup-pending` (added in 0.23).

**Documents attached to a new project (added in 0.131; ADR 0076; standalone plan `attached-documents`).** Under the paragraph the project screen has "Attach a document" (4.2). A picked file asks "What is it about?" and then waits as a chip with its name, which "Take <name> off this message" removes; nothing is sent while the wizard has no team, because `document.attach` (5.17) needs a Product Manager or an Architect to keep the document. The files are kept in the page's memory, not on disk, so reloading the page forgets them. The finish screen's start button sends them one at a time, in the order they were picked, with `document.attach`, and then starts the team as before; a file the daemon refuses is dropped, its refusal said above the button (5.17 gives the words), and the start goes on. The Product Manager's interview (4.3) then lists them.

**A project with no lockfile (added in 0.122; ADR 0069).** The scan names a toolchain by its lockfile. A tracked `package.json` with no lockfile is an npm project, so its `lint` and `test` scripts become the checks `npm run lint` and `npm run test` and its start script the preview's suggestion; `bun.lock` is Bun's, as `bun.lockb` is. A project with neither a lockfile nor a `package.json` has no toolchain, as before.

They then build the team. "Your team" shows a card per way to start above one list of who is on it, on one screen (added in 0.35; changed in 0.103 and 0.125): first, full width and marked "Suggested", the ready-made team (3) the folder fits best, with one line under the title saying why ("Picked for your TypeScript project and its tests."); then the other ready-made teams, "One agent" (4.4, one agent alone), each saved team (3) with its faces, and "Build your own", which is from scratch. The order of the ready-made teams is `team.propose`'s `suggested_teams`, worked out from the folder's tracked paths: code (a language the scan knows, or a manifest) puts Software product first, spreadsheets and ledgers Financial analysis, a shop's files Online store, the most files winning and code winning a tie; a folder with nothing tracked puts Software product first (added in 0.125). A first visit starts on the first card. Each row of the list is the agent's picture in its role's ring, its name over its role, and its model and effort in words ("Opus 5.5", "High effort"); pressing it opens the agent's sheet: its name, its job (fixed for a team's agent; a choice for one agent alone and for an agent added here), what it focuses on (its persona), its model as a segmented choice of the newest model of each family the price table knows, its effort as a segmented choice of five, its temperature as "Set by the model" (4.4), whether it is on the team, and, for the UI/UX Designer, how its app opens (added in 0.125). A ready-made team fills the rows as a saved team does, with its answers carried to the later screens and the permission screen skipped, and is available without a state folder (added in 0.103). A saved team fills the rows with its agents, each active (the screen's intro stays above the starts, and "Filled from <name>" sits between the starts and the rows; 0.35 fix wave), with its role's suggested persona, picture, model and connectors wherever the template has none; its answers fill the later screens, already chosen; and its permission answers carry over (the founder, 2026-09-30): the two permission questions are not asked again, the last screen lists them in words under "What they may do, from <name>", and Settings changes them later. Setup does not use the switching rules of 4.4, since the starter team it replaces is the setup's own. From scratch is two rows, a Product Manager and a Developer, their roles fixed and their names empty, with "Add someone" (changed in 0.103): the Product Manager's row is fixed, the Developer's has a tick box, and Continue waits until everyone ticked is named and at least two are ticked. "Add someone" bases its newcomer on the suggested Developer, so it works on a team without one (added in 0.103). "A saved team" is offered but cannot be chosen when none is saved, or when Catervas has no state folder (8.4), and says which. `team.propose` still answers the suggested six (the Product Manager, the Scrum Master, the Architect, the Developer, the UI/UX Designer and the Marketing Specialist), which every start draws its agents' defaults from, and `role_defaults`, every role's shipped model, effort and persona; the six are no longer a card of their own: Software product holds the Product Manager, the Architect, the Developer, the UI/UX Designer and the Marketing Specialist (changed in 0.125). Each agent gets a generated name and avatar that the user can change, and a short persona line ("terse, prefers to show rather than tell"). In the wizard each row says the role's job in a sentence, the UI/UX Designer's naming the Product Manager who agrees its plans; the persona shows on the Team page (added in 0.31). Adding a seventh agent means picking a role again; two developers is the common case. An added agent's picture is the first of the extra pictures that nobody on the team has, never the UI/UX Designer's own or the Finance Specialist's (added in 0.31). The UI/UX Designer's row says its job ends by checking every screen the Developer builds (added in 0.33). The UI/UX Designer works only with Docker's sandbox, because its browser runs there (the founder, 2026-09-30; added in 0.33): in no-sandbox mode, or when Docker cannot be reached, the suggestion names it unavailable (`team.propose`'s `unavailable`, with `designer_needs_sandbox`), and its row starts unticked and cannot be ticked, a saved team's UI/UX Designer's too whatever its id, since the row is held off by role (0.35 fix wave), says "Needs Docker's sandbox" and why, and offers "Check again" and a link to how to install Docker. While the Designer is ticked, a card under its row, "<name> needs to know how to open your app", asks for the project's preview (8.3): "Get it ready", the `prepare` command, optional; "Start it", the `start` command; the port, optional (changed in 0.106); and the first page, `/` by default. When the scan found a start script (`dev`, `start` or `preview`, in that order, of a toolchain whose commands are scripts), `project.scan` answers it as `app_start { prepare, start }` and `team.propose` proposes it as the team's preview when the team has none (a scan that fails proposes none), and the card then reads "<name> opens your app with “<start>”." with a quiet "Change how it starts" that opens the fields (added in 0.106).
