The owner's own Claude Code usage is read from the `replies` of `machine.db`, one row per reply, so a resumed session, a fork, a teleported copy or an overlapping export counts a reply once, for the sessions placed `owner` in the team's project folder and its member repositories; each reply is priced by `catervas_core::pricing`'s shipped table by its model and its four token counters, and a reply on a model the table has no row for counts its tokens for nothing and is counted in `unpriced_replies` ("n replies on models without a price"). Sessions of Catervas's own agents are placed `catervas` and left out of it. The team's agents' usage is the sum of its log's `cost.recorded` `cost_usd` in the period. `billing` is `api` when Claude Code's account is a subscription (`account.status` `kind: subscription`), and the page then says "What this would cost on the API" with an info button ("You pay a monthly Claude plan." and what the amounts are); on a console or environment account it is `spent` and the page says "What you spent". Owner usage in a project no team holds is `watched_usd`; claude.ai conversations updated in the period are counted as activity only, since the export carries no usage figures. The workflow is: sessions, the owner's with a reply in the period plus the team's `session.started`; active hours, the owner's replies less than five minutes apart (the gaps between them added) plus the agents' session durations; commits, from `git rev-list --count --no-merges --since --until` on the integration branch of each root, those authored as `catervas@localhost` being the team's and the rest the owner's; pull requests, those created in the period from GitHub (`GET /repos/{full}/pulls?state=all&per_page=100`) when it is connected and knows the repositories, else the team's `pull_request.opened` events, and left out when neither has any; the three tools the owner's sessions called most, a built-in named in words ("Editing files", "Running commands", "Reading files", "Searching files", "Searching the web") and a service by its catalog name; and the sessions of each day. The blockers, each with a count and up to three examples and none shown at zero: what waits on the owner (`waiting.list`'s count and the oldest one's age), failing, silent or turned-off schedules and failed deploys (the daily digest's items, by name), tasks blocked over three days, forgotten sessions (the digest's count), and the period's `tool.denied` events. A team's `analytics.mine` adds `cycle_days`, the mean days from a task's first `in_progress` to `accepted` for the tasks accepted in the period, and `throughput`, how many were. The pages: `/analytics`, "Analytics" in the rail of All teams and This computer, with "This week" and "This month", "Usage per team" (a stacked bar per team, "You, in Claude Code" and "The team’s agents", the two amounts written beside it as "$41.20 + $18.60", "Watched $1.30", the claude.ai line, and "See as a table"), "Workflow" (the four numbers, the sessions each day with the number above each bar, "Used most") and "Blockers"; and a team's Costs page with the tabs "Spending", which is the page as it was, and "Activity", with the week's usage bar, "1.6 days a task, start to done", "9 tasks done", "14 · 12 commits: you · team" and "1 waiting on you". Charts are plain SVG in the app's tokens (`BarChart` of `@catervas/ui`); every bar carries its numbers in text and each chart has a table behind a disclosure.

### 4.5 Reading and changing the team's documents (added in 0.97; ADR 0051; phase 8 step 04b)

"Files" is a place of the rail, after "Chats"; on a phone the bar keeps its five places and Team's page links to "Files" before "Settings". Its routes are `/files` and `/files/<path under docs/catervas/>` (`/files/product/roadmap.md`); `/files` opens the first document of the first folder that has one, and a path the tree does not list says "There is no such document.". On a wide screen the folders are a tree beside the document: one folder for each active role (5.17), each with its owner's picture, a tag in the folder role's colour reading the folder's name, and the owner's name, the open document's folder open and its document marked as the current page; a folder with no document says "Nothing here yet". On a phone the tree is a picker labelled "File" above the document, one group for each folder ("<Folder>, <owner>") whose options read "<Folder> › <document>", an empty folder one disabled option, with the owner's picture and "<owner>’s folder, <Folder>" under it, and a "Back" link to Team. The document stays where it is on the page when the screen changes size, so a draft survives it.

A document is read in the version for you. A pair (5.17) has a "Which version" switch of "For you", pressed when it opens, and "For the team", the agent version (`.agent.md` or `.agent.html`). Under the document's name a line says who changed the shown version last, when and in which task: "Changed by <who> <when>", then ", in <task>" linking to the task when the change names one; <who> is the agent's name when it is on the team, "you" when the owner made it, else the commit's author, and <when> is "just now" under a minute, else the largest whole unit of minutes, hours, days, months or years in words ("5 days ago", "yesterday"); there is no line when no commit changed it. A one-file document says "Written for your team. You can read it and change it." The team's version says "This is how your team reads the <document>. To change it, change the version for you; <owner> keeps this one in step.", and when it is stale, before that line, either the owner's picture with "<owner> is bringing this up to date with your change." (a task that brings it up to date is open) or "The team’s version is older than yours" naming no agent (the twin was made stale by the owner's own commit, which gets no re-derive). The team's version has no "Edit", and neither has a document that `files.read` says is not editable: a marketing plan changes through a new version on its own page.

**An attached document (added in 0.131; ADR 0076; standalone plan `attached-documents`).** A document the owner attached (5.17) has under its name the line "Attached by you from <name>", <name> the file's own name (`Trip spec.pdf`), which `files.read` answers as `attached: { name }` and `attached: null` for every other document. The page is a pair as any other (above): the document is the Markdown Catervas made from the file, `Edit` changes it as it changes any document, and the team's version is the one the folder's owner writes once the owner's change is integrated.

"Edit" turns the document into a plain text box labelled "<document> text", with a "Write" and a "Preview" switch, the hint "A line starting with # is a heading, one starting with - is a list item, and **two stars** make words bold.", "Save" and "Cancel". For a pair the page says "You are changing the version for you."; a draft is the owner's own state, based on the blob the document had when "Edit" was pressed, and nothing the page asks again after an event changes it. "Save" sends `files.save` (5.17) as the owner's change; the page says, beside the buttons, what saving does: "Saving puts your change in a pull request; it is in your project once that is merged.", for a pair followed by who updates the team's version (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: the sentences for `auto_merge` and `manual` are gone). Once saved, and while the change waits (`waiting`), the page shows the owner's text, with no "Edit", and a line: "Saved. It goes out with a pull request." (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: it also had two lines for the other policies); "at once" is said nowhere else. A save refused with `file_changed` keeps the owner's text in the box, says "This file changed while you were editing. Your text is still here; copy it, then reload to see the new version." with "Reload", which puts the new version's text and blob in the box; `file_busy`, `change_waiting`, `is_a_link`, `marketing_plan` and `too_large` are said in plain words above the box, the draft kept ("This file was also changed on your computer, outside Catervas. Finish or undo that change, then save here again.", "An earlier change to this file is not in your project yet. Edit it once it is.", "This is too long to save here: a document can be at most about 256 KB."). Today's card of the product plan's changes (5.7) has "Open in Files" under each document's name, linking to that document's page.

Markdown is read with raw HTML off, so that every `<`, `>`, `&` and `"` of a document shows as itself, and a link or image whose address is `javascript:`, `vbscript:`, `file:` or a `data:` that is not an image stays text. A `mermaid` fence is drawn only on a page that has one, by `mermaid` loaded then, with `securityLevel: "strict"`, as an image whose picture the page's content policy lets through; a diagram it cannot draw stays as its text under "This diagram could not be drawn.".

HTML documents (added in 0.108; ADR 0058; standalone plan `html-documents`). A document in `.html` is shown in `<iframe sandbox src="/documents/raw?path=…">` with no `allow-*` token, titled with its name, in place of the drawn text (5.17 gives the route). The frame takes the reading column's full width and the window's height below the page's header (at least 60% of the window), scrolls inside itself, and is fitted to the screen, a phone's included; on Today the product plan card's frames are 50vh high, at least 16rem, since the card holds two. Above it, "Open full page" opens the same route in a new tab (`rel="noopener"`). "For you" and "For the team" switch between the pair's two files as for Markdown. Below it, "Ask for a change" is a box, "What should change?", with "Send to <agent name>" (the name of the agent whose folder holds the document), which sends `files.ask_change` (5.17); it is shown for every document `files.read` says is `askable`, either format, and not on the Scrum Master's `delivery/` documents. Under Advanced, "Edit source" turns the HTML into the text box above with "Save" and "Cancel", no "Write"/"Preview" switch and no live preview, since an unsaved page has no route to be served from; the frame shows the saved document once the save is in. A Markdown document keeps "Edit" with "Preview", unchanged. A marketing plan waiting for approval whose `marketing_plan.proposed` has `format: "html"` is shown in the same frame on its page, in place of plain text. A link from one document to another inside the frame opens nothing useful (the frame is its own origin and the route answers `401`); documents are reached through the tree. In the owner's "changes to approve" an HTML document's changed lines are shown with their tags removed.

**Documents kept on this computer (added in 0.129; ADR 0074).** While `team.get` says `documents_mode` is `local`, "Saving" says "Saving changes the document on this computer." and, once saved, the page says "Saved."; nothing waits on a pull request, so there is no "Saved. It goes out with a pull request.". "Changed by" names who wrote the document last through Catervas (you, an agent, or a task and its assignee) and when, from the log (5.17); a document nobody has written since the switch has no line, and a twin is stale when its document was written after it. While the documents move (`taking_out` or `putting_back`) no document has "Edit" or "Ask for a change", and the page says "Documents can't be changed until you merge the pull request that moves them." `files.save` is refused `documents_switching` then.

## 5. The harness

This section is the heart of the specification. Everything else could be rebuilt; this is what makes Catervas worth building.

### 5.1 Principles

Contracts before work. No agent starts a task that lacks a contract passing the Definition of Ready. This applies to tasks the user creates by hand too. Every request from the user is triaged and becomes an epic contract or a single task contract first; tasks otherwise exist only as the breakdown of an approved epic (5.16).

Nobody grades their own homework, and only code is reviewed by an agent (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). A code task is one of the Software Developer or the UI/UX Designer (`changes_code`); its reviewer is never its assignee, and the human's send-back of a result comes after the reviewer has finished (5.2; added in 0.25). For the developer's code, the reviewer is the Architect; if the team has none, another Developer, since a Software Developer may review another Developer's work but never its own; if there is neither, no contract for a Developer can pass the Definition of Ready, and the Product Manager asks the human to add a reviewer agent, an Architect or a second Developer (decided 2026-09-15). The UI/UX Designer's code is reviewed by the Architect, and by a Developer when the team has no active Architect; a Designer's task has a reviewer only while the team has an active Architect or Developer, and the Definition of Ready says so otherwise (5.3; 6.8; changed in 0.103, since a team needs only a Product Manager, F1; added in 0.31). The human does not stand in as reviewer: the harness verifies agents' code with agents. A bug hunt (5.16) is the one code-role task no agent reviews (changed in 0.117; ADR 0063): the governor accepts it on its criterion. No other task is reviewed by an agent, and none has a reviewer session or waits for the Product Manager's or the human's acceptance: the Architect's designs and plans, the Product Manager's, Scrum Master's, Marketing, Finance and Procurement Specialists' tasks, and an epic are accepted or rejected by the governor on the exit criteria Catervas runs itself, `command`, `test` and `artifact`, and the Definition of Ready refuses a `review` or `human` criterion on them (5.3, `no_review_outside_code`). Catervas writes the review note for them itself (5.4). Nobody grades their own homework still holds there, since the agent that wrote the work does not run the criteria that accept it. The Product Manager's contracts are checked by the Definition of Ready's rules alone: no agent judges them (the judge of 0.10 and 0.26 is gone, 5.3), and no contract waits for the human's approval (5.16 item 2). The human does not run commands: when a result waits for the human (a code task's `human` criterion, or an epic filed before ADR 0061 that Catervas does not verify alone, 5.4), Catervas runs its `command`, `test`, and `artifact` criteria for them, and the human answers the rest (5.4; ADR 0013; added in 0.8).

Governance is code, not prompts. The prompts tell agents what good behavior looks like. The governor makes bad behavior impossible or expensive. A system prompt that says "never push to main" is a suggestion; a governor that returns a permission error is a rule.

Bounded everything. Every session has a token budget, a wall clock limit, a tool call limit, and an iteration limit. Hitting any of them is a normal, handled outcome that produces an escalation, not a crash.

Chat is not command. The channel exists for coordination and for the humans watching. The only way work enters the system is as a task with a contract. This rule is what stops a chatty team from talking itself into a rewrite. It holds through one tool (added in 0.14): the only way from the channel to work is `catervas_create_task` without a parent, a request that goes to triage (an incident's fix is the one exception, 6.9; changed in 0.32) like one of the user's (5.16). A conversation session is given that tool and refused a `parent` on it, so it cannot file a task under an epic, and no other tool it has creates or moves work. A one-to-one chat (4.3; added in 0.34) holds the rule more tightly still: its session has neither that tool nor any other that files or moves work, only the reading tools and its reply, and a request its reply proposes is filed only when the user sends it, as the user's own. (Changed in 0.117; ADR 0063.) The ways from a one-to-one chat to work are two: the owner's, "Send as a request" under a proposal and "Send as a task" on a message, and `catervas_take_task`, by which the chat session files a task given to its own agent from the owner's message; a chat session still files and moves nothing else.

Everything is a file, every action is an event. Contracts, decisions, memories, and role definitions are plain files in `.catervas/`. Every tool call, state transition, message, and expense is an event in an append-only log. The user can reconstruct exactly what happened and why.

### 5.2 Task lifecycle

```
draft ──▶ refining ──▶ ready ──▶ assigned ──▶ in_progress ──▶ verifying ──▶ accepted
                        │            │             │               │
                        │            │             ▼               ▼
                        │            │          blocked         rejected ──▶ in_progress (bounded)
                        │            │             │
                        ▼            ▼             ▼
                    escalated    escalated     escalated ──▶ (human decides) ──▶ any state or cancelled

verifying ──▶ blocked      (the reviewer is stuck; added in 0.122; ADR 0069)
blocked ──▶ verifying | refining   (the answer goes back where the block came from, or to the plan)
refining ──▶ blocked      (the Product Manager is stuck)
ready ──▶ refining        (a dependency of the task was cancelled; the owner sends the task back to its plan; added in 0.134; ADR 0079)
accepted ──▶ assigned     (the pull request no longer merges and the merge left conflicts)
```

Transitions and who may trigger them:

| From | To | Triggered by | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| draft | refining | Product Manager picks it up | the request has been triaged (5.16; added in 0.3) |
| refining | ready | Governor, after PM submits contract | Definition of Ready (5.3); the human's acceptance of the contract is no longer asked, whatever the risk, the kind or the team's policy (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061) |
| refining | escalated | Governor | contract fails DoR `policy.readiness_attempts` times, three when it is left out (changed in 0.136; ADR 0080; 1 to 100, set on Settings → Rules). The rows for a contract that needs the human's acceptance (risk `high`, the policy, an epic) stay in the table so that older logs read, and never open for a new contract; an escalation of reason `approval` or `risk_gate` already open in a log is still resolved by the human's acceptance of the contract (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061) |
| refining | blocked | Product Manager, or the agent a chat gave the task to | a written blocker with what is needed (added in 0.122; ADR 0069) |
| ready | assigned | Scrum Master, or the Product Manager when the team has no active Scrum Master, within WIP limits (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062: a task that is stuck fills no agent's limit, below) | assignee role matches the contract, an epic's assignee being the Scrum Master, or the Product Manager when the team has no active one (5.16 item 3); for a code task the reviewer holds the contract's reviewer role and is never the assignee (5.1); the reviewer field is still filled for every task and checked as before, but no agent reviews a task that changes no code, an epic included (5.1, 5.16 item 4; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061); the assignee is below the team's work-in-progress limit, which counts the tasks it holds in `assigned`, `in_progress` or `rejected` that do not wait on the human, and none in `verifying`, `blocked` or `escalated` (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062, below; changed in 0.118; ADR 0064: a task under review is its reviewer's work, and when it comes back it counts again from its rejection, so its author takes no new work while it waits, and a sent-back task is never handed to another agent, unlike a blocked, escalated or waiting one (0.116's hand-over); before it counted every task neither `accepted` nor `cancelled`, and `assigned` and `rejected` still count, because nothing gates `assigned -> in_progress` and `rejected -> in_progress` hands a task straight back to the same agent, so counting only the started ones would let the limit be walked around, added in 0.3); every dependency accepted, whether or not it is integrated yet (5.14; added in 0.2; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061); a task of a role with a private folder (the Finance Specialist's, 6.6) is not assigned while another task holds that folder, whatever the assignee's room under the work-in-progress limit and however many agents of the role the team has: another task assigned to an agent, in any status but `accepted` and `cancelled`, whose own contract names a role with that folder, holds it (the task's role, not its agent's current one, so an agent who has left the team does not free it), so one sent back, blocked or escalated does, since `rejected -> in_progress` and `blocked -> in_progress` pass no assignment gate; the human's own moves of an escalated task (`escalated -> assigned`, `escalated -> in_progress`) are the existing override of the `escalated -> any` row and do not wait for the folder; the refusal is `private_folder_busy`, and the orchestrator passes over such a task rather than asking for it (added in 0.21; as built in 0.62); the tasks of one lane of an epic's plan are built by one agent, in order: a task with a `lane` and a parent is refused any assignee but its lane's builder, the assignee of the highest-numbered other task of the same epic, lane and assignee role that is not cancelled and whose assignee is active, with "lane_taken: lane <n> of <epic> is <builder>'s, who builds its tasks in order; assign <task> to <builder>", while the first task of a lane to be assigned goes to any agent of the role, and the orchestrator offers a lane's task to its builder alone and waits while the builder has no room (added in 0.98; ADR 0051); under autopilot an agent with no session running may be assigned a `ready` task of its role past `wip_limit_per_agent`, though not past a limit of zero (added in 0.138; ADR 0082) |
| ready | refining | Governor | a dependency the contract lists was cancelled (gate `dependency_cancelled`; added in 0.134; ADR 0079). On a tick the governor moves each `ready` task that depends on a cancelled task, with the reason "<id> was cancelled", and the channel says of each "sent it back to refining: <id> was cancelled". The Definition of Ready then fails on the cancelled dependency (5.3), which opens a refine session for the Product Manager |
| ready | refining | human | none; the owner's words are required (added in 0.134, after the second live look; ADR 0079). The task page of a `ready` task offers "Change the plan", which asks "What should change?" and sends the move with the words as its reason. A refine session for the Product Manager follows, carrying the owner's words (see "A send-back to refining" below) |
| ready | refining | Product Manager, to re-plan a task no one holds (added in 0.133; ADR 0078) | none |
| assigned | in_progress | assignee starts session | none |
| in_progress | verifying | assignee declares done | every exit criterion the assignee can run has a recorded result with evidence from its own run, a `human` criterion being the human's to answer and a `review` one the reviewer's, both checked at acceptance instead (5.3, 5.4), and the task branch has at least one commit and a clean worktree (added in 0.2), or, for a task in a private folder (6.6), which has no branch, the assignee names the workbooks it wrote in `catervas_request_transition`'s `workbooks`, one to twenty paths in the folder such as `books.xlsx`, and each is a file in the folder reached through no link: a request naming none is refused "name the workbooks you wrote", and each path that is no such file "<path> is not in your folder" (added in 0.21; as built in 0.62); an epic is asked none of that and asked instead that every task under it is accepted or cancelled and at least one is accepted, which is the whole of its gate (5.16 item 4; added in 0.3) |
| in_progress | blocked | assignee | a written blocker with what is needed |
| assigned | blocked | assignee | a written blocker with what is needed; Catervas moves it so when the user retires the task's assignee before it started (added in 0.37) |
| blocked | in_progress | Scrum Master or human | blocker resolved, with a written resolution, so that the next session knows what changed (added in 0.3); for a block from `assigned` or `in_progress`, or with no record of where it came from (changed in 0.122; ADR 0069) |
| blocked | verifying | Scrum Master or human | a written resolution, for a block from `verifying`: the reviewer finishes its review (added in 0.122; ADR 0069) |
| blocked | refining | human | a written resolution, for a block from any status: the Product Manager changes the plan (added in 0.122; ADR 0069) |
| blocked | escalated | Governor | blocked for the configured limit or longer (default: 24 hours) |
| verifying | accepted | reviewer, then Product Manager | Definition of Done (5.4), for a code task. The result waits for the human only for a `human` criterion (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: risk `high` and a task that may change the product plan no longer wait). A task in a private folder's move carries the effect `nothing_to_integrate` (5.14; added in 0.62) |
| verifying | accepted | Governor | Definition of Done (5.4), for a task that changes no code and whose every exit criterion is a `command`, `test` or `artifact` one, which Catervas has run itself; refused otherwise with "Catervas accepts or rejects on its own only a task that changes no code and whose every criterion it runs (ADR 0061)" (added in 0.115; ADR 0061) |
| verifying | rejected | reviewer | written reasons mapped to failed criteria |
| verifying | rejected | Governor | the failed criteria's ids with the reasons Catervas wrote from its own runs, under the same conditions as the governor's acceptance above (added in 0.115; ADR 0061) |
| verifying | rejected | human | the result waits for the human (5.4: a code task's `human` criterion, or an epic filed before ADR 0061 that Catervas does not verify alone), and, for a task, its review has passed; a written message, and optionally the failed criteria's ids (added in 0.25; ADR 0024; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061) |
| verifying | blocked | reviewer | a written blocker with what is needed, for something the reviewer cannot change and that stops its review: a check Catervas could not run, or something only the owner can give (added in 0.122; ADR 0069) |
| rejected | in_progress | Governor | iteration count below limit (default 3, plus the extra tries the human granted, 5.7) |
| rejected | escalated | Governor | iteration limit reached, the limit being the default plus the extra tries granted (5.7) |
| accepted | assigned | Governor | the task's pull request no longer merges and Catervas's merge of the integration branch into its branch left conflicts (5.14; added in 0.122; ADR 0069) |
| any | escalated | Governor | a budget whose consequence is escalation is exhausted — the task's dollars or its sessions (5.5), a move Catervas asks for on the task's behalf as soon as it sees the budget spent, whatever the task's status other than terminal, `escalated`, or waiting on the human (changed in 0.13) — or a permission was denied on a required action, or Catervas could not run one of the task's criteria for its reviewer for a reason that is not the work's (5.4; added in 0.8), or a UI/UX Designer's plans for the task were returned as many times as the iteration limit, the default plus the extra tries granted, which escalates with the reason `iterations` and is checked after the budgets and before a denied permission (6.8; added in 0.31); a `stop` from the user takes the human's row below, which needs no gate, because the governor is not what hears the user (added in 0.3); the user's stop of a running session also aborts it, at once when Catervas runs it in the process that heard the stop, and every later tool call of it is denied (added in 0.8) |
| any | cancelled | human only | none (added in 0.2) |
| escalated | any | human only | none |

**Tools' changes outside a task's paths (added in 0.121; ADR 0068).** A preview or a build the assignee runs may rewrite tracked files outside the task's allowed paths (`next dev` and `npm run build` rewrite `next-env.d.ts` and `tsconfig.json`), which the agent can neither write nor restore. Before a move into `verifying` is judged, Catervas reads the task's worktree with git on the host. Each tracked file changed, deleted or retyped there (staged or not) that matches none of the allowed paths is restored from the task branch's last commit. Each untracked file outside them that git does not ignore is deleted. Catervas then records `worktree.tidied { put_back, removed }` on the task. A change inside the allowed paths is the agent's own work: it is never touched, and the clean-worktree rule still refuses the move. Added, renamed and conflicted paths are left alone, and a task in a private folder or with no worktree has nothing to tidy. The tidy also runs before each implement session (changed in 0.122; ADR 0069), as Catervas's act with no agent and no session, so that a Developer in the middle of a task is never stuck on a file it cannot restore; and it does nothing while a merge is in progress in the worktree (5.14), whose staged changes outside the paths are the integration branch's.

**A send-back to refining, and a task that has not started (added in 0.134; ADR 0079).** A task the human moved into `refining` ("Ask the Product Manager to change the plan", or any move of the human's into it) is not judged as filed whole (5.16 item 2) until a refine session has run since that move, so the move always costs the Product Manager one session; that session's prompt carries the human's words, in an `untrusted` block. While a task is in `draft`, `refining` or `ready` and not `locked`, the Product Manager may write its `dependencies` and its `parent` (5.11), `parent` only to an existing epic; the write leaves the status as it is. After assignment, and for every other writer, `parent` stays fixed. In a session about an epic (purposes `plan` and `refine`) the Product Manager's `catervas_write_contract` and `catervas_request_transition` take an optional `task_id` (added after the second live look): a child of that epic in `draft`, `refining` or `ready`, which the call then acts on instead of the epic, under the same gates as for a session of that task (the writes above; a move the table allows). Without `task_id` they act on the session's own task. Any other `task_id`, from another role or for a task outside the epic or past `ready`, is refused with "task_id: <id> is not a waiting task of <epic>". The epic's `plan` prompts say so, so that a re-plan changes the waiting tasks itself instead of asking the owner.

**A task whose documents stay on this computer (added in 0.129; ADR 0074).** With the documents kept on this computer (5.17) a task works on a copy of the folder in its worktree, and a task whose every allowed path lies within `docs/catervas/` has no branch: its worktree is detached, it reaches `verifying` with no commit once it changed a document ("the task changed no document in docs/catervas/" otherwise; the clean-worktree check stays), `catervas_git_commit` refuses a path under `docs/catervas/` (`documents_stay_local`), and its move into `accepted` carries `nothing_to_integrate`, as a private-folder task's does, so that it opens no pull request and counts as integrated for its dependants. The tidy before `verifying` also puts back, from the task's start copy, a document changed outside the allowed paths, and removes one added there, and lists them in `worktree.tidied`.

More than one row can carry one move: three send a `refining` contract to `escalated` (two of them never open since 0.115), and a blocked or rejected task has its own row and the governor's. The rows are taken in the order they appear here and the first whose gate opens is the one recorded, so the more specific reason is the one the user reads; when none opens, the refusal says what every gate it tried was waiting for. A row whose actor is the assignee or the reviewer is open only to the agent the contract names in that field, so one Developer cannot declare another's task done (5.1), and who asked for an assignment is the actor of the request rather than anything the runtime repeats back. A move to `escalated` raises an escalation whose reason is the row's: the readiness failures, an epic's approval or a task's risk gate (both only in a log older than 0.115), the blocker's age, the iteration limit, the exhausted budget (the task's sessions being their own reason), the denied permission, a criterion Catervas could not run, which asks the human and so is `explicit_request` (added in 0.8), or the user's own request on the human's row (5.7). A contract that now passes is not escalated on its earlier failures, however many the runtime counted, so a contract that has been fixed is readied rather than escalated as a failure (the approval row that once mirrored it never opens since 0.115). `iteration` counts returns: it goes up by one as the task goes from `rejected` back to `in_progress`, which is what `max_iterations` bounds, so a task gets `max_iterations` + 1 tries, plus the extra tries granted, and the web UI says the try in progress as `iteration` + 1 of that many (changed in 0.26 by step 08's landing review), and every move into `in_progress` clears the blocker and its time, including the one the human makes from `escalated`, because a task that escalated out of `blocked` kept its blocker and a stale one would age again. A block the runtime recorded no time for cannot be aged, so the governor refuses to escalate it and says so, as it does for any value it was not given; the time is stamped by the same decision that blocks the task, so that it is recorded rather than remembered. An agent id is compared once trimmed and a blank names nobody, which is why a task the contract names no assignee for cannot be moved by one (added in 0.3).

A UI/UX Designer's task (added in 0.31) stays `in_progress` from its first `explore` session to its `implement` session: its plan gate (6.8) adds events, not states, so the diagram and the table are unchanged but for the escalation above. Until the task's latest plan is approved, the governor refuses the Designer's `write_workspace`, `execute`, `git_local` and `git_remote` calls, and its `external_effect` connector calls without asking the human (changed in 0.39), in any session of the task with `design_plan_not_approved` (5.6), so no commit, and therefore no move to `verifying`, comes before the approval. Since 0.115 (ADR 0061) the approval is Catervas's: when a plan is proposed, the orchestrator records `design_plan.approved` at once, with no agent and no session on the envelope and the reason "Catervas approved it: no agent approves a design plan, and the finished change is reviewed (ADR 0061)", and starts the `implement` session in the same tick. A plan an older log left proposed is approved on the first tick after the upgrade; a plan the Product Manager returned in an older log still counts as returned.

A dependency counts once it is accepted (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061; it counted as integrated, accepted and no longer awaiting integration, from 0.113), in whichever repository of a project folder it went, so a task in one member does not wait for a task in another to be merged. The task's worktree starts from the dependency's branch when that is not merged yet (5.14). The governor judges an assignment on what the runtime tells it, and refuses rather than guessing when what it is told cannot be true: an assignment the runtime named no assignee for, a task that lists itself as a dependency, and two reports about the state of one dependency, or of one task under an epic, are all refused, because a dependency has one state and taking the first report would make the answer depend on the order they arrived in. A work-in-progress limit of zero refuses every assignment, which is how a team pauses an agent without retiring it. An epic needs no reviewer agent (5.16 item 4; changed in 0.115).

A one-to-one chat (4.3; added in 0.34) is no task and has no place in this lifecycle. Its rule is the first of a tick scoped to no task, before the delivery rules and the rules of work, and it is the one rule that runs while the team is paused (section 3), except while the pause is Catervas's for a key the provider refused (5.5) (5.9).

`accepted` and `cancelled` are terminal: no transition leaves them but the one row `accepted | assigned` (changed in 0.122; ADR 0069: a task whose pull request stopped merging goes back to its assignee, and `accepted` still counts as done for the work-in-progress limit, the cleanup and the tasks that depend on it), `any` in the table excludes them, and `any` never means staying in the same status. The governor is the only actor allowed to write the `status` field for transitions marked as its own. Agents request transitions through a tool; the governor evaluates and either applies them or refuses with a reason that goes back to the agent and into the log. A contract is frozen once its task leaves `refining` (5.11). The blocked-age rule measures from the moment the runtime stamped, so the runtime must never persist a block time later than the present and must re-stamp it if its clock is corrected backwards: the governor cannot age a task whose block time has not arrived, and it keeps waiting rather than escalating every blocked task the instant a clock steps back. When the orchestrator asks for a move on a task's behalf that it does not start a session for (an assigned task's start, a rejected task's return or escalation, an old block's escalation) and the governor refuses it, the task is passed over and that move is not asked again until the task next moves, so a refusal is recorded once and left on the board for the human rather than recorded on every pass (added in 0.8). A blocked task returns where its block came from (changed in 0.122; ADR 0069): the governor reads the status of the last move into `blocked`, and `blocked → verifying` opens only for a block from `verifying`, `blocked → in_progress` only for one from `assigned` or `in_progress` (or an older log with no record), and `blocked → refining` for any. Whoever holds a task and cannot finish it blocks it: the assignee in `assigned` and `in_progress`, the reviewer in `verifying`, the Product Manager (or the agent the task was given to in its chat, ADR 0063) in `refining`; `catervas_declare_blocked` asks as the caller's own actor. `rejected` and `ready` have no holder, and the UI/UX Designer's design review is a check, not a held task. A move out of `blocked` or `escalated` into `verifying` or `refining` resets the blocker, and the review that follows runs Catervas's checks again and the Designer's look again.

The work-in-progress limit leaves out an epic for its own tasks (added in 0.101; ADR 0051; phase 8 step 07). When the assignee of a task under an epic is counted, the epic itself is left out: `open_tasks` takes the task's parent, as the rule that offers assignees (rule 8) takes it, so that with no Scrum Master the Product Manager that holds the Catervafication's epic can take its own docs task under it at a limit of one.

**A stuck task frees its agent (added in 0.116; ADR 0062).** The work-in-progress limit counts a task its assignee holds in `assigned`, `in_progress` or `rejected` that does not wait on the human (a task in `verifying` counts for no one: the row above says why) (an unanswered question, tool approval or marketing plan). A `blocked`, `escalated`, `accepted` or `cancelled` task, or one waiting on the human, counts for no one, so an agent whose task is stuck is assigned the next ready task of its role. The rule is written once, in the store (`counts_towards_wip`), and the assignment gate, the rules that start work and the agents' activity all read it. An agent's counted tasks are ordered by when each last began to count (`counted_seq` on the projection: the event that moved it into a counted status from another, cleared its last wait on the human, or handed it over; a row made before it was kept ranks first) and then by the task's number, and the first `max(wip_limit_per_agent, 1)` of them are the ones its agent works (`within_limit`; a limit of 0 still lets the task under way finish). An epic is always within, its assignee coordinating it. A task whose wait cleared resumes with its previous assignee when it is within the limit. When the assignee began other tasks meanwhile and the task is past the limit, it is returning, and the rule that follows rule 5 hands it, when it is `assigned` or `in_progress` (a `rejected` one waits for its author), to the first active agent in team order whose role is the contract's assignee role, that has room, that is not its current assignee and that, unless the role reviews its own work, is not its reviewer. The governor checks the hand-over (`check_reassignment`), records `task.reassigned { from, to, reason: "resumed" }` and writes the contract's `assignee`; the reviewer is unchanged, and the new assignee's next session resumes from the last commit and note in the task's own worktree. `check_reassignment` refuses an epic, a task with a lane (it waits for its lane's builder), a status but `assigned` or `in_progress`, a task that is not returning, and a candidate that is not active, lacks the role, has no room, already holds the task or is the reviewer; a refusal records nothing, and the task waits with its assignee and is tried again on the next tick. A task has one holder, `assignee_id`, set only by an assignment (`ready -> assigned`) and by that hand-over; one process drives a project, its ticks taking turns (8.2); and nobody reviews their own work. A private folder (6.6) is still held by a blocked or escalated task. An agent with no session running that holds a counted task in `assigned`, `in_progress` or `rejected` within its limit shows as working ("Building <title>") in `team.activity` (F3).

**A task given in a chat (added in 0.117; ADR 0063).** A task whose `task.created` names an agent in `given_to` is that agent's while the agent is on the team and not retired and the contract's `assignee_role` is still the agent's (the human may change any field, which makes it an ordinary task again). Rule 8 takes the ready tasks in two passes, first those given in a chat and then the rest, each in board order. A given task is assigned to its agent with no session, on the assigner's behalf (the Scrum Master's, else the Product Manager's), when the agent has room under the work-in-progress limit, the move was not refused since the task became `ready`, an assigner and a reviewer exist and the governor's conditions for the assignment hold; the reviewer is the first active agent, in team order, of the contract's `reviewer_role` that is not the assignee, else the assignee when the role reviews its own work. The tick says "assigned it to <agent>, who was given it in its chat". It is next in its agent's queue: while the agent is at its limit the task waits, and in the first tick the agent has room it is assigned before any other ready task. A task given to a paused agent waits. Its code is reviewed as any code is (5.4).

**Autopilot's rows (added in 0.138; ADR 0082).** Seven rows give the Product Manager, under the gate `Autopilot`, the moves the table gives the human, but `ready -> refining`, which the Product Manager already holds: `blocked -> in_progress`, `blocked -> verifying`, `blocked -> refining`, `verifying -> rejected`, `any -> escalated`, `any -> cancelled` and `escalated -> any`; the table has 40 rows. The gate opens only while autopilot is on (5.12), only for a task that is `blocked` or `escalated`, and only when the human's own row of the same move would open, with its gate: the Product Manager needs what the human needs. The `verifying -> rejected` twin, for a task that is neither, never opens; the result that waits on the owner is accepted or sent back through `catervas_decide` (5.7), not through it. A move recorded through the gate carries `gate: autopilot`, and the actor is the Product Manager's agent. The rest of the table, and the Governor's own rows, are unchanged.

**Work for an idle agent (added in 0.138; ADR 0082).** Under autopilot, each tick, an active agent with no session running is offered a `ready` task of its role that nobody holds, even when it holds `wip_limit_per_agent` tasks, and the governor lets that assignment pass: the runtime tells it the agent is idle, and a limit of zero is still held. The order of work, the reviewer rules and every other gate are unchanged. An agent with a session running, a task of another role, and autopilot off change nothing. When no task of its role is ready the agent stays idle: the team does not file work for an idle agent.

### 5.3 Definition of Ready

A contract passes when all of the following hold. The governor checks every rule mechanically; no agent judges a contract (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061, which removes the judgment part that 0.10 and 0.26 gave the team's judge).

Structural (mechanical):
- Intent is non-empty and states the user-facing reason for the task.
- At least one exit criterion exists, and every criterion has a `verification` with a `method` that is one of `command`, `test`, `artifact`, `review`, `human`. A `review` criterion is a rubric the reviewer answers and a `human` one a question only the user answers; neither is the assignee's to run, because nobody grades their own homework (5.1), so the gate on `in_progress -> verifying` does not ask the assignee for them and the Definition of Done asks the reviewer instead (added in 0.3). Only a code task has a reviewer: a `review` or `human` criterion on any other task is refused by `no_review_outside_code` (below; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061).
- Every `command` and `test` criterion has the command to run and what a passing result looks like.
- A contract that is not reviewed by an agent, which is every contract but a Software Developer's or a UI/UX Designer's task, has no `review` and no `human` criterion (`no_review_outside_code`; added in 0.115; ADR 0061): "<ids> ask for a review or the human, and only a code change is reviewed (ADR 0061): use command, test or artifact criteria", in plain words "This task asks for a review, and only code is reviewed. Check it with a command, a test or a file instead." Catervas runs `command`, `test` and `artifact` criteria itself and accepts the task on them (5.4). The rule `required_criteria_present` leaves a required `review` or `human` method out for such a contract, as it leaves `command` and `test` out of what a task that runs none is asked for. A contract written before the rule, and still carrying such a criterion, keeps the old path (5.4).
- Budget is set, and does not exceed the team's `max_task_budget_usd` when the team sets one, and a task's budget does not exceed what is left of its epic's (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062).
- For a code task, the reviewer will not be the assignee (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: no other task is reviewed by an agent, though its reviewer field is still filled and checked). When the reviewer role differs from the assignee role, the team has at least one active agent of the reviewer role; when they are the same role (two Developers reviewing each other), the team has at least two active agents of it. The governor picks a reviewer agent other than the assignee at assignment (decided 2026-09-15). A Product Manager's own docs task needs one active Product Manager (changed in 0.103).
- The team has at least one active agent of the contract's assignee role, the human excepted, and an epic too, since the Scrum Master or the Product Manager takes every epic; a task for a role nobody on the team holds is refused in words that name the role, "nobody can take this task: the team has no active <role>; add one on the Team page" (added in 0.103; ADR 0055).
- Risk level is set.
- Scope lists at least one `out_of_scope` item. (An empty exclusion list is a reliable predictor of scope creep, so we require the PM to think about it.)
- Every listed dependency exists and is at least `ready` (added in 0.2; moved here from the judgment list because it is mechanical).
- When no agent can review, the readiness result says which role to add (added in 0.3).
- The contract satisfies the team rules (5.12): the required verification methods are present, `allowed_paths` fall within the ceiling, and the budget is within the team maximum (added in 0.2).
- No `allowed_paths` entry reaches under `.catervas/`, whatever the role or kind, because the files there change only through Catervas's tools (5.8): an entry is refused when its first segment, after `.` segments are dropped and each `{a,b}` is expanded, contains `**` or matches `.catervas` regardless of letter case, and it goes on below it or is `.catervas` itself, so `.catervas/**`, `**`, `**/*.md`, and `*/memory.md` are refused and `*.md` and `src/**` are not; the failure names the entries (added in 0.17). An entry with a backslash is refused outright, because the glob engine reads `\` as an escape and would otherwise match under `.catervas/` through a segment this rule reads as not reaching it (added in 0.17). The one exception (added in 0.21; as built in 0.62) is a task of a role with a private folder (6.6), a task and not an epic: its `allowed_paths` may reach under its own folder, `.catervas/local/finance/` for the Finance Specialist and `.catervas/local/procurement/` for the Procurement Specialist (added in 0.70), and nowhere else under `.catervas/`. An entry is within the folder as a path is within the team's ceiling (5.12): `.catervas/local/finance/**`, a path in the folder and the folder itself are, and `.catervas/local/**`, the sibling `.catervas/local/financeX/**`, `**` and an entry with `..` are not, and the first three of those are still refused here as reaching under `.catervas/`. Such a task is held to its folder by one rule of its own, `private_folder_task`, which takes the place of the ceiling and of the document paths below: every `allowed_paths` entry lies within the folder; no criterion is a `command`, a `test`, a `review` or a `human` one (the last two since 0.115, ADR 0061), since the task has no worktree to run a command in and no reviewer; an `artifact` criterion names a file as the folder holds it, by the path rule of 6.6 (a workbook, and in the procurement folder a note ending `.md`, added in 0.70) and never starting `.catervas/`, and has no `must_contain`, since a workbook is not text and a note is checked for being there alone; and the task has no `parent`, since an epic's paths cannot name `.catervas/`. A command or a test the team's rules require (5.12) is not asked of it, and every other method they require still is. Its plain words name no role, since the rule holds both folders' tasks (changed in 0.70): "A task in a private folder works only there: no commands, no tests, no text searched in a workbook or a note, and no parent epic." The words of the rule read "use artifact criteria" in place of "use artifact, review and human criteria" (changed in 0.115). Its reviewer field names the Product Manager alone (the founder's decision of 2026-10-07, "Only the Product Manager"; added in 0.70): a task that works in a role's private folder is read by that role and by the Product Manager, and by no other role, so each folder stays its own role's. Since 0.115 (ADR 0061) no agent reviews it: Catervas checks its `artifact` criteria and accepts it (5.4). A contract whose `reviewer_role` is any other role, the other folder's among them (a finance task naming the Procurement Specialist, a procurement task naming the Finance Specialist), is refused by a rule of its own, `private_folder_reviewer`, whose message names the folder and says to name `product_manager`, in plain words: "A task in a private folder is reviewed by the Product Manager alone, and this plan names someone else." An epic works in no folder and is not held to it.
- A task assigned to any role but the Software Developer and the UI/UX Designer keeps its `allowed_paths` inside the team's `document_paths` (5.12), because only those two change code; the failure names the paths outside (added in 0.11; the Designer added in 0.31). An allowed path is inside when it lies within a document glob as a path lies within the ceiling (`docs/adr/**` within `docs/**`), or when it has no wildcard and a document glob matches it (`README.md` and `notes/plan.md` by `**/*.md`). A path with a wildcard that lies within no document glob is outside (`notes/**`, `notes/*.md`), because it could name code. A document glob that does not compile puts every path outside, as 5.6 says of any glob, and the failure names the glob. An epic is not held to the rule; each of its tasks is, against its own assignee role. A task in a private folder is excepted here too, and from the team's ceiling (5.12), by the rule above (6.6; added in 0.21; as built in 0.62): its `allowed_paths` lie under `.catervas/local/finance/`, which no document glob names.
- While a role that owns a folder under `docs/catervas/` (5.17) has an active agent, a task assigned to any other role names no path that could reach that folder; the failure, `folder_owned`, names the paths and the folders (added in 0.52 as `marketing_paths_owned`, for `docs/catervas/marketing/` and the Marketing Specialist alone, ADR 0042; widened in 0.91 to every role's folder, ADR 0051). An entry could reach a folder when, after backslashes become `/`, `.` segments are dropped and each `{a,b}` is expanded, it is read segment by segment against the folder's (`docs/catervas/product` has three): a segment that contains `**`, or does not compile, reaches (the check fails closed, as for `.catervas/` above); one that does not name the folder's segment, regardless of letter case, does not; and an entry that goes on below the folder, or ends at or before it with a last segment that is no wildcard, reaches, since a literal directory names what is under it. So `docs`, `docs/catervas`, `docs/**`, `**`, `**/*.md`, `Docs/Catervas/Product/x.md`, `docs/catervas/{product,adr}/**`, `docs[/]catervas/product/x` and `docs/*/product/**` reach `docs/catervas/product`, and `docs/adr/**`, `docs/*`, `docs/catervas/*.md`, `docs/catervas/product*`, `src/**` and `*.md` do not. A task is held for each folder whose owner is another role than its assignee and has at least one active agent now; a folder whose owner has no active agent (none on the team, paused or retired) is anyone's, so the Product Manager's task may name `docs/catervas/architecture/plans/**` on a team with no active Architect. An epic is not held to it, each of its tasks is, and a role's own task may name its own folder. The message, exactly: `allowed paths <the reaching paths, in the contract's order, joined by ", "> could reach folders other roles own: <each reached folder as "<folder>/ (<role>)", in the table's order (5.17), joined by ", ">; name narrower paths, or give the task to the folder's owner`. The rule reads the agents active now, so a task made ready before an owner joined is not checked again, and the Definition of Done does not hold ownership a second time (5.4). The Product Manager's `writing-task-contracts` and the Scrum Master's `keeping-work-flowing` tell them to name the folder a task needs, such as `docs/adr/**` or `src/**/*.rs`, never `docs/**`, `docs/catervas/**`, `docs`, `**` or `**/*.md`, while a role that owns a folder has an active agent. Its plain words: "Only a folder's owner changes the documents in it, and this plan lets someone else."
- A task's `lane` is no more than the team's active builders, the Software Developers and UI/UX Designers (the roles that change code), one lane each. The failure, `lane_beyond_builders`, reads "lane <n> is beyond the team's builders: it has <b> active, Software Developers and UI/UX Designers, one lane each", in plain words "The plan splits the work into more parallel parts than your team has builders." A lane is read only on a task with a parent, and it is content, frozen from `ready`, so only refining renumbers it and a failure goes back to the Product Manager who writes it; a builder paused later strands no lane, since one builder may hold several (added in 0.98; ADR 0051).
- No allowed path of a task in a lane could meet one of another task of its epic that is not cancelled and is in another lane. The failure, `lanes_overlap`, reads "lane <n> could meet <id> in lane <m> (<ours> and <theirs>)", a clause for each such task joined by ", ", then "; tasks in different lanes are built side by side, so their allowed paths must part before their first wildcard: narrow the paths, or put the tasks in one lane", in plain words "Two parts of this work that run side by side could change the same files." Two globs could meet unless, after each `{a,b}` is expanded, backslashes are read as `/` and empty and `.` segments are dropped, the segments before each one's first wildcard segment differ at some position, ignoring letter case; a glob with a `..` segment meets anything. This is a conservative test with a known ceiling: `src/*.rs` and `src/*.ts` are taken to meet although no path matches both, and the Architect narrows the paths or puts the tasks in one lane. Each pair is checked when the later of the two becomes ready (added in 0.98; ADR 0051).
- No allowed path is a protected path (5.6), which no tool may write, so such a task could never be done; a path under `.catervas/` or with a `..` segment is the rules' above (added in 0.133; ADR 0078). The failure, `protected_path_allowed`, names the paths.
- A task names the member repository it changes only where one belongs, and always where one does (added in 0.111; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 02). In a project folder a task that names a `repo` works in that member and may change anything there; a task that names none works in the project folder, which holds documents and no code, so a builder's task with no `repo` keeps every allowed path to the team's document paths (5.12). Three rules, reported in this order after the assignee rule. `repo_not_allowed` fails when `repo` is set and the project is one repository ("this project is one repository, so repo is left out"), or the contract is an epic, which spans the project's repositories whatever role it names ("an epic spans the project's repositories, so repo is left out"), or the assignee's role does not change code ("the <role>'s task works in the project's own folder, so repo is left out"), the first that holds. `repo_required` fails when the project is a project folder, the contract is a task, `repo` is not set, the assignee's role changes code, and some allowed path is not a document path ("this project has several repositories: set repo to the one this task changes (<names>), or keep its allowed paths to the project's documents"); a team document glob that does not compile leaves it silent, and `document_paths_only` reports the glob. `repo_unknown` fails when `repo` is set where one belongs and is not a member ("<repo> is not one of this project's repositories: <names>"). A contract fails at most one of the three. The paths of a task and of its epic are compared, by `paths_within_parent` and `lanes_overlap`, without their repositories until a later step says how. An epic in a project folder runs no command (added in 0.112; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 02b): the rule `epic_command_in_project_folder`, after `repo_unknown`, fails when the project is a project folder, the contract is an epic and an exit criterion's method is `command` or `test` ("an epic in a project of several repositories runs no command: give <ids> to its tasks instead"), and `required_criteria_present` leaves `command` and `test` out of what the team rules require of such an epic, as it does of a task in a private folder, so Catervas's runs on the integration branch (5.4) check an epic's `artifact` criteria alone, in the project folder. Thirty rules in all (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: `no_review_outside_code` is added, and `summary_present`, `judgment_recorded` and `judgment_answers` are gone).
- A new project plans nothing but its product plan until the product plan's task is accepted (added in 0.99; ADR 0051; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: the owner no longer approves the plan). While a project whose log holds `project.started` has no task created with `product_plan: true` that is `accepted`, every task and epic but the product plan task (5.16) fails `product_plan_first`: "this new project's product plan is not accepted yet: only its own task is planned until Catervas accepts that task", in plain words "A new project plans nothing until the owner approves its product plan." Nothing is stored for the acceptance and git is not read: `Transitions::awaits_the_product_plan` is the one question, asked by readiness, rule 9, the interview's prompt and opening, the command and the query, and rule 9 waits for the acceptance, not for the merge. Rule 9 passes over a contract while it is true, the product plan task excepted: no refine session and no governor ask, so no readiness attempt is spent and nothing is escalated after three (5.2); triage still runs, and once the plan's task is accepted the next tick refines the contract against the spec as the task's branch holds it, or as the integration branch does once it is merged.

No judgment (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). Until 0.115 a team's judge, the Architect, else the Scrum Master, else the Product Manager, answered the team's questions about every plan that passed the mechanical rules (is it small enough for its budget, would its criteria notice the failure its intent worries about) in a session of its own, with `catervas_record_judgment`, and the rules `judgment_recorded` and `judgment_answers` held a contract until it had. The founder removed it on 2026-10-16 ("Remove it"): it is a review of a plan by an agent, and only code is reviewed. Rule 9 now asks the governor straight away, `escalated` first, a row that opens only on three readiness failures, then `ready`, and no session starts for a contract that passes. The tool, its prompt and message, the judge's retire refusal (`last_judge`) and the answers `judges` of `team.get` and `team.check` are gone. `policy.judgment` in `team.yaml` is accepted on load and ignored, `validate_team` asking nothing of it (no judge must be held, no question asked), and Catervas drops it when it writes the file or a saved team; the schema keeps the key so that older files load. A `contract.judged` in an older log still loads (8.5) and nothing reads it. The Definition of Ready is evaluated in one pass, in the order of the rules above.

### 5.4 Definition of Done

A task is accepted when (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: items 1, 4 and 5 are said for a task an agent reviews, which is a code task, and the paragraph "A task Catervas verifies alone" below says how every other task is accepted):

1. Every exit criterion has been run by the reviewer, independently of the assignee's run, and passed. A recorded result from the reviewer counts only when it carries evidence: a result with nothing in it is the "I ran the tests and they passed" this section exists to refuse. `human` criteria, which only a code task may carry, are satisfied only by an explicit human acceptance event, which needs no evidence of its own because the acceptance is the evidence.
2. No file outside the contract's `allowed_paths` was changed, and no protected path (5.6) was, even one inside them (added in 0.9), nor any path under `.catervas/`, whatever the role (5.8; added in 0.17). The governor computes this from the git diff and refuses acceptance otherwise, naming the protected paths and the paths under `.catervas/` apart from the ones outside the allowed paths. It also refuses a diff that changes one file of a human document's pair without the other (`pair_changed_alone`; added in 0.91, 5.17): the document for people or its agent version (`.agent.md` or `.agent.html`) alone, except a twin that is stale (5.17; added in 0.96): behind the document the owner changed, it may change alone, since bringing it up to date is that diff. The runtime lists the stale twins in the evidence only when a changed path is a twin, from the integration branch. Ownership of a folder is not asked again here: the diff is held to the allowed paths, which `folder_owned` checked against the owners when the task became ready (5.3), and an owner made active after that does not reopen it. A twin changed alone is refused like any other half pair until the owner's edits and a stale twin are built (5.17).
3. The assignee wrote a completion note: what changed, what was not done, and anything the reviewer should look at first.
4. The reviewer wrote a review note that maps each criterion to evidence (a command output, a file path, a test name). When the reviewer is the assignee (5.1), its review runs in a fresh session given no memory, no decisions from the human about the task and no `catervas_write_memory`; the review note is refused from the session that did the work (`review_in_implement`), and the completion note from the review session (`completion_in_review`) (added in 0.103).
5. A code task with a `human` criterion has the human's acceptance, which stands for each `human` criterion (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). Risk `high` and a task whose `allowed_paths` may change the product's `spec` or `roadmap` (the rule `may_change_an_owner_document` of 0.95 is gone) no longer wait for the human, and neither does an epic filed since 0.115, which Catervas verifies alone (below). An epic filed before it, whose criteria Catervas does not all run, keeps the old path and waits for the human, and a contract written before readiness refused a `review` or `human` criterion on a task that is not code keeps the old path too.
6. A Software Developer's change to the interface has passed the UI/UX Designer's design review, when the team has a Designer (below; added in 0.33).

Verification runs in a fresh session for the reviewer. The reviewer does not receive the assignee's transcript, only the contract, the diff, the completion note, and the tools to run the criteria. This is deliberate: a reviewer that reads "I ran the tests and they passed" is measurably worse than one that runs the tests.

How this release verifies (added in 0.8). When a task reaches `verifying`, Catervas runs the contract's `command`, `test`, and `artifact` criteria itself, one at a time, in a sandbox of the task's made afresh for them rather than the one the assignee's commands ran in, so that nothing those commands left outside the worktree reaches the run, and records each result as the reviewer's run, recorded by the governor: that is item 1's run by the reviewer, independently of the assignee, and the reviewer is shown the results. The sandbox is fresh, but it mounts the task's worktree, so gitignored build output inside it, such as `target/`, is still what the assignee left (added in 0.9). A criterion Catervas could not run because the task's container went, which the work's own commands can cause, is recorded as failed with the error as its evidence, and the next one runs in a new sandbox; one it could not run for any other reason (git, the base-branch sandbox, a file it could not write, a command that would not start) is not the work's fault, so the governor escalates the task with reason `explicit_request` and the error as its detail, rather than send it back to an assignee who cannot fix it. The reviewer may not record those criteria itself, so that it cannot record a pass over Catervas's failure, and no agent records a `human` criterion, which only the human's acceptance answers. The reviewer answers the `review` criteria and writes the review note; it may not commit or push, because nobody rewrites what they grade. When a criterion the reviewer ran failed, Catervas files the rejection in the reviewer's name, with the failed criteria's ids and the review note as its reasons. When every criterion passed, the Product Manager's session is asked to accept a code task; a task with a `human` criterion waits for the human instead (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). A request the governor refused during a verification is left on the board for the human rather than asked again, whoever made it: a refused request from the reviewer's or the Product Manager's own session, a rejection the reviewer asked for itself among them, leaves the task waiting for the human even where Catervas would otherwise have filed the rejection from the review note. Once the human has accepted the result of a task with a `human` criterion, the Product Manager's session is asked to accept it, the acceptance standing for each `human` criterion. Each verification is summed up once in a `review.recorded` event. The reviewer's session is given Claude Code's read-only built-in tools alone: the `PreToolUse` hook judges a call by the agent's tiers, or by its kit tag for a connector's tool (5.6, 6.7; added in 0.22), rather than by the session's purpose, so a reviewer whose role holds `write_workspace` would otherwise be allowed to write in the worktree it reviews, and that allowlist is what stops it. Neither the reviewer's session nor the Product Manager's acceptance session is offered `catervas_exec`, `catervas_git_commit`, or `catervas_git_push`: neither has a sandbox to run a command in, and git writes are refused to anyone but the assignee, so the tools are left off the session's list rather than offered and refused; `catervas_git_status` and `catervas_git_diff`, which only read, stay for an agent whose tiers hold `git_local` (added in 0.9).

A task Catervas verifies alone (added in 0.115; ADR 0061). A task that changes no code, one of the Product Manager's, the Architect's, the Scrum Master's, the Marketing, Finance or Procurement Specialist's, and an epic, whose every exit criterion is a `command`, `test` or `artifact` one (`catervas_verifies_alone`), has no reviewer session, no Product Manager acceptance session and no wait for the human. When it reaches `verifying` (an epic once its tasks are integrated and its criteria have run on the integration branch, below), Catervas runs its criteria as above and records them as the reviewer's runs, recorded by the governor; then, in the same tick, the governor accepts it on the row `verifying -> accepted` when every criterion passed and the Definition of Done holds, or rejects it on the row `verifying -> rejected` with the failed criteria's ids and the reasons Catervas wrote, which is a try as any rejection is. Agents cannot ask as the governor, so the log names no false actor. Catervas writes the review note itself, `note.written { kind: review, written_by: "catervas" }` with no agent and no session on its envelope: "Catervas ran every criterion of this task itself; only a code change is reviewed by an agent (ADR 0061).", a blank line, and one line for each criterion, `<id>: passed|failed: <evidence>`. No `review.recorded` is written. Every other rule of the Definition of Done holds as for a code task, the `human_accepted` rule alone excepted, the human's acceptance of a result being asked of no task of this kind. The task page says "Catervas checks it" in place of the reviewer's name, and signs the summary "Catervas checked it".

A task's checks run in its member (added in 0.112; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 02b). Catervas resolves the task's repository once for its runs: a task that names a `repo` has its `command`, `test` and `artifact` criteria run in the sandbox made for its worktree, which is a worktree of the member under the project folder, so a command runs at the member's root, where `allowed_paths` are relative to; and `new_tests_required` is judged against that member's integration branch, with the member's git, the diff being the member's. The base worktree of that check, `.catervas/local/worktrees/CTV-<n>-base`, is made under the project folder and removed after the run, however the run ended, so nothing of Catervas's goes into a member's own folder. A task whose member is missing is passed over before anything runs, as 5.14 says of every rule that resolves its repository; a repository that cannot be had for another reason, a name the project does not list, is a refusal that names the task and the cause.

A task in a private folder (a Finance Specialist's, added in 0.21 and built in 0.62, or a Procurement Specialist's, built in 0.70) has no diff and no worktree. Its criteria are `artifact` ones (5.3; `review` and `human` ones, which readiness refused only from 0.115, are gone, ADR 0061), and Catervas verifies it alone (above). Catervas checks each `artifact` criterion itself, on the host and with no sandbox, as the reviewer's run: the path, a workbook or, in the procurement folder, a note named as the folder holds it (6.6), passes when it is a regular file in the folder reached through no link, none of the folder's parts from the project's root down (`.catervas`, `.catervas/local`, the folder) being one and none of the artifact's, and fails, with its reason as the evidence, when it is missing, a folder, a link or through one, or not a workbook's path; a criterion that searches a workbook for text fails. A `command` or `test` criterion of such a task, which readiness refuses, is one Catervas cannot run, and escalates it as any criterion it cannot run. Item 2 is checked against the folder: when the task is assigned, Catervas copies every regular file of the folder but `.history/` to `.history/<task-id>/`, once, so a task sent back and assigned again keeps its first copy; the files that differ from that copy (their bytes, not their times), are new to it, or are gone from it are the task's diff, each path under the folder, and `allowed_paths` hold them as they hold a branch's. The protected paths (5.6) and `.catervas/` (item 2 above, 5.3) except the task's own folder and nothing else under it: a path that climbs out, the sibling `.catervas/local/financeX/`, and any other path under `.catervas/` are refused as for any task. One piece of work touches the folder at a time (5.2, 6.6), so the copy is the state the task started from. Its reviewer's first message, in place of a diff, lists each changed file in one untrusted block: its path, whether it is new, changed or removed, and its size, a removed file's being the copy's, with how to read each: a workbook with `catervas_read_sheet` and its copy from the start of the task with `catervas_read_sheet` and `baseline: true` (6.6), and, when the list holds a note, a note with `Read` at its path in the folder, which is the session's working directory, and its copy with `Read` at `.history/<task-id>/` followed by that path (added in 0.70). The sentence names no file: a file's name is its writer's word, and stays in the untrusted list. An older task in a private folder, whose reviewer and Product Manager still run in the folder, with no executor, are given `catervas_read_sheet` for it. `task.diff` answers such a task with `diff` empty, `files` the changed paths in the folder (none until the task has its copy, which its assignment takes), `added` and `removed` 0 and `private_folder: true`, and the task's page and its gate say where the changes are and list the names, and its page says there is nothing to add to the project, since acceptance was its end; `catervas task show --diff` prints no diff. Until the task is accepted, the list is read against the folder as it is when asked, which the reviewer does while the task is the only one holding the folder. Its move into `accepted` records the files it changed (`changed` on `task.transitioned`, 8.5), and `task.diff` answers an accepted task from that move, so a later task's changes in the folder are not shown as its own (added in 0.70); a log from before the move recorded them is answered from the folder as it is asked.

A UI/UX Designer's task (added in 0.31) is verified as a Developer's is, items 1 to 5 unchanged. Its reviewer is the Architect, else a Developer (5.1), and the reviewer's session can come only after the Designer's `implement` session, which Catervas starts once it has recorded the approval of the task's plan, at once (6.8; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061).

The design review (added in 0.33; ADR 0026, the founder's decision of 2026-09-30). A Software Developer's change to the interface is checked by the UI/UX Designer in the browser before the Architect reviews it, and only a change it passed reaches the Architect. A change is to the interface when the task's assignee is a Software Developer and either its contract sets `ui_change: true`, a content field (5.11), or a path its branch changed since its merge base with the integration branch matches the team rule `ui_paths` (5.12); the worktree is never read, since Catervas's own criterion runs write into it. A glob of `ui_paths` that does not compile, or a path that climbs with `..`, counts as a change to the interface. A team's document, any path under `docs/catervas/`, is never one, whatever its extension (changed in 0.122; ADR 0069: a bug-hunt report as `.html` had waited for a design review a document never gets); a contract's `ui_change: true` still counts. A task of any other role's is never one. When a task with such a change reaches `verifying` on a team with a Designer that is not retired, Catervas runs its criteria as above and then, before the reviewer's session, reads the latest `design_review.recorded` since the task entered `verifying`: one that passed lets the Architect's review go ahead; one that failed is filed as the rejection, `verifying → rejected` in the Designer's name, with the review's reasons and no failed criterion, which the governor admits from the Designer alone and only with written reasons (5.2); it counts as a try, as any rejection does, and after it the next `verifying` needs the Designer's pass again. A recorded answer is acted on even if the preview or the Designer has since gone, since it needs neither. With none recorded, the task waits, and no session starts, while the team has no preview set (`preview_missing`), while the Designer cannot open the app because the sandbox is off or Docker is gone (`designer_needs_sandbox`), while the active Designer has Playwright off (`designer_needs_browser`; added in the step's fix wave, since a Designer without its browser is given no work), and while every Designer is paused (`waiting_on_designer`); otherwise Catervas starts the first active Designer's design review, a `verify` session in the task's worktree with the read tier's built-ins, the Playwright connector (5.6), and seven Catervas tools: `catervas_read_task`, `catervas_read_board`, `catervas_read_rules`, `catervas_read_criteria`, `catervas_read_decisions`, `catervas_check_page`, and `catervas_record_design_review`, with no `catervas_exec`. Its message holds the diff, as untrusted text, and the preview's first page. It checks the page at 360 and at 1280 pixels, each in the light and the dark theme, with `catervas_check_page` (8.3), and ends with `catervas_record_design_review { pass, reasons }`, which records `design_review.recorded` with a copy of the session's latest check of each of the four. The tool is refused with `design_review_refused` to anyone but the Designer in a `verify` session about a task, with `blank_reason` for blank reasons, and with `design_review_incomplete`, naming the checks missing, until all four exist, so Catervas's own measurement, not the agent's word, stands behind a pass (5.1).
