If recorded again in the same session, the latest counts. A design review session that ends with no record is started again, and each restart counts toward the contract's sessions allowance (5.5). Without a Designer, or with every Designer retired, the Architect reviews alone, and item 6 holds.

**A review that cannot finish, and what a reviewer is told (added in 0.122; ADR 0069).** Rule 5 passes over a task in `verifying` only for a `transition.refused` of the governor's own since the task entered `verifying`, not for an agent's refused request: the reviewer's next session is told "Catervas refused your last request:" with the refusals as untrusted text, and the reviewer's budgets bound the retries. When the governor's own acceptance or rejection of a task it verifies alone is refused, Catervas escalates the task with the refusal's words (`criterion_unrunnable`) instead of passing it over, and the owner answers on Today. The governor judges a contract by asking `refining → ready` first and `refining → escalated` only when that is refused, so a passing contract records no refusal. The reviewer's first message for a change to the interface carries the Designer's latest `design_review.recorded` since `verifying` (its pass, reasons and checks, as untrusted text) and says how a page looks and behaves in a browser is the UI/UX Designer's check, never the owner's; the reviewer gets neither the preview nor the browser. The closing instructions of the Verify and Refine sessions say to end with `catervas_declare_blocked`, saying what is in the way and what is needed, when something only the owner can give stops the work, and a refine session that follows a block is told the blocker's words.

An epic (added in 0.8 for an epic the human reviews; ADR 0013; changed in 0.10 to every epic, whoever reviews it; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). While any task under the epic is still awaiting integration, nothing is run, because its criteria are meant for the integrated work. Then Catervas runs each of the epic's `command`, `test`, and `artifact` criteria once per verification, on a detached worktree of the integration branch's head with the network off, and records each as the reviewer's run, recorded by the governor, its evidence opening with the commit it ran at. A `test` criterion's new-tests check stays with the epic's tasks, since an epic has no branch to compare. An epic filed since 0.115 carries machine criteria alone, and Catervas verifies it alone (above): after those runs the governor writes the note and accepts the epic when they passed, or rejects it with the failed criteria's ids, and its assignee's close-out `plan` session is then given the rejection (5.16 item 4). The Catervafication's epic, for example, asks for its product spec as an `artifact` criterion. The paragraphs that follow are the old path, which an epic filed before 0.115 with a `review` or `human` criterion still takes: the human may accept it only once every one of those runs passed, and only with a message, and then the acceptance stands for the reviewer's answer to each `review` criterion and the human's to each `human` criterion; when a run failed, the human escalates the epic and sends it back to `in_progress` with a message saying what is missing, and the Product Manager files the tasks for it.

An epic the Product Manager reviews (added in 0.10; only an epic filed before 0.115 that Catervas does not verify alone takes this path since ADR 0061), which is one the Scrum Master holds (5.16 item 4), starts as every epic does, with nothing run while a task under it awaits integration and then Catervas's runs on the integration branch. Then the Product Manager's `verify` session reviews it, with the read-only built-in tools a task's reviewer has, in the project root, since an epic has no worktree; its first message holds the epic's contract, Catervas's results, and each task under the epic with its status and its last completion note, in place of a diff. It answers the `review` criteria and writes the review note, and at the end of that session the epic's `review.recorded` names the Product Manager as its reviewer. When a criterion failed, Catervas files the rejection in the Product Manager's name, with the failed criteria's ids and the review note as its reasons, as it does for a task, and the governor's row returns the epic to `in_progress` (5.16 item 4). When the review note is written but a criterion other than a `human` one has no result of the reviewer's, the Product Manager's review session runs again, told which criteria are still unanswered, as a task's reviewer's does, and the epic waits for no acceptance until they are answered. When every criterion passed, the epic waits for the human's acceptance, which an epic of this kind needs (item 5) and which may come before or after the review; then the Product Manager's session, told the human accepted, asks for `accepted`.

What a human gate shows (added in 0.18; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). Two gates wait for the human where they used to be three: a code task's `human` criterion (item 5) and the result of an epic filed before 0.115 that Catervas does not verify alone, and the money gates of 5.7. No contract waits for the human's approval, no task waits for it because of its risk or the documents its paths may reach, and an epic of 0.115 and after waits for no one. Each gate that remains shows the human three things, so that a user who cannot read code can decide and one who can may check. The first is a plain-language summary, written by the agent that asks: for a result, the opening of the assignee's completion note (item 3) and of the review note (item 4), each of which starts with one. The second is the diff: a task's branch against the integration branch, an epic's as its tasks' integrated diffs. The diff is always one step away and never required. The third is Catervas's check results: Catervas's runs of the mechanical criteria (above) for a result. A completion note and a review note must open with a summary: the first paragraph, up to the first blank line, of 20 to 600 characters, and `catervas_write_note` refuses one that does not with `summary_missing: open the note with two or three plain sentences for the user, then a blank line`. Progress notes, an agent's or Catervas's, are exempt, and so is the review note Catervas writes for a task it verifies alone. A contract's `summary` is a string of 20 to 600 characters, optional in the schema and no longer a readiness rule (`summary_present` is gone, since no human decides on a plan before work starts); the contract's summary is shown wherever it is given. The contract's `summary` is a different thing from the `summary` on `task.created` and `contract.written`, which is the log's one line. The human sends a result back (5.2) with `catervas send-back <task> <message> [--criterion <id>]…` or the web UI; a task's send-back is refused with `review_first` until its review has passed (a review passing is the latest `review.recorded` since the task entered `verifying`), and a result that does not wait for the human with `not_waiting_for_the_human`. The criteria a send-back names are held as a reviewer's rejection's are: a blank id, or one the contract has no criterion of, refuses it; a send-back may name none (added in 0.25's landing review). The send-back counts as a try, as any rejection does. What waits on the human, as the web UI and `catervas run` and `catervas plan` list it, holds a task's result once its review has passed since it last entered `verifying`, and an old epic's as soon as it is there (added in 0.25's landing review). A contract awaiting approval in an older log is sent back to `refining` the same way, with `not_awaiting_approval` otherwise.
A task's document changes (added in 0.129; ADR 0074). With the documents kept on this computer, the changed paths of a task include the documents that differ from, are new to, or are gone from its start copy of `docs/catervas/`, as repository paths; the Definition of Done holds them to `allowed_paths` and to the pair rule as it holds a branch's paths. The task's diff names them and has no `branch` for a task that has none.

**Autopilot accepts for the owner (added in 0.138; ADR 0082).** While the team decides (5.7), a result that waits on the owner's acceptance (an epic's, or a task with a `human` criterion once its reviewer passed it) is accepted by the Product Manager in a `decide` session with `catervas_decide { choice: accept_result, reason }`, after reading the criteria and the results recorded. The acceptance is recorded as `human.accepted` with `accepted_by` the Product Manager's agent id and the reason as its message; the Definition of Done is still checked as for the owner. A `human` criterion is answered by the same acceptance.


### 5.5 Budgets and limits

Five budgets, each enforced by the governor when it is set, all configurable per team, the three dollar ones optional (ADR 0015), the others with role-based defaults:

| Budget | Default | On exhaustion |
|---|---|---|
| Per session (tokens) | 400k input, 40k output | session ends with a note from Catervas; the task keeps its status and the next session resumes from the note (changed in 0.13, which no longer moves the task to `blocked`) |
| Per task (dollars) | set in contract, PM proposes | task to `escalated` |
| Per task (sessions) | `max_sessions` in the contract, default 14 (added in 0.2; the default raised from 5 in 0.9, and to 14 in 0.17); only work sessions count (changed in 0.134) | task to `escalated` |
| Per day, team-wide (dollars) | set by the user, optional | everything pauses; user is notified |

The marketing budget (added in 0.72; ADR 0042, 6.5) is a limit beside these four, and it is money spent outside the team's AI account: a marketing plan's Google Ads budget and each of its campaigns' budgets, in the plan's currency, counted by Google's own figures. It is a hard stop: no mode (`ask` or `auto`, ADR 0041), no allowance (5.6) and no agent goes past it. Catervas itself pauses a plan's campaigns when the spend Google reports reaches a budget, with no model and while the team is paused (6.5), and an agent's enabling of a campaign is refused once the spend has reached one (6.7). It is not part of the day's budget, which counts what the AI account costs.

Plus non-monetary limits: a session wall clock (default 30 minutes), a tool-call count per session (default 200), and the rejection iteration limit (default 3; the human may grant more tries, 5.7). Per-role defaults: the Scrum Master's session budget is 200k input and 20k output tokens; every other role uses the team default. Catervas ships no dollar limit: the daily budget and the team's cap on a task's budget (5.12) are each the user's to set, and one left out is no limit of that kind (ADR 0015); the token, wall-clock, tool-call, session, and iteration limits ship as above, because they bound a loop rather than spending.

More than one budget can be exhausted at the same moment, and every consequence applies. The governor reports all of them rather than the first, because none of these consequences subsumes another: stopping new assignments does not end a session that is already running, so a task that has run out must never hide a day that has. A budget is exhausted when what was spent reaches its limit, and a spend that is not a number counts as exhausted.

Costs are computed from the usage fields returned by the model API and from the model's published price table, which Catervas ships as a versioned file the user can override at `.catervas/prices.json` (added in 0.6). An override whose `version` this program does not read is refused rather than read as the version it knows, because a later format priced as this one would price a session by guesswork. An override replaces the shipped table as a whole rather than being merged into it, so a model the user took out of it is not priced. Each usage report a session returns is recorded as one `cost.recorded` event carrying the dollars computed at that moment, so a later change to the prices does not rewrite what was charged; a report for a model the table in use does not price is recorded with its tokens, a cost of zero and `unpriced: true`, and no dollar limit counts it, so that an agent can run on any model its user chooses (ADR 0015); `catervas doctor` and every start of `catervas run` name such a model. A budget's `budget.exhausted` event is recorded once, when it crosses from having room to none (added in 0.8). The daily budget's day is the UTC date the cost was recorded on, because the log does not know the user's time zone; a team eight hours behind UTC sees its day end at four in the afternoon (added in 0.8).

The period of a connector allowance (added in 0.45; ADR 0037) is the UTC day as the daily budget counts it (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062).

An agent's own session limits (added in 0.136; ADR 0080). An agent's `session` in `team.yaml` (`max_input_tokens`, `max_output_tokens`, `max_wall_clock_seconds`, `max_tool_calls`, the shape of `budgets.session`) is applied after the team's, field by field: a session of that agent starts from the role's defaults, then the team's `budgets.session`, then the agent's own, and a field the agent leaves out keeps what the team or the role gave. A session about no agent has the team's. The owner sets the team's limits on Settings → Rules, under "How long one session may run", and an agent's on its page, under "Rules for <name>"; both are saved through `team.save`. The team's readiness attempts, rejections before escalation, hours blocked, work per agent and hours an escalation may wait (`policy.readiness_attempts`, `max_iterations`, `blocked_limit_hours`, `wip_limit_per_agent`, `escalation_age_hours`) are on the same page, under "When work stops and asks you"; they are the team's alone.

A goal adds no budget (added in 0.130; ADR 0075). The daily budget is the only limit on what a goal's work spends, and a goal is refused (`goal_needs_daily_budget`) on a team with none; when the day is spent no goal session starts, as no other session does, and the team carries on the next UTC day. The two bounds of the goal's loop (5.18), that no round starts before the board is quiet and that a goal waits for the owner after a round that filed nothing or five rounds with no progress, bound a loop as a session's tool-call limit does and spend nothing: neither is a budget.

This release enforces the table above (changed in 0.13; 0.8 enforced its minimum): every session's cost is recorded, one that reports no usage as a session costing nothing; a session the orchestrator cannot go on with, because something failed after it started, is aborted and recorded as ended with `error` before the failure is reported; token and dollar budgets are checked when a session reports its usage, which Claude Code does once, at the session's end, so a live session is bounded by its wall clock and its tool-call limit alone (corrected in 0.9); a session limit, its task's dollars, or a daily budget that is set, crossed by what a session reported, is recorded as exhausted then, a session limit with the consequence `end_session_with_note`, and a task's dollars or a daily budget crossed during a session stops the next one from starting rather than cutting that one short; with sessions of several agents running at once (8.2), a daily budget that a session's cost crosses also stops every other session running in the process then, with the reason `the team's daily budget is spent`: each ends `aborted`, its task keeps its status, and nothing is escalated, so the overshoot is what the running sessions had used by then (added in 0.118; ADR 0064). An `implement` session, the one purpose whose next session reads the task's last note (8.2), that ended at a limit (its wall clock or its turns) or at its model provider's limit, or whose usage crossed its tokens, its wall clock, or its tool calls, gets one `note.written` of kind `progress`, written by `catervas`, naming each cause and what the session said, and quoting the agent's own last progress note of that session when it wrote one, so the agent's words are kept: "This session stopped at <causes>: <detail>. Your last note in it: <text>. Resume from the last commit and this note." The task keeps its status. A session of any other purpose leaves no note, and its next session is asked again from its own first message. A task whose dollars or sessions are spent is escalated by the governor (5.2), with the reason `budget` or `sessions`, before the other rules look at it, so a `verifying` task out of sessions is escalated before Catervas runs its criteria; `catervas plan` and `catervas contract new`, which do not govern work in progress, pass such a task over as before. A session that ended at the provider's limit counts toward its task's `max_sessions` like any other work session that started (below). The default of 14 is what a task's normal path needs before its iteration limit escalates it (changed in 0.17): triage, refinement, plan, and acceptance (the Scrum Master's judgment of 0.17 is gone, 0.115), then an implementation and a review for each of `max_iterations` 3 passes and the one after them, plus one for a session a provider's limit cut short, so that a task that passes on its last allowed iteration is accepted rather than escalated for its sessions, and `max_sessions` bounds only the loops the iteration limit cannot see. No session starts for anyone once a daily budget that is set is spent, until there is room again; no agent is paused for it, and the channel line that tells the user comes with the channel. The governor's own moves, which cost nothing, still run. A one-to-one chat's session (added in 0.34) is recorded with the purpose `chat` and no task, so it counts toward the day and toward no task; no chat session starts while the daily budget is spent, the user's message being kept and answered once there is room again, and the chat saying why (F8). The Costs page shows today's chat spending as "Conversations today" (F17).

A task's caps (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062). A task's dollars and sessions are limited by its contract's `budget`, `max_cost_usd` and `max_sessions`, plus the room the human gave it: `task.room_granted { sessions, cost_usd, granted_by }` (5.7), whose sums the budget rule and the session's own check add to the contract's, so the next tick sees the new caps; the contract file is not changed. A session already running is not aborted for a budget. The daily budget stays enforced as above.

What a task's sessions are (added in 0.134; ADR 0079). The sessions counted against a task's `max_sessions` are its work: `refine`, `explore`, `implement` and `verify`. Triage, assignment (`plan`) and chat sessions do not count, nor does any other session about no task of the task's own. The one exception is an epic: planning is an epic's work, so its own `plan` sessions count toward its budget, which keeps an empty breakdown bounded by sessions; a child task's `plan` sessions do not. The budget rule skips a task in `ready`, `assigned` or `blocked`, which starts no session and so spends none; a task in any other status that has spent its dollars or its counted sessions is escalated as before, except that a `refining` task the human moved there (the send-back of 5.2) is left alone while its refine session has not run (changed in 0.137; ADR 0081). The first `refine` session after each such move of the human's is not counted against `max_sessions`, so a send-back never costs the task a session; the second and later refine sessions are counted as before. The escalation says what was spent in its detail (and in the channel's line and on Today), "spent 6 of 6 sessions" or "spent $20.40 of $20.00", where it said only the gate's name before; the figures are those of the task's caps, the room granted included (above).

A model provider's usage limit (added in 0.13). A session can stop because the account that pays for it has used what its model provider allows for now, which is none of the budgets above. Catervas reads it from the session's stream (8.2): a session whose result is an error ended at its provider's limit when the last rate-limit report of the session has a status that does not start with `allowed` (so a warning is not a limit, and neither is a report with no status), when the result's API status is 429, or when what the result says contains `usage limit` or `rate limit` in any letter case. It reads all three because no capture of a session its provider refused exists yet, Claude Code 2.1.280's captures showing only `allowed`: each form is tested on a synthetic transcript, and a refusal in a shape none of them matches ends as an ordinary `error`, the residual this rule accepts. The session ends `provider_limit`, and its agent sleeps: Catervas records `agent.slept` with the time the agent wakes, the reset time the provider last reported when that is later than now, else one hour from now. An agent is asleep while its last `agent.slept` names a time later than now. Sleep is not a status: the team file is not written, the agent stays `active` (F1), and work is still assigned to it within its work-in-progress limit; only its own sessions wait, no rule starting one or making a sandbox for it until it wakes. Catervas's own criterion runs are not an agent's and are not held up. A tick with nothing to do but wait for a sleeping agent says so, naming the agent and when it wakes, and the run waits until the first one wakes and ticks again rather than ending (8.2), because a run that ended would leave the sleeping agent's work for nobody. A key the model provider refuses (added in 0.30). A session whose result is an error with the API status 401 ended because the provider refused the AI account's credential, which Claude Code 2.1.285 reports after retrying: its captured transcript is the test. A result with the API status 403, which is how the provider refuses a key whose organisation is revoked or disabled, is the same refusal, and so is a third retry of a 401 or a 403: Claude Code retries a refused subscription token twice before its result, but a refused API key ten times over about three minutes, so the session ends at the third retry of one request, which the retry's own attempt number says, and the user is not left waiting in silence; single retries spread over a session, as when a subscription token is refreshed, never add up (changed in 0.37). The session ends `credential_refused`. It is not its task's fault, so it does not count toward the task's `max_sessions`, leaves no note, and puts no agent to sleep; and since the same key fails every session alike, Catervas pauses the team at once with one `team.paused` whose `by` is `catervas`, its `reason` `credential_refused`, and its `detail` what the provider said, unless the user paused the team while the session ended, whose pause then stands. No session starts after it until the user signs in again or the connection check passes, either of which resumes a team paused for this reason, or resumes the team themselves; a team the user paused stays paused (changed in 0.141; ADR 0084). Catervas tries the account only when the user signs in or presses "Check connection", with one request that costs well under a cent (8.6), never on its own; a transient 401 therefore pauses the team too, and the user resumes it. A ceremony that stopped at a limit or at the provider's limit is asked again (5.9).

Limits shared by the teams of one serve (added in 0.144; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 05). Three limits are shared by every team a `catervas serve` drives, each off by default so that one team works exactly as before; `catervas run` and `catervas start` have none. "Agents working at once" (1 to 16, in `state.json`) caps the agent sessions that run across the teams, a chat session among them; a session that waits for a place records nothing until it is given one, and a freed place goes to the next team after the one served last, in the order the teams first asked, so that no team waits behind another's whole queue; a change applies to the next session and never stops a running one. When a session ends at the AI account's limit, every team waits until it resets: the session's agent sleeps as above (`agent.slept`), and no other team's agent is written to, but no session of any team starts before the reset; it is held in memory, so a restart forgets it and the next session that hits the limit sets it again. The computer's daily cap (`daily_cap_usd` in `state.json`, above 0 and at most 100000) counts what every team spent on this UTC day together: when the sum reaches it no session starts in any team until the next UTC day, the idle reason is "all your teams together reached this computer's daily limit; they go on tomorrow (UTC)", the team whose session crossed it stops its other sessions as for its own day (ADR 0064), and the running sessions of the other teams finish.

### 5.6 Permissions

Permissions are capability tiers attached to a role, overridable per agent by the user. The governor checks them on every tool call.

| Tier | What it allows | Default for |
|---|---|---|
| `read` | read files in the project, read `.catervas/`, search | everyone |
| `write_workspace` | write files under `allowed_paths` in the task contract | Developer, UI/UX Designer (added in 0.31), Architect, Marketing, PM (added in 0.92) |
| `execute` | run commands inside the sandbox | Developer, UI/UX Designer, Architect |
| `network` | outbound HTTP from the sandbox, web search | everyone (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: the Developer, the UI/UX Designer and the Scrum Master hold it too, and research is free; it was Marketing, Architect, PM, Finance and Procurement, added in 0.21 and 0.70) |
| `git_local` | commit on a task branch | Developer, UI/UX Designer, Architect, Marketing, PM (added in 0.92) |
| `git_remote` | push, open pull requests | nobody by default; user grants explicitly |
| `external_effect` | anything that changes state outside the sandbox: posting to services, sending mail, deploying | nobody by default, for the agent's own tool calls (a connector's tool is judged by its tag instead, below); a connector's tool tagged `external_effect` runs without asking and each use is recorded, and only one tagged `paid` waits for the human, who allows that one call (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061), or, for the DevOps Engineer's `catervas_deploy`, `catervas_restart` and `catervas_roll_back`, approved as 6.9 says (changed in 0.32), or, for a post and a Google Ads change the owner's approved marketing plan covers, approved by that plan as 6.5 says (ADR 0042; changed in 0.52), and a post outside the plan goes out like one inside it, shown on Today with a Stop and holding no task (changed in 0.115; it waited for the owner's yes from 0.57); from phase 12 step 01, a team whose `approvals` policy is `auto` runs a connector's `paid` call without asking, within its allowance and the spending limits (ADR 0041; changed in 0.50) |

The Architect, the Marketing Specialist and the Product Manager hold `write_workspace` and `git_local` because a task reaches `verifying` only with a commit on its branch, and each commits the documents that are its work; none writes application code (6.1, 6.3, 6.5; changed in 0.10, when the Architect's `write_workspace` was for spikes and neither held `git_local`; the Product Manager's added in 0.92, for the docs tasks of its folder, 5.17). Only an implement session about a task changes the project (added in 0.92; ADR 0051): in any other session, whatever the agent's tiers and whatever its role, the hook and `call_tool` refuse the built-ins `Edit`, `Write`, `MultiEdit` and `NotebookEdit` and the Catervas tools `catervas_exec`, `catervas_git_commit`, `catervas_git_push` and `catervas_propose_marketing_plan` with `no_task_no_write: <tool> changes the project, and only an implement session working on a task changes it`, after the check of the tiers and paths and after the Designer's plan gate, and such a session is not offered them. A Catervas tool of the `read` tier that writes under `.catervas/` keeps its own rules, and a connector is still judged by its tag. `catervas_write_folder_doc` (added in 0.94; 5.17) is the one tool that changes the project's files from a session that is not about a task: a `read`-tier tool offered in a ceremony session, it writes nothing in the session's tree and asks Catervas to commit a document of the caller's own folder as a folder change on a branch of its own (5.14), which Catervas makes with its own hand under the integration lock, so the check of tiers and paths asks `read` and names no path. The user's setup screen asks about `execute` and `git_remote` explicitly because those are the two that can hurt. The two answers are the team's policy `permissions: { run_commands, push }` in `team.yaml` (defaults `true` and `false`), and they apply to every agent of the role, one added later among them: an agent's tiers are its role's defaults, without `execute` for Developers, UI/UX Designers and Architects when `run_commands` is `false`, with `git_remote` for Developers and UI/UX Designers when `push` is `true` (the Designer added in 0.31), and then its own grants and revokes, a revoke winning. A UI/UX Designer's `write_workspace`, `execute`, `git_local` and `git_remote`, and its `external_effect` connector calls (changed in 0.39), are further held by its plan gate, which the hook and Catervas's tool server read from the log at each call (5.2, 6.8; added in 0.31). A "No" to commands leaves every check to Catervas, which runs them itself (added in 0.26). `git_remote` governs what an agent's session may do. When Catervas itself pushes accepted work or opens a pull request, it does so by pull request, whatever the team file says (5.14; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). No agent is acting, so no tier applies. The setup screen and `catervas init` therefore say that accepted work is pushed to `origin` and opened as a pull request for the owner to merge, and, with no `origin`, that the owner merges it by hand (`team.get` answers `online`: the repository, and for a project folder every member's, has an `origin`); the push question is about work in progress only (changed in 0.124) (ADR 0012; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). Catervas's coordination tools (reading the board, triage, writing a contract, asking for a transition, recording a result, writing a note, asking the human) all need only `read`, which every role holds: what governs each is the rule it names (5.2, 5.11, 5.16), checked by the tool itself, not a tier of its own (added in 0.8; writing a product document left the list in 0.91, with its tool, 5.17). `catervas_exec` needs `execute`; git is four tools, `catervas_git_status`, `catervas_git_diff`, and `catervas_git_commit` under `git_local` and `catervas_git_push` under `git_remote`, so that each is checked as its own tool. `catervas_git_commit` gives git each path it names as a path, never as a glob or a pathspec, and refuses one that is a directory in the worktree, because the path checks judge the name the agent gave, and a directory or a pattern would stage a protected file under it that no check saw (added in 0.9). It also takes `removed`, paths to delete and commit as removed (added in 0.108): each goes through the protected-paths and allowed-paths checks like a written path, must be a regular file inside the worktree with no link on the way, and is refused when it is a directory or is not there, so that a task of a role without `catervas_exec` can remove the document it replaces. `catervas_exec` refuses a command when any segment of it (split on `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`, and newlines, without parsing quotes) runs git, because git is a Catervas tool with its own tiers (ADR 0004), except read-only git (changed in 0.134; ADR 0079): a segment whose git subcommand is one of `status`, `diff`, `log`, `show`, `ls-files`, `grep`, `rev-parse` or `blame` runs, so that an agent can run a contract's own criterion, `git ls-files` or `git grep`. Any other subcommand is refused as before, and so is a read-only one given `--output` or `--open-files-in-pager`, which write a file or run a program. The owner can allow more (added in 0.136; ADR 0080): `rules.git_subcommands`, and an agent's own `git_subcommands` (5.12), list lower-case subcommands that run on top of the eight, with any options, so `fetch` listed lets `git fetch origin` run; the eight cannot be removed, since they change nothing. A pushing subcommand listed there is the owner's choice and is not held to `policy.push_remotes` (5.14), and the web app says so. A segment runs git when its first word is `git`, or when its first word is a `NAME=value` assignment or one of the wrappers `env`, `sudo`, `doas`, `command`, `exec`, `nohup`, `time`, `timeout`, `nice`, `setsid`, `xargs` and `git` appears anywhere later in the segment, which catches `sudo -u root git push` at the cost of refusing `sudo apt install git`. A word is read bare: quotes and shell punctuation are stripped, a path keeps only its last segment, a `.exe` suffix is dropped, and a redirection is not a command name. A call hidden in a subshell, a variable, or a script (`$(git push)`, `GIT=git; $GIT push`, `sh -c "git push"`) is the residual ADR 0004 accepts.

Protected paths (added in 0.2). A team rule (5.12) lists globs that no tool may read or write whatever the tier, so that secrets kept in the repository never enter a session. The default list is `.env`, `.env.*`, `**/*.pem`, `**/*.key`, and `.catervas/local/**`. The owner can change the list (added in 0.136; ADR 0080): each of those five can be lifted, by naming it in `rules.lifted_paths` (a team file written before 0.136 lists only its own additions in `protected_paths`, so it keeps the shipped five and no upgrade loosens a team), and the owner's own globs are `protected_paths` as before; an agent's page can lift or add paths for that agent alone (5.12). A lifted path shows a warning in the web app that says what it kept out of reach. Read only is a third answer (added in 0.136): `rules.read_only_paths` lists globs an agent may read and no tool may write, matched as the protected globs are; a call of the `write_workspace` tier that names one is refused `path_read_only: <path> is read only: the owner lets agents read it, not change it`, and a lifted path is not made read only by lifting it, the owner chooses "Read only" as a separate answer. Catervas's own state and keys are a floor under every rule (added in 0.136): whatever the owner lifts, no call of the `write_workspace` tier writes a path under `.catervas/local/**` (refused `path_read_only`, from the constant `CATERVAS_STATE`, never read from the team file), and no call reads `.catervas/local/daemon.json` or `.catervas/local/sessions/**`, which hold the daemon's token (refused `path_protected`, from `CATERVAS_KEYS`). Lifting `.catervas/local/**` therefore leaves the rest of it readable and unwritable; Catervas's own tools (5.8, 6.6) still write their files as before. The Definition of Done (5.4 item 2) holds a task's diff to its assignee's protected and read-only paths. An env template, a file named `.env.example`, `.env.sample` or `.env.template` in any folder and letter case, lists a project's keys with empty values and holds no secret: a glob such as `.env.*` does not protect it, and only a protected glob that is its own path does (added in 0.133; ADR 0078); the deny rules written into a Claude session leave out such a glob too, so the template can be read and therefore written (0.137). Protected and allowed globs match the whole path relative to the project root, after backslashes become `/` and `.` segments are dropped: `*` stays within one directory, `**` crosses directories, a bare name such as `.env` names the root file only and `**/.env` names it anywhere, protected globs match without regard to letter case and protect a directory they name along with its children, an absolute path, an empty path, or a path with a `..` segment is always refused, and a glob that does not compile refuses the check rather than matching nothing. The Definition of Done holds a task's diff to the same list (5.4 item 2), because a command run under `execute` can write a protected file that no tool call named (added in 0.9).

Tools that write to a private folder of Catervas's own (added in 0.56). A tool of the `read` tier may write to Catervas's own files: `catervas_write_memory` the agent's notebook (5.8), and `catervas_write_sheet` a workbook in the private folder of the Finance Specialist, `.catervas/local/finance/` (6.6), or of the Procurement Specialist, `.catervas/local/procurement/`, which `catervas_write_evaluation` writes a note in (6.10; added in 0.70). A tool that writes to a private folder reports no path to the check above and holds its own folder line instead: it refuses a path outside its folder, a path through a link and a path of another shape (`private_path_refused`), so `.catervas/local/**` stays a protected path for every other call. A session about a task in a private folder runs with that folder as its working directory (8.2), and the hook judges each path of a built-in tool against the working directory, so such a session reaches the folder and nothing outside it, and no exception to the protected `.catervas/local/**` is made for it (as built in 0.62). A procurement session is held the same way (0.70): its working directory is `.catervas/local/procurement/`, so the finance folder is as far from it as the database, and the hook reads no role.

An MCP tool is tagged, not tiered (changed in 0.38). When the user connects an MCP server of their own to an agent, Catervas lists the server's tools and the user labels each one (6.7; changed in 0.38, from "read-only or side-effecting"); a connector from a role's kit comes tagged, and the user tags nothing (6.7; added in 0.22). A tag (added in 0.22) is `network`, `external_effect`, `paid` (added in 0.115; ADR 0061), `ask` (added in 0.136; ADR 0080), or `denied`; `denied` is not a tier but a tool the agent is never offered, and `paid` means the service charges for the call. `ask` means the owner chose to be asked before the tool runs: the hook treats it as `paid` in every step below, so a call waits for the human, or uses the tool's allowance, and a grant allows it once, but it costs nothing, and outside a task its refusal says "<tool> of <server> asks you first", not that it costs money (added in 0.136). On an agent's page each tool of a connector is "Runs", "Asks first" or "Never": "Runs" is the tool's shipped `network` or `external_effect` label, "Asks first" is `ask` (or, for a tool shipped `paid`, `paid`), and "Never" is `denied`. A tool shipped `paid` offers "Asks first" and "Never" alone, since no tool pays without the owner (ADR 0041), and a tool the owner's marketing plan marks (below) shows no choice: `team.get` carries the kit row's `plan_approved`, the tools the plan marks, sorted, for the page to read. A tool's tag governs the call whatever the agent's own tiers, a kit's, the built-in's and a user's server's alike, so a Developer without `network` reads library documentation through its connector: the hook judges a connector's call by its tag alone and asks no tier (changed in 0.38, from a tier check at `network` after the tag). A tool of a custom connector that the user did not label is `paid` (changed in 0.115; it was `external_effect`), so that a tool whose cost nobody stated still asks. `preauthorized_external_tools` never applies to a connector's tool: the hook does not consult it for an `mcp__<server>__<tool>` call (added in 0.38). A `paid` connector tool stays offered, and a call to it waits for the human, who allows that one call or refuses it (changed in 0.39, from refused `external_effect_refused` in 0.38; ADR 0031; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: only `paid` asks; a call to an `external_effect` tool runs at once and is recorded as every call is, `tool.called`, with no approval). With no grant that matches it, the hook records `tool_approval.requested { server, tool, input, input_sha256 }`, whose sequence number is the approval's id, and denies the call `approval_needed: <server> <tool> waits for the human (approval <seq>)`, which stops the session (8.2); the task then waits on the human (5.7). `input` is the call's whole input as compact JSON, never cut, so the human sees all of what they allow. An input whose compact JSON is over 64 KiB is not asked about: it is denied `tool_input_too_large: <tool>'s input is over 64 KiB, too long to show you, so it is refused`, grant or not, and only its `tool.denied` is recorded. A grant allows exactly one later call: by the agent that asked, on the same task, to the same server and tool, with the same `input_sha256`, the sha256 of the input's canonical JSON (compact, object keys sorted at every depth, as `spec_sha256`'s, 6.7), in a session of that agent about the task that started after the grant. That call is allowed, and its `tool.called` carries `approval: <seq>`, which uses the grant up; the hook finds the grant and records its use while holding the daemon's one sessions lock, so two identical calls after one grant cannot both run, and the second asks again. The grant lapses when a session of the asking agent about the task that started after it ends without the call, and a later call asks again. Another agent's session about the task, a reviewer's, cannot use it, and a changed field asks again. A session about no task has nothing to wait on, and a user's servers are given to none (8.2): its call is refused `external_effect_refused: <tool> of <server> costs money, and only a session about a task can ask you to allow it`, without asking (added in 0.39; changed in 0.115). A session is given Catervas's own server, the one built-in connector where the next paragraph says, and its agent's own servers where 8.2 says, and no other (added in 0.8; the built-in connector added in 0.33, the user's servers in 0.38); the hook takes any tool named `mcp__<server>__<tool>` that is not Catervas's for a connector's, and denies one whose server the session was not given `connector_not_in_session` (changed in 0.38, from `tool_not_allowed`, no tier).

The order of a connector call in the hook (added in 0.45; ADR 0037; changed in 0.71 and 0.115; ADR 0061 removes the call's sites, since no session is held to approved sites): the session's connector, the tag, `denied`, the preview's `url`s, the Designer's plan gate, the 64 KiB limit, the human's grant for this exact call, then, for a `paid` tool, the tool's allowance while the agent's calls of it this period are under it, then the ask; an `external_effect` tool is let through after the 64 KiB limit and the Designer's plan gate, and its `tool.called` is recorded. A grant is used before the allowance. The count and the `tool.called` it is checked against are read and recorded under the daemon's one sessions lock, so two calls at the last place cannot both run; a call the allowance lets through records `allowance: <n>`.

Research is open to every role (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). The Procurement Specialist was held to approved sites from 0.71 (ADR 0039's amendment of 2026-10-07; phase 7 step 10b2), a `web` registration of `approved_sites` for it alone, and the hook refused a `WebFetch` or a connector call whose address was not on the owner's list; that is gone, with `catervas_request_sites`, `catervas_read_sites`, the Procurement Specialist's `approved_sites.yaml`, the `site.requested` waiting row, `catervas site` and the `sites.list` query. `site.requested` and its decisions in older logs still load and nothing lists them, and `site_decide`, `site_add` and `site_remove` answer `sites_gone: Catervas no longer keeps a list of sites (ADR 0061)`. Every session is given `WebFetch` and `WebSearch` when its agent holds `network`, which every role does by default; an explore or a chat session is registered with `network` as well as `read` when the agent holds it, and a session whose built-ins are the read tier's alone (a verify session) is given them too. An agent the team file took `network` from (`revokes`) gets neither in any session, unless the browser adds it as 6.7 says. The helper that reads an address's host (`site_of`) stays for the seller messages, the data pipeline requests and the waiting rows. What still keeps a page from steering an agent to leak: the protected paths and the keychain, the model credential, connector keys and OAuth tokens stay out of every session's reach (5.6, 8.6), and a page's text is untrusted (8.6).

Reading is open (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). The Marketing Specialist read two folders of the project, the Product Manager's `docs/catervas/product/` and its own `docs/catervas/marketing/`, from 0.93 (ADR 0051; phase 8 step 02; the founder's "Read all; Marketing reads PM only"); it now reads the whole project like every other role. The `reads` registration, the hook's `judge_reads` and every `read_not_allowed` refusal are gone, and `catervas_exec` and `catervas_git_diff` are no longer refused to it for that reason. The protected paths (above) still hold for every role, and so do the working folder and the read roots (below).

Read roots (added in 0.114; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 03). In a project folder a session may read, with `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob` and `LS`, every present member repository but its task's own, in `repos.yaml` order, and the project folder (named `project`) unless the session works in it: the Developer's task in `app` reads `infra` and the Architect's documents, and the Architect's planning session at the project root reads every member. It writes only inside its own working folder, under its task's `allowed_paths`; any other tool, or a write, outside it stays `path_outside_workspace`. A session has no read root in a one-repository project or when `repos.yaml` cannot be read; the session then still starts and reads fail closed. The Marketing Specialist's and a private-folder task's sessions have them like any other (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). A member whose path holds a parenthesis, a backslash, a control character or a glob character is not a root, since Claude Code cannot be given a rule for it. The hook resolves the path through links, so a link is judged by where it points, takes a path inside the working folder as the working folder's, and judges one inside a root against the team's `protected_paths` and `.git/**` read relative to the root (`path_protected: <root>: <path> is protected`); a `Grep` or `Glob` whose folder is the root's top, or holds or is held by the literal folder of a protected glob (`.catervas/local` for `.catervas/local/**`, `.git`), is refused, as is an `LS` of the top. Claude Code is given each root with `--add-dir`, and a `Read` deny rule `//<root>/<glob>` for each protected glob and `.git/**` of each root (5.12).

A plan-marked call (added in 0.68; ADR 0042, ADR 0038; phase 7 step 08f). A kit's `stdio` connector that is exactly `catervas connector <name>` may list `plan_approved: [<tool>]`, each tool tagged `paid` (`plan_mark_not_paid`; it was `external_effect` and `plan_mark_not_external` before 0.115), none with an allowance (`plan_mark_with_allowance`), and only on Catervas's own connector (`plan_mark_not_catervas`), since only Catervas's own server can be trusted to check the plan; the mark is the kit's, in neither the team entry nor its hash, and the session's connector carries it (`plan_tools`) only for an entry that is exactly the kit's (`matches_kit`). A marked call comes in the order above after the 64 KiB limit and before the grant: while a marketing plan is active (read from the log by the daemon's clock, only for a marked tool) it runs as the plan's own call, with neither a grant nor an allowance, and `tool.called` records `marketing_plan: "MP-<n>"`; with no active plan it is denied `no_active_marketing_plan: <tool> of <server> runs only inside a marketing plan the owner approved`, never asked, so `auto` (ADR 0041) never runs it either. Catervas's own server then refuses every call the active plan does not cover (`not_in_marketing_plan`, 6.7).

Connectors per agent (added in 0.33; ADR 0026). An agent's `mcp_servers` in `team.yaml` lists the connectors it is given, each `{ name, source: builtin }` or, added in 0.38, a server of the user's own, `source: custom` (6.7), at most 20 and no name twice on one agent (`connector_name_twice`, added in 0.38); a name is lower-case letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter, at most 40, never an underscore, because the hook splits `mcp__<server>__<tool>` at the first `__` (changed in 0.38); and a built-in name Catervas does not ship is refused with `unknown_connector` at the entry. This release ships one, `playwright`, the Playwright MCP server, a browser confined to the project's preview and the owner's computer (8.3; changed in 0.120; ADR 0067). A connector may also be `source: kit` (added in 0.44; 6.7, ADR 0036): a service of the agent's role's kit, written whole into the team file with the kit's tags as its `tools`, held to every rule of a custom entry, and refused at connect unless it is exactly the kit's. The browser's definition now lives in the Designer's kit. Any agent may have it, and the team builder gives it to the UI/UX Designer; the agent page switches it on and off (F9). A session is given it when its agent has it, its purpose is `explore`, `implement`, or the Designer's design review (5.4), and a preview can open: a preview is set and Docker's sandbox is on and reachable. The Designer's own connector being off takes it from no one else; it counts only where the Designer's assignment and design review are decided (5.4, 6.8). Such a session is registered with `network` added to its tiers (6.7), which a user's server never adds (changed in 0.38). Every tool of the connector is tagged in its pinned list (6.7): the tools that browse, `network`, reach only the preview; every other is `denied`, never offered and also passed to Claude Code as `--disallowedTools`. The hook judges a call to any connector's tool in this order (changed in 0.38, from a built-in connector's): the connector must be the session's (`connector_not_in_session`), the tool tagged (`tool_not_tagged`) and not `denied` (`tool_denied`), and, for a connector confined to the preview, every field named `url`, at any depth of the call's input, a string that is the preview's origin, `http://localhost:<port>`, exactly or followed by `/`, `?`, or `#` (`url_outside_preview`, which a `url` that is not a string gets too), whatever the tool's tag, so a grant never takes a call outside the preview (changed in 0.39, from `network` tools alone); a user's server has no such confinement. An `external_effect` or `paid` call is first held by the Designer's plan gate, which refuses a UI/UX Designer's call before its plan is approved `design_plan_not_approved`, as it refuses a write, and asks nothing (5.2, 6.8); once the checks above pass, a `paid` call is refused `tool_input_too_large` over 64 KiB, allowed with a matching grant, or asked about (above; changed in 0.39, from `external_effect_refused`), and an `external_effect` one runs and is recorded (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061). Nothing else follows: the tier check at `network` no longer runs for a connector's call (changed in 0.38), and the plan gate runs for no other tag. `tool.called` and `tool.denied` record the server and the tag (8.5).

What the hook cannot see (added in 0.8). The hook judges a search by the directory it names, and a protected glob protects files, not the directories they sit in, so a `Grep` or `Glob` over a directory reads a protected file under it without naming it. For those, Catervas relies on Claude Code: each protected path is given to the session as a `permissions.deny` rule `Read(<glob>)`, which Claude Code applies to its reading tools, searches included. That is enforcement by the program Catervas drives, not by Catervas, and it is the residual this rule accepts. The deny rules are built for each session from its agent's rules (changed in 0.136; ADR 0080): `Read(<glob>)` for the agent's protected paths and for Catervas's keys, `.catervas/local/daemon.json` and `.catervas/local/sessions/**`, and `Edit(<glob>)` for its read-only paths and for `.catervas/local/**`. A glob Claude Code cannot be given as a rule still refuses the session, as a protected one does. A finance session's deny list is the team's, with no glob left out: its working directory is the finance folder, and Claude Code reads a `Read(<glob>)` rule relative to the working directory, so `Read(.catervas/local/**)` names nothing it can reach, and the folder's workbooks are read through `catervas_read_sheet` (6.6; changed in 0.62, from a deny list that left the folder out).

### 5.7 Escalation

An escalation is a task state and a message to the user. It carries: the task, the reason, what the agent tried, and the options the agent proposes. There are eleven reasons, written on the wire as `budget`, `sessions`, `iterations`, `blocker_age`, `permission`, `risk_gate`, `approval` (a contract waiting for the user's approval, 5.16; since 0.115 only in an older log, ADR 0061, no contract waiting for the human; the contract's own `high` risk was `risk_gate` instead), `readiness_failures` (a contract that failed the Definition of Ready `policy.readiness_attempts` times, three unless the owner set another, 5.2; changed in 0.136; ADR 0080), `integration` (5.14), `explicit_request`, and `preview` (changed in 0.33 from ten). A `preview` escalation is a preview Catervas could not open for a session that needed it (8.3): a `prepare` that failed or ran past its fifteen minutes, a `start` that never answered, or Docker gone. Its detail is the error and the output's error lines, those that say `error` or `ERR` and are not option help, at most eight, or the last eight lines when none do, without npm's `notice` and `warn` lines (changed in 0.134 and 0.137; ADR 0081; the full 40-line tail stays in the session's log), `preview.stopped` records the reason, and no session starts; the human fixes the commands in Settings and resolves it. Catervas does not retry, since a broken command fails the same way each time. An `integration` escalation is the one that moves nothing: the task it is about is `accepted`, which no row leaves, so it stays there, awaiting integration, with the escalation as a message to the user until they run `catervas integrate` (5.14; added in 0.8). The user resolves it from the board or from the channel. Nothing else on the board waits for an escalation unless it depends on that task. A resolution names the status the task moves to and carries a message: the task moves out of `escalated` as the human asked, and on the move `escalation.resolved` records the status and the message, so a move the governor refuses leaves only its refusal. A resolution never takes a contract awaiting the user's approval to `ready`: approving it does, which records `human.accepted` of the contract and then moves it, so that a move the governor refuses leaves the approval on a contract still awaiting it. Nor does it take to `ready` an epic whose contract the user has not approved, one escalated for failing the Definition of Ready three times among them: that epic goes back to `refining`, and once its contract passes it waits for the approval (5.16 item 2). More tries (added in 0.25; ADR 0024). A resolution of an `iterations` escalation may carry `extra_tries`, from 1 to 5, recorded on `escalation.resolved`; on any other reason, or with a move to any status but `in_progress`, since more tries resume the work, it is refused with `extra_tries_only_for_tries` (the move added in 0.25's landing review), and a value outside 1 to 5 as invalid. The task's limit becomes the iteration limit plus the sum of its granted tries, and the resolve raises `iteration` by one, so the resumed attempt is counted and N more tries mean N more attempts; a resolution without `extra_tries` leaves `iteration` alone. The task's session limit grows by four for each try granted. The `integration` escalation moves no status: its one choice is to open the pull request again with `task_integrate` (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062; Catervas never merges, ADR 0061, 5.14). A `budget` or `sessions` escalation resolved to a working status while the task's dollars or sessions are still spent is raised again on the next tick, which is how Catervas says the budget is still spent: the user gives a task room with `extra_room` (below; changed in 0.116; ADR 0062), or by raising its `max_cost_usd` or `max_sessions`, a change to its content, which sends it back to `refining` (5.11; added in 0.13). Outside an escalation the user moves a task from any other status with a reason, which the move records, and which out of `blocked` is also the blocker's resolution and into `escalated` the escalation's words (added in 0.8).

**Choices (added in 0.116; ADR 0062).** Every escalation a user can answer lists named choices, and the web app (4.2) and the command line read one list, `escalation.choices { task_id }`, built once in `catervas_runtime::choices`. A choice is `{ label, next, suggested, kind, body?, path? }`: `label` is the button's words; `next` says in plain words what happens next, naming the agent that holds the task (`{who}`, its display name on the board when the list is read, else "The team") and the Product Manager (`{pm}`, the active one's display name, else "The Product Manager"); `suggested` is true for exactly one choice, the first; `kind` is `command`, with `body` the command to send (`escalation_resolve`, or `task_integrate`), or `open`, with `path`, a page of the web app to go to, which sends nothing. No two choices send the same command. The list, suggested first, by reason (`before` being the status the task left for `escalated`, in lower case, and `Cancel` the choice "Cancel the task", a resolve to `cancelled`: "{id} stops for good. Its branch is kept, and nothing is merged."):
- `iterations`: "Give 2 more tries" (to `in_progress` with `extra_tries` 2: "{who} picks up {id} again with 2 more tries."), "Ask {pm} to change the plan" (to `refining`: "{pm} rewrites the plan of {id}; it is assigned again once it is ready."), Cancel.
- `budget` and `sessions`: "Give it more room" (to `before` with `extra_room`: "{who} carries on with {id}, with up to {n} more sessions and ${x} more to spend.", `{n}` and `{x}` the contract's `max_sessions` and `max_cost_usd`; offered only when `before` is known), Cancel. Asking the Product Manager to change the plan is not offered: a resolve while the task is still spent is escalated again on the next tick (below).
- `blocker_age`, for an escalation of a blocked task: the three choices of a blocked task below; otherwise "Answer and carry on" (to `in_progress`: "{who} reads your answer and carries on with {id}."), "Change the plan" (to `refining`, the words of the second choice above), Cancel (changed in 0.122; ADR 0069).
- `permission` and `explicit_request`: "Carry on" (to `before`: "{id} goes back to {before} and {who} is told what you wrote."; only when `before` is known and is neither `refining` nor `escalated`), "Change the plan", Cancel.
- `readiness_failures`: "Ask {pm} to try the plan again" (to `refining`: "{pm} writes the plan of {id} again with your note."), Cancel.
- `approval` and `risk_gate`, only in a log made before ADR 0061 that left one open: "Review the plan" (`open`, `/tasks/{id}/plan`: "You read the plan of {id} and approve it or send it back."), Cancel.
- `integration`: "Open the pull request again" (`task_integrate`: "Catervas pushes the branch of {id} and opens its pull request again, for you to merge."), alone, since an accepted task cannot be cancelled (5.2).
- `preview`: "Fix how your app opens" (`open`, `/settings/your-app`: "You tell Catervas in Settings how to start your app; then come back to {id} and choose Carry on."), "Carry on" (to `before`: "{id} goes back to {before} and {who} opens your app again."), Cancel.
- Any other reason: "Change the plan" and Cancel.
- A blocked task (added in 0.121; ADR 0068), with no escalation open: its reason is `blocked`; "Answer and carry on" (back where the block came from, changed in 0.122; ADR 0069: to `verifying` for a reviewer's block, `refining` for the Product Manager's, `in_progress` for the assignee's; "{who} reads your answer and carries on with {id}."), "Ask {pm} to change the plan" (to `refining`, the refine session told the blocker's words, unless the block came from `refining`), Cancel. {who} is the agent that blocked the task, not its assignee: Today's line "{agent} is stuck: …" names it too. Every task in `blocked` is listed in "Waiting on you" (`waiting.list`) as a `help` row, "{agent} is stuck: {the blocker's description}". `escalation_resolve` and `catervas resolve` accept it as they accept an escalation, with no `extra_tries` or `extra_room`. The message is the move's blocker resolution and, recorded as `escalation.resolved`, reaches the next session. The task page shows the blocker's words with the same choice.

Answering a block (changed in 0.134; ADR 0079). An answer needs words. The web app's help page refuses "Answer and carry on" and "Ask {pm} to change the plan" without a note and no longer sends the button's own label as the answer; Cancel needs none, and neither do "Give it more room" and "Give it more tries" (changed after the live run), which send their label when the note is empty. The page's heading ("{who} needs your help with ..."), the explanation ("{who}, your {role}, explains what happened") and "What {who} tried" name {who} as the note's label does. The note's label names {who}, the agent who raised the block, so that a reviewer's block is answered to the reviewer. A block is also answered from the channel: a human message that mentions the assignee of a task blocked on the human and writes that task's id (as written, `CTV-<n>`) resolves the block as "Answer and carry on" with the message as the note, back where the block came from; a resolution the governor refuses is ignored and the message stands as an ordinary one. Before each `implement` session on a task whose worktree exists, and after the tidy (5.2), and (changed after the live run) before each `verify` session of a task's reviewer, Catervas fetches the integration branch and, when the task's branch lacks commits of it, merges it into the worktree with the message `chore: bring up to date with <branch>`, so that a file the owner or another task put on the integration branch is there when the agent looks for it. A merge that conflicts is aborted, the session starts as before, and its prompt (the implement or the verify prompt) says the branch is behind the integration branch and conflicts. No event records it: the merge commit is the record, and the prompt says the branch may start on a commit the agent did not make. The owner's answers stay with the task for its whole try: a session's first message also carries, under "The owner's answers on this task:", the owner's answers to the task's blocks and escalations (`escalation.resolved` with `resolved_by: human`) since the task last entered `in_progress` from `assigned` or `ready`, the newest three, oldest first, besides those given after the session before it.
`task.tries` (changed in 0.137; ADR 0081) answers `{ try, of, sessions, max_sessions }`: `sessions` and `max_sessions` are the task's sessions and its allowance as the budget counts them (5.5), the extra room granted included. The web app's help page of a `sessions` or `budget` escalation shows "Sessions 6 of 6" in "About this task" in place of the tries.

`escalation.choices` answers `{ choices: [] }` for a task with no open escalation and not blocked; the open `integration` escalation of an accepted task is one. More room: a resolution of a `budget` or `sessions` escalation may carry `extra_room` (`escalation_resolve`'s boolean, `catervas resolve --extra-room`), and Catervas first records `task.room_granted { sessions, cost_usd, granted_by }` on the task, `sessions` the contract's `max_sessions` and `cost_usd` its `max_cost_usd`, then moves the task as any resolve does; a task's caps are the contract's plus the sum of its grants (5.5), so the contract file is not changed. It is refused `extra_room_only_for_spent` on any other reason and `extra_room_or_extra_tries` when `extra_tries` is also given. `catervas resolve` takes `--extra-tries <n>` (1 to 5) and `--extra-room` before the message, and not both.

The Scrum Master is responsible for making sure escalations do not pile up silently (changed in 0.15). Its review (5.9), the Product Manager's when the team has no active Scrum Master, is given a digest in its first message and posts it in the review thread: every open escalation with its task, title, reason, detail, and the hours it has waited, and every daily budget spent since the delivery started (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062). An open escalation is a task in `escalated`, with the reason and detail of its last `escalation.raised`, waiting since then, or an `accepted` task whose last `integration` escalation since it was accepted has no `task.integrated` after it. An escalation left waiting past the team policy `escalation_age_hours`, from 1 to 720, default 24, is aged once: Catervas records `escalation.aged` with the hours it has waited, rounded down, and posts the system line `<task> has waited <hours> hours on the human: <reason>`, which mentions no one. One escalation is aged per tick, the oldest first, and only in `catervas run` in a tick about no one task, after the channel's conversation rule. Aging happens only while something ticks: `catervas run` ends when the board is idle, so an escalation that ages while no process drives the project is said on the next run. A new escalation of the same task is aged again. The web app's notification of it comes with phase 14, and the desktop app's with phase 18 (changed in 0.18, from the desktop app's in phase 6, and in 0.20; renumbered in 0.24 and by ADRs 0025 and 0029).

Questions (added in 0.2). An agent that needs an answer from the human before it can continue, a Product Manager refining a contract most often, asks it through the `catervas_ask_human` tool. The session ends, the task keeps its status and is shown as waiting on the human, the question appears on the board and in the channel, and the human's answer starts the next session with the answer in its prompt. A question is not an escalation: nothing has gone wrong, and the answer is context, not a state decision. Escalations that carry a message from the human work the same way: the next session for that task starts with the message. A question is answered once, by the sequence number of its `question.asked`; the answer is recorded as `question.answered` with the question's task, and a task is shown as waiting on the human while any question about it is unanswered. The next session about a task is given, as the human's message, every answer (each after its question, which is marked as the asking agent's words), every resolution's message, and every acceptance's words recorded on the task since the last session about it started, in the order they were given (added in 0.8).

A connector's call that waits for the human (added in 0.39; ADR 0031). A `paid` connector call with no grant (5.6) waits as a question does (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: an `external_effect` one runs without asking), and is not an escalation either: the session ends (8.2), the task keeps its status, does not raise its `iteration`, raises no escalation, and counts the session towards `max_sessions` as any session counts. While the approval waits, the asking agent's line in `team.activity` and the team band reads "Waiting on you: may <agent name> use <server>?" (changed in 0.39). The task's projection holds `open_approvals` beside `open_questions`, raised by `tool_approval.requested` and lowered by `tool_approval.granted` or `tool_approval.refused`, and the task waits on the human while either is above zero, so the orchestrator starts no session for it and the board marks it "Waiting on you" (F3). The human answers with the command `tool_approve { approval, note? }`, which allows that one call, or `tool_refuse { approval, note? }`, by the approval's id, the sequence number of its `tool_approval.requested`; each records `tool_approval.granted` or `tool_approval.refused { approval, note? }` on the request's task with no agent or session, `note` absent when none was given, and says "Allowed <tool> once for <agent> (approval <n>)." or "Not allowed: <tool> for <agent> (approval <n>).", `<agent>` the asking agent's id, and on a second line "Input: <the call's whole input, as it was recorded>", so that a terminal decides with the input in front of it (8.6; changed in 0.39). The check that no decision exists and the write of the decision are one step under one lock, so two decisions at once (a browser tab and a command) let exactly one through, `open_approvals` is lowered once for it, and the other is refused `approval_decided`. A seq that is no `tool_approval.requested` is refused `unknown_approval`, and a second decision on one approval, either way, `approval_decided`. Only the asking agent's next session about the task is told the decision, as the human's message, beside what the paragraph above gives it: each decision on a call it asked about since its own last session about the task started, "You may call `mcp__<server>__<tool>` once, with exactly the input you asked for (approval <n>), which is this, your own words quoted, never cut:" and then that input, the canonical JSON the grant's hash covers, in an `untrusted` block as a question is quoted (8.6), because the session starts fresh and a call whose input differs by a word asks again, with "The human adds: <note>" after it when there is a note (changed in 0.39); or "The human did not allow `mcp__<server>__<tool>` (approval <n>).", with the human's note after a colon in place of the full stop. Another agent's session about the task is not told.

A marketing plan that waits for the owner (added in 0.55; ADR 0042). A plan the Marketing Specialist proposes (6.5) that has money in it waits as a question does (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: a plan whose total budget and every channel's and campaign's budget are zero is approved by Catervas at once, `marketing_plan.approved` with no agent and no session and the note "Catervas approved it: it spends nothing (ADR 0061).", and holds nothing), and is not an escalation either: the session ends, the task keeps its status, and the task's projection holds `open_plans` beside `open_questions` and `open_approvals`, raised by `marketing_plan.proposed` and lowered by `marketing_plan.approved` or `marketing_plan.returned`. The task waits on the human while any of the three is above zero, so the orchestrator starts no session for it, the rules that act on a task pass it over, and the board marks it "Waiting on you" (F3). Its assignee cannot hand it in meanwhile: while the plan is proposed, `catervas_request_transition` refuses the move to `verifying` with `marketing_plan_waiting: MP-<n> waits for the owner; end your turn`, and nothing is recorded. The owner decides on Today or with `catervas marketing plan` (6.5). The next session about the task is told, as the human's message, each decision on its plans since the last session started: "The owner approved your marketing plan MP-<n>." with "The owner adds: <note>" after it when there is a note, or "The owner sent back your marketing plan MP-<n>: <reason>", the reason exactly as the owner wrote it and not in an `untrusted` block, since it is the human's own words (ADR 0011) and the agent is to answer it. A decision whose envelope names an agent or a session is not the owner's and is not told.

A change to a document the owner approved waited for the owner (added in 0.94; not any more since 0.115, ADR 0061, as the paragraph's end says; ADR 0051; phase 8 step 03). `catervas_write_folder_doc` (5.17) proposes a change to the product's `spec` or `roadmap` at a delivery's review as `folder_doc.proposed`, whose sequence number is the proposal's number. It is neither a question nor an escalation and it holds no task: the proposal is about no task, nothing waits on it, no task projection counts it, and the session ends as any ceremony's. A newer proposal of the same path replaces an older one still waiting, with no event of its own. The owner decides the proposals of one card, all of one agent's, with `folder_doc_decide { proposals, decision: approve | return, note? }`, on `POST /command` behind the daemon's token or the browser's `command` behind its cookie: `proposals` holds 1 to 20 distinct numbers, `note` at most 600 characters, required for `return` and optional for `approve`. Only the owner decides, under `ask` and `auto` alike (ADR 0041), and a proposal whose agent was paused or retired since may still be decided. The decision is all or nothing, made under the integration lock with the log read again first, and refused `folder_doc_proposals` (none, over 20, or one twice), `folder_doc_note_too_long`, `folder_doc_reason_needed`, `unknown_folder_doc`, `folder_doc_decided`, `folder_doc_superseded`, `folder_doc_mixed` (two agents' proposals) and, for an approval, `folder_doc_busy`, `folder_doc_link` and `folder_doc_waiting` (5.14). An approval makes one folder change of both files of each proposal, the path with its `text` and its twin with its `agent_text`, authored for the proposing agent (its id when it has left the team), and records `folder_doc.approved { proposals, change?, sha?, note? }`, `change` and `sha` absent when the files already said it all and nothing was made; its answer says what the team's policy does next (5.17). A return makes nothing and records `folder_doc.returned { proposals, reason }`. Neither event carries an agent, a session or a task, and a decision recorded with one counts for nothing, as for a marketing plan's. The owner's words reach the agent at its next review (5.9), not wrapped as untrusted text, as a returned marketing plan's reach its task. Today's card for the proposals (added in 0.95; phase 8 step 03b). `folder_doc_proposals.list {}` answers `{ integration, cards }`, `integration` the team's policy (`pull_request` since 0.115, whatever the file says) and `cards` one for each review and agent, made from the proposals still waiting and ordered by the first proposal of each: `{ <the review's key, 8.5>, agent_id, summary, documents }`, `summary` the card's summaries in proposal order joined by one space and `documents` its proposals in order, each `{ proposal, path, lines }`. `lines` are the document's changed lines (`changed_lines` in `catervas-core`), between the integration branch's file, empty when git has none, and the proposed text, each `{ change: same | added | removed, text }`: a trailing `\r` and blank lines are left out, the middle is compared by longest common subsequence, each run of changes lists its removed lines before its added ones, and what is shown is every changed line, the unchanged line just before and just after each run and the nearest unchanged line starting with `#` above it. A middle whose two lengths multiply past 1,000,000 is not compared but shown whole, every old line removed and every new one added. A proposal is not a row of `waiting.list`, which is about a task. Today shows each card after the waiting rows, counted with them, as "Product plan changes to approve": the agent's picture, "From <name>, after the team's review", the summary, "Lines marked + are added; lines marked − are removed.", and each document under its name ("Roadmap", "Product description", else its path) with its lines, a heading without its `#`s, a bullet without its mark, an added line marked + and a removed one −, each also read out as "Added: " or "Removed: ", or "Only the version for the team changes." when only its twin changes; then "Notes for <name>" ("(needed to send it back)"), "Approve" and "Send back". "Approve" sends `folder_doc_decide` with every proposal of the card, the note trimmed and left out when empty; "Send back" with blank notes sends nothing and says "Write what <name> should change first.". Beside the buttons a note says what approving does: "Nothing changes until you approve. Then Catervas opens a pull request, and the change is in your project once it is merged." (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: the sentences for `auto_merge` and `manual` are gone). A refusal shows in words. The agent's line in the team band is "Waiting on you: product plan changes" while it has a proposal waiting and no waiting row of a task, and "What moved since yesterday" says "<name> proposed a change to the product plan at the team's review.", or "<name> proposed <k> changes to the product plan at the team's review." for <k> distinct documents, at the latest proposal's time. "Open in Files" on the card is step 04b's. Since 0.115 (ADR 0061) nothing is proposed any more: `catervas_write_folder_doc` lands a change to the spec or the roadmap at the review as one folder change of both files like any other document (5.17), and the card and the command stay only for the proposals an older log holds.

A post outside the plan goes out like one inside it (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061; from 0.57 it waited for the owner's yes as `social_post.requested`). A post the Marketing Specialist writes with no slot (6.5), or with no active plan, is recorded `social_post.scheduled { approved_by: "catervas" }` at once, at least three hours ahead (`post_too_soon` otherwise), and shown on Today with a Stop as a planned post is; it is no question and no escalation and it holds no task, the session going on and the task keeping its status. `social_post.requested` is never written again and `social_post_decide` stays for open requests. The agent is told of it in its next `implement` session's message, after the rest, from its previous session on: each of its posts missed or failed, which the owner could not save, with the reason as untrusted text, each the owner declined, with their note as their own words, and each the owner stopped (6.5). Posts go out between sessions: the hand-over is a rule with no model that runs on a tick, and a session runs to its end before the next tick, so a post can be handed over late by one running session, and a session limit over 55 minutes (`max_wall_clock_seconds`) can make one missed.

A site the Procurement Specialist asked to read (added in 0.71; ADR 0039) no longer waits for the owner (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061): `catervas_request_sites` is gone with the approved sites (5.6), `site.requested` in an older log still loads, and its row on Today, `catervas site approve` and `decline`, and the agent's line "Waiting on you: may <agent name> read <host>?" are gone. The task's projection no longer counts `open_sites`.

A purchase order that waits for the owner (added in 0.74; ADR 0039's amendment of 2026-10-07, "suggest, then track"; phase 7 step 10c). An order the Procurement Specialist drafts with `catervas_draft_purchase_order` (6.10) is recorded `purchase_order.drafted` and waits for the owner as a post outside the plan does: it is neither a question nor an escalation, and it holds no task.
