The session goes on, the task keeps its status and may be handed in, and no task projection counts the order, so the board does not mark the task "Waiting on you" for it. `waiting.list` gives one row of kind `purchase_order` for each order drafted and not yet decided, after the marketing plans, with `task_id`, `agent_id`, `title` (its task's) and `line`, which reads "<agent name> set up an order from <seller>: <total> <currency>", and `order` (its number, the n of PO-n), `seller`, `seller_contact`, `lines` (each `item`, `quantity`, `unit`, `unit_price` and `line_total`), `currency`, `period`, `total` (two decimals), `delivery`, `terms`, `url` (the seller's page exactly as the agent wrote it, or empty), `host` (the site that address names, in its ASCII form, absent with no `url`), `evaluation`, `why`, `at` (when it was drafted) and `expires_at` (when Catervas closes it by itself, 6.10); every text in it is the agent's own and untrusted (8.6). While it waits, the agent's line in `team.activity` reads "Waiting on you: <the row's line>". Today shows it as a row of its own: each line with its amounts and currency (the first five, then how many more), the total and its period, the seller's contact, delivery and terms, the seller's page with its host in bold and the address as text beside a link that opens in a tab that cannot reach the page, why in a frame that says whose words they are, "Read the comparison" (the evaluation note, read when it is opened and shown as text in the same frame), "Download PO-<n>.xlsx", the day it closes by itself, and "Approve, I'll place it myself" and "Reject", each asking for an optional note the agent reads with `catervas_read_purchase_orders`. Approving places nothing and pays nothing: the owner places the order and pays for it themselves, then marks it placed (6.10). The owner decides with `purchase_order_decide { order, decision, note? }`, `decision` `approve` or `reject`, or `catervas order approve <n>` and `catervas order reject <n>`; the check that nothing decided the order yet and the write of the decision are one step under one lock, so that two decisions at once let one through and the other is refused `purchase_order_decided`. A number that is no drafted order is `unknown_purchase_order`, an order Catervas closed by itself `purchase_order_expired`, a received or closed one `purchase_order_ended`, and a note over 600 characters `purchase_order_note_too_long`. Only the daemon's token on `POST /command` and the browser's session on its command carry the decision, under `ask` and `auto` alike (ADR 0041): no agent's session reaches them, and `purchase_order.approved` and `rejected` count only from an event whose envelope names no agent and no session. An order not decided within 30 days of its drafting is closed by Catervas (6.10).

Messages to sellers and their replies (added in 0.77; ADR 0039; phase 7 step 10f). A message the Procurement Specialist drafted (`seller_message.drafted`, 6.10) and a reply from a seller (`seller_reply.received`) wait for the owner in Today's own sections, "Messages to sellers" and "Replies from sellers", and are neither a question nor an escalation nor a row of `waiting.list`, so the board marks no task "Waiting on you" for them and `team.activity` says nothing of them. An order's message is not in the first section: it is the `send` of its order's row, which gains `{ message, to, domain, new_domain, subject, body }` while its message waits, and Today offers "Approve and send to <seller>" beside "Approve, I'll place it myself" when the mailbox is connected and fewer than 50 messages have gone today.

A data pipeline that waits for the owner (added in 0.76; phase 7 step 10e). A request that Catervas escalates, on the request itself and with no agent and no session on the envelope, because it costs money, its cost is not known or it sends the project's data to another service (6.10; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: the Product Manager no longer decides a data source, and a free source that sends nothing out is filed at once), waits for the owner as a purchase order does: it is neither a question nor an escalation of a task and it holds no task. The task keeps its status and its assignee may hand it in, and no task projection counts the request. `waiting.list` gives one row of kind `data_pipeline` for each escalated request not yet decided, after the purchase orders, with `task_id`, `agent_id`, `title` (its task's) and `line`, which reads "<agent name> asks for a data source: <name>", and `pipeline` (its number), `name`, `what`, `url`, `host` (the address's site in its ASCII form), `why`, `cost`, `needs_account`, `sends_project_data`, `reason` (Catervas's: "It costs money, or its cost is not known, so you decide (ADR 0061).", or, for a free source that sends your project's data out, "It sends your project's data to another service, so you decide (ADR 0061)."; an older log's is the Product Manager's), `at` and `request_text` (the text the request would be filed with). The agent's activity line reads "Waiting on you: <line>", and a run's end lists it with `catervas pipeline approve <n>, or catervas pipeline decline <n>`. The owner decides with `data_pipeline_decide { pipeline, decision: "approve" | "decline", note? }` (changed in 0.76 after review), a note of at most 600 characters (`pipeline_note_too_long`), refused `pipeline_not_escalated` for a request that was not escalated, `pipeline_decided` for one decided and `unknown_pipeline` for a number that is none; the decision names no agent and no session, and approving files the request (5.16).

A marketing plan's ads and their budget (added in 0.72; ADR 0042; phase 7 step 08g). What Catervas did, or could not do, with a plan's ads is not an escalation and holds no task. `waiting.list` gives one row for each plan, ahead of every other row since it is the owner's money, with `task_id` the plan's proposing task, `agent_id` its proposer, `plan`, `plan_title`, `ends_on`, `currency` and amounts as decimal strings; the page words each one from these fields, with Catervas's picture, the plan's title and a campaign's name as text. By precedence, one kind for a plan: `marketing_budget`, for the active plan with a `marketing_budget.reached` recorded, until the plan ends, titled "Ads budget reached: <plan>", with `google_ads` (the plan's Google Ads budget), `spent` (its spend as last read, else as its caps recorded it), `read_at` (when it was read, when it was), `cap` (the budget the row's words are about: the newest, or, when an older cap's pause was refused and a campaign of it has no pause recorded since, that one, with `reason`, Google's words or Catervas's own when no sign-in could be used), `caps` (every budget reached, oldest first, each `{ scope, key?, name?, spent, budget }`), `campaigns` (each of the plan's, `{ key, name, budget, spent }`) and `raising` (the task of the owner's open request for a new version); it says "Its ads reached their budget: <spent> of <budget> <currency>. Catervas paused them." ("Its campaign <name> reached its budget: … Catervas paused it." at a campaign's), or, while a campaign of that cap is unpaused, "… Catervas could not pause them: <reason> Catervas tries again every 15 minutes; pause them in Google Ads.", with the facts "Google Ads: <spent> of <google_ads> <currency> spent" and "Ends <ends_on>", and offers "Raise the budget" (not while a raise is open, when the line adds "You asked <agent> for a new version with a raised budget. It waits for you here when it is ready."), "End the plan" (the End question of the plan's page, 6.5) and, when Catervas could not pause, "Open Google Ads" (ads.google.com, in a new tab). `marketing_ads_running`, for a plan whose ads Catervas could not pause when it ended or when Google Ads was removed (a plan with a `marketing_budget` row has it folded into that row), titled "Ads still running: <plan>": "Catervas could not pause its ads: <reason> They keep running at Google until <ends_on> or their budget there. Pause them in Google Ads." `marketing_spend_unread`, for the active plan whose last read failed, titled "Can't read the ad spend: <plan>": "Catervas can't read its ad spend: <reason> Any of its ads still running keep running at Google until <ends_on> or their budget there; pause them in Google Ads.", with "Last read <when>: <spent> of <google_ads> <currency>" once a read worked. The last two offer "Open Google Ads" and nothing to decide. The reason is Google's words as `Google answered “<words>”`, or Catervas's own sentence when no sign-in could be used ("<agent>'s sign-in to Google has ended; sign <agent> in again on <agent>'s page", "no Marketing Specialist on the team has Google Ads connected"), cut at 300 characters. What the watch read and could not pause is kept in memory, so a restart forgets it, but not the warning: an ended plan's pause is tried again at the watch's first wake and the active plan's read fails while no connection is left, so one of the rows says it again within a minute. A row of a kind the page does not know is skipped.

The user answers, approves, accepts, and resolves from any terminal, while a process drives the project or not (section 3, ADR 0014), and from the web and desktop apps. Every approval and acceptance the user is asked for shows the plain-language summary written by the agent that asks, the diff, and Catervas's check results, as 5.4 says of a human gate (added in 0.18). While the team is paused because the provider refused the key (5.5), Today's list of what waits on the user starts with one row, "Your AI account's key was refused", with "The team is paused until you sign in again.", which links to Settings to sign in again (added in 0.30; changed in 0.141). The chats' line for an agent that cannot answer says the same and links to Settings. A design review that cannot start (5.4) is listed there too (added in 0.33): with no preview set, "Tell Catervas how to open your app", which opens Settings at "How to open your app"; and while the Designer cannot open the app, "<name> needs Docker's sandbox", with the words "The UI/UX Designer needs Docker's sandbox to open your app. Turn the sandbox on, or retire the Designer.", which opens the Team page; and while the Designer has its Playwright connector off, "<name>'s browser is off", with the words "<name> opens your app with Playwright. Turn Playwright on for <name> on the Team page; until then <name> takes no work, and nobody checks the screens <Developer> builds.", which opens that Designer's page on the Team page (`designer_needs_browser`, added in the step's fix wave). A connector's call waiting for the human is listed there too (added in 0.39): `waiting.list` gives it a row of kind `tool_approval` carrying `approval`, `server`, `tool` and the whole `input`, which reads "<agent name> wants to use <server>", then "To <tool, its underscores as spaces>, for <task> <title>. <agent name> waits until you decide.", and offers "Review", which opens `ToolApproval` (F9). A post outside the plan waiting for the owner is listed there too (added in 0.57): `waiting.list` gives it a row of kind `social_post` carrying `post`, `channel`, `text`, `media` and `at`, which reads "<agent name> wants to post on <Network>", after the marketing plans, and Today shows it with the post's words and pictures, "Post it" and "Don't post"; the agent's activity line is "Waiting on you: may <agent name> post on <Network>?". A site a Procurement Specialist asks to read is listed there too (added in 0.71): `waiting.list` gives it a row of kind `site_request` carrying `request`, `host`, `url` and `why`, which reads "<agent name> asks to read <host>", after the posts outside the plan, and Today shows it with the site, the page as text and never a link, the reason as the agent's own words in a frame that says so, a warning for a name written in another alphabet, and "Allow" and "Don't allow", each asking for an optional note. A purchase order the Procurement Specialist drafted is listed there too (added in 0.74): `waiting.list` gives it a row of kind `purchase_order`, after the site requests, which reads "<agent name> set up an order from <seller>: <total> <currency>", and Today shows it as the paragraph on a purchase order above says. A marketing plan waiting for the owner is listed there too (added in 0.55): `waiting.list` gives it a row of kind `marketing_plan` carrying `plan`, `summary`, `total`, `currency`, `starts_on` and `ends_on`, which reads "<agent name> proposes a marketing plan: <title>", the plan's own title, after the connector calls and before the approvals, and offers "Review", which opens the plan's page (6.5). When a process driving the project ends, it says what waits on the user, in this order and by task: each unanswered question with the command that answers it; each connector call waiting for the human, "<task> waits: <agent name> wants to use <server>: catervas tool approve <n>, or catervas tool refuse <n>" and, on the next line, "  input: <the call's whole input>" (added in 0.39; the input line with `--json` is an `input` field); each marketing plan waiting for the owner, "<task> waits: <agent name> proposes a marketing plan: <title>: catervas marketing plan approve <plan>, or catervas marketing plan return <plan> --reason <text>", with `--json` a `plan` field (added in 0.55); each post outside the plan waiting for the owner, "<task> waits: <agent name> wants to post on <Network>: catervas marketing post send <n>, or catervas marketing post decline <n>", with `--json` a `post` field (added in 0.57); each site waiting for the owner, "<task> waits: <agent name> asks to read <host>: catervas site approve <n>, or catervas site decline <n>", with `--json` a `request` field (added in 0.71); each purchase order waiting for the owner, "<task> waits: <agent name> set up an order from <seller>: <total> <currency>: catervas order approve <n>, or catervas order reject <n>", with `--json` an `order` field (added in 0.74); each contract awaiting approval in an older log; each other escalation with its last reason and, under it, one line for each of its choices (above; changed in 0.116); each `verifying` result that waits for the user's acceptance (a code task's `human` criterion, or an older epic; changed in 0.115; ADR 0061); and each accepted task waiting to be merged (added in 0.8; under every team file since 0.115). A choice's line is two spaces, the command that makes it, two spaces, `# `, what happens next, and ` (suggested)` after the suggested one's: `catervas resolve <task> <status> [--extra-tries <n> | --extra-room] "<your message>"`, `catervas integrate <task>`, or `in the web app: <path>` for a choice that opens a page; with `--json` the item gains `choices`, a list of `{ command, next, suggested }` (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062). Today's "What moved since yesterday" shows the moves newest first as cards, each with the picture, name and time of whoever made it, three at first, and "Show more" adds the next three; `moved.since` gives each move's `by`: `human`, `catervas`, or another actor id (added in 0.88).

**Autopilot: the team decides (added in 0.138; ADR 0082).** While autopilot is on (5.12) and the team has an active Product Manager or is one agent alone, no question and no escalation reaches the owner; with neither, nothing changes and the owner decides. (1) `catervas_ask_human` is offered to no session, and every agent but the Product Manager and a solo agent is offered `catervas_ask_team { question (1 to 2000 characters), about: product | technical }`: the task waits as it waits for the owner and the agent is freed, `team.question_asked` is recorded, and a `decide` session of the Product Manager (`product`), or of the Architect (`technical`, the Product Manager when the team has none or the asker is the Architect), answers with `catervas_answer_question { question_seq, answer }`, recorded as `team.question_answered`; the answer resumes the task as the owner's does. The Product Manager's own questions, and a solo agent's, are not asked: the prompt says to decide, write the decision and its reason in the task's notes and go on. (2) Every open escalation, and every block that has stood an hour, gets a `decide` session of the Product Manager whose only acting tool is `catervas_decide { task_id, choice, reason }`, recorded as `team.decided`. The choices are the owner's own for that reason, under the same names, and `flag` is always the last: `more_tries` and `more_room` (at most three of the two together per task, after which only `back_to_plan`, `cancel` and `flag` are offered for `iterations`, `budget` and `sessions`), `back_to_plan`, `try_readiness_again`, `reopen_integration` (at most three per task), `answer_block` (with the answer), `cancel`, `approve_plan` and `accept_result` (5.4, 5.16), `carry_on` after a `permission`, `explicit_request` or `preview` escalation when the task came from another status than `refining`, and `retry_folder_change` (5.14). "Fix how your app opens" is a Settings change and has no choice: the Product Manager flags it. (3) `flag { needs }` is for what only the owner can give: a sign-in, a key, a connector to connect, a confirmation of a cloned skill's or connector's hash, a purchase to place, a legal or account step, money above the day's limit. The task stays where it is, `task.flagged { needs, flagged_by }` is recorded, and a flagged task gets no session while autopilot is on, so the agent takes other work; Today lists it under "Flagged by the team" (4.2). When the owner acts on it, or turns autopilot off, the task resumes as it does without autopilot. Catervas flags a wait itself (`flagged_by: catervas`) when three `decide` sessions about it decided nothing, and flags a task whose agent kept calling a paid tool (8.6). (4) Rule 4 and the aged rule leave the team's waits alone: an escalation does not age while the team decides. Turning autopilot off puts every wait back on the owner, who may also answer a team question at any time; what was decided stays decided.

### 5.8 Memory

Three memories, all files in `.catervas/`. Files under `.catervas/` change only through Catervas's tools, never through a task's commit: the Definition of Ready refuses a contract whose allowed paths reach there (5.3) and the Definition of Done a diff that changes a path there (5.4), for every role, the Finance Specialist's own `.catervas/local/finance/` excepted (6.6; changed in 0.21) (added in 0.17).

- `decisions/` holds architecture decision records and product decisions, written by the Architect and PM, one file each, immutable once written (changed in 0.16, from "once accepted": nothing accepts a decision). A decision is written only through `catervas_write_decision { title, text }`, a tool of the read tier that refuses anyone but the Architect and the Product Manager with `decision_refused: only the Architect and the Product Manager write decisions`. Its title is 1 to 120 characters once trimmed, on one line with no control characters, and its text 1 to 32,000 characters and not blank; anything else is refused with `decision_refused`. It is numbered one past the highest number among the decision files, in four digits, and a project that has 9999 is refused. Its file is `decisions/<NNNN>-<slug>.md`. The slug is the title in lower case, with each run of characters other than `a-z` and `0-9` turned into one `-`, trimmed of `-`, cut at 60 characters and trimmed again, or `decision` when nothing is left. The file holds `# <NNNN>. <title>`, a blank line, `Date: <UTC date>`, `By: <agent id>`, a blank line, and then the text. The file is written under a temporary name and then hard-linked to its own name, which fails when that name exists, so a crash never leaves a half-written decision and no decision is written over. When another writer took the number first, whatever title it gave, the tool tries the next number, three times at most, and then refuses. No tool edits a decision. Each decision is recorded as `decision.written`. Every agent reads the decisions through `catervas_read_decisions { number? }`, a tool of the read tier offered wherever `catervas_read_rules` is. With no number it answers every decision's number, title, date, and author, oldest first; with a number it answers that decision's whole file; an unknown number is refused with `no_such_decision: <n>`. It is a tool rather than the file tools because the decisions live in the project's own checkout, which a task's worktree is not (5.14). A file named `NNNN-<slug>.md` in that form and written by hand is listed too: its title comes from its `# ` heading, else its slug, and its date and author from its `Date:` and `By:` lines when it has them. Any other file there is ignored (added in 0.16).
- `agents/<name>/memory.md` is the agent's own notebook. It is included in every session for that agent. The agent may edit it. It is capped at a size (default 8k tokens) and the agent is told to prune. The agent writes it only through `catervas_write_memory { text }`, which replaces the whole notebook; an empty text empties it. The tool is of the read tier and offered in every session but the one given one tool alone, triage (added in 0.16; the judgment's session of 0.10 is gone, 0.115). The cap is the team policy `memory_cap_tokens`, from 500 to 16,000, default 8,000. A text's tokens are a quarter of its characters, rounded up, which is also how the channel summary is measured (5.9). A text past the cap is refused with `memory_refused: <n> tokens is past your cap of <cap>; prune it`, and nothing is written or recorded. A write is recorded as `memory.written` with the whole text (added in 0.16). Every session's prompt says how full the notebook is, as `<n> of <cap> tokens.`, a line Catervas writes outside the notebook's `untrusted` block. When `n` is past 80 percent of the cap and the session can call `catervas_write_memory`, the line goes on: `Prune it with catervas_write_memory before it reaches the cap.` The prompt cuts the notebook at four characters for each token of the cap, never splitting a character, so a notebook within its cap is never cut (8.2; added in 0.16).
- `team/retro.md` accumulates retrospective learnings. Appended after each delivery by whoever runs the retro ceremony: the Scrum Master, or the Product Manager on a team with no active one (changed in 0.17). It is written only by the retro ceremony (5.9), with `catervas_append_retro`, once per delivery whichever session asks: a text that is not blank and holds at most 4,000 characters, appended under a heading `## D<n> (<date>)`, the latest closed delivery's id and the UTC date of the append (an older log's sections keep their own headings), in a file Catervas starts with a `# Retro` title when it is missing, and recorded as `retro.appended`. Anywhere else, and for a delivery whose retro is written, the tool is refused with `retro_refused` (`retro_refused: D<n>'s retro is written`, or, with no delivery closed since the last retro, `no delivery has closed since the last retro`), and it answers `{ "delivery_id": "D<n>" }`. The retro is given its last 16 KiB (added in 0.15; changed in 0.116; ADR 0062).

The project scan from onboarding is stored as `project.md` and refreshed after an integration when what it reads has changed (changed in 0.16, from "whenever the tree changes materially"). The refresh runs once for each integration that records `task.integrated`: Catervas's merge, the human's `catervas integrate`, a pull request merged on the forge, and a branch the human merged by hand (5.14). A task that was already integrated is not scanned again. The scan reads the working tree at the project's root, so the refresh runs only when the project's own checkout is on the integration branch; on another branch, detached, or unreadable, it is skipped, and the reason is given. It compares the new scan with the last `project.scanned`: the read-back without its closing part about the last commit (`last commit ...` or `no commits yet`), and the names of the criteria found. A new commit alone is no change, and neither is a detected command that changes under the same name. A project with no `project.scanned` counts as changed. When the two differ, Catervas rewrites `project.md`, reseeds the criterion library as `catervas init` does (5.13), writing it and recording `criteria.updated` by `governor` when it changed, and records `project.scanned` last. Each event is about the integrated task, and no model is involved. A refresh that fails never fails the integration, though what it wrote before the failure stays written; since it recorded no `project.scanned`, the next integration does it again. The integration's own words then end with "; the project scan was refreshed", with nothing when it was unchanged, or with "; the project scan was not refreshed: <why>", in `catervas run`'s line and in `catervas integrate`'s answer; so do the words of an escalation that follows a merge, such as a failed push (added in 0.16). A project folder's own scan never runs (added in 0.112): an integration in a project folder, a documents task's among them, reports nothing about the scan and leaves the library as it is, since the folder's criteria are its members' (4.1, 5.13); a rescan of a member after a task integrates into it comes with integration in a member.

There is no vector store in the first release. Grep over the repository and these files is enough for repositories of the size the target users have. This is a known limit to revisit.

### 5.9 The channel

Agents post to the channel in a conversational register. The persona line and a shared style guide control tone. What triggers a post:

- State transitions on tasks the agent owns or reviews (assigned, done, blocked, rejected with the one-line reason).
- Mentions from other agents or the user.
- A review and a retro for each delivery (3), which are structured conversations that run in the channel (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062).
- A configurable "ambient" allowance: a small number of unprompted messages per day per agent, so the team feels alive without becoming expensive. Default is one, and reactions are one or two sentences (decided 2026-09-15: keep the register minimal).

A message (added in 0.14) is a `message.posted` event, and the log is the channel's only storage. It has an author, a kind, one line of text, the agents it mentions, a ceremony thread when it belongs to one, and the message it answers when it is a reply. The author is an agent, `human`, or `catervas`. The text is not blank and holds at most 2,000 characters, and Catervas turns each line break in it into a space. There are six kinds:

A post's attachments (added in 0.131; ADR 0076; standalone plan `attached-documents`). A `message.posted` with `author` `human` may have `attachments`, 1 to 5 paths of documents the owner attached (5.17), from `message_post { text, attachments }`; the words are still needed. A conversation session started by a post that names documents reads them as 5.17 says. `channel.messages` answers each message's `attachments` as `[{ path, name }]`, `name` the file's own name, and leaves the key out of a message with none. The Channel page's box has "Attach a document" and chips as Today's has (4.2), and a sent post shows its chips as links to Files.

- `reaction`: an agent's first post in a session that is not a conversation, about the move that session made.
- `ambient`: each later post of such a session, from the agent's allowance.
- `reply`: the one post of a conversation session.
- `ceremony`: a post of a ceremony session, in its thread (changed in 0.15).
- `system`: Catervas's line, written with no model.
- `human`: the human's post, from `catervas say`.

Mentions are read by Catervas from the text, never taken from the agent: each `@<id>` naming an agent of the team, active or not, once each, leaving out the author. `@human` is not a mention, because the human reads the channel. A system line mentions no one.

The team in every prompt (added in 0.137; ADR 0081). The system prompt (8.2) has a section "Your team", after the agent's name and persona: one line per agent not retired, `- <name>, <role>`, the agent's own marked ` (you)`, then "Anyone else named in your notes, memory or the channel has left the team." Retiring an agent posts the system line "<name> has left the team."; replacing one posts "<new> replaces <old> as <role>." in its place.

A message to no one (added in 0.134; ADR 0079). A human message that mentions no agent is addressed to the Product Manager, or to the one agent of a team of one: Catervas records the Product Manager's id as its mention, and the text is unchanged, so the message gets that agent a conversation session as if it had named it. The Product Manager decides who else is needed. A message that names an agent keeps its own mentions. A message that also answers a block is described in 5.7.

An agent posts with `catervas_post_message`, tier `read`, which every session has except a one-tool session (triage; the judgment's is gone, 0.115) and a one-to-one chat's session (added in 0.34). Catervas decides the kind from the session's purpose, and a refusal says `channel_limit`. The tool's description is the style guide: one or two sentences, what happened and what is next, no instruction to anyone.

The reaction comes from the session that made the move, on that session's model (changed in 0.14; this replaces "ambient and reaction messages use a cheaper model than task work"). The closing instruction of `refine`, `plan`, `implement`, and `verify` sessions asks for it: after asking for a move, post one or two sentences about it in the persona's voice, naming the task. No session is started only to react. A reaction's and an ambient message's envelope names the session's task.

Catervas posts a system line with no model:

- for a move made by the governor or the human, which has no session;
- for the rejection Catervas files in a reviewer's name once the review session has ended;
- when the daily budget is spent;
- when an agent sleeps at its model provider's limit (5.5).

A move's line reads `<task> <from> → <to> (by <who>)`, followed by `: <reason>` when the move carries one: the escalation's detail, the failed criteria and the reviewer's reasons for a rejection, the blocker, the resolution, the human's reason, or the criterion Catervas could not run. It is cut to 2,000 characters ending in `…`, so a line never fails a move that is recorded. It is posted after the move's own events. The moves Catervas makes on an agent's behalf post nothing, which keeps the register minimal: a triaged draft to `refining`, an assigned task to `in_progress`, an epic's assignment.

The ambient allowance is the team policy `ambient_messages_per_day`, from 0 to 20, default 1 (added in 0.14; changed in 0.116; ADR 0062: an older period counted it, and 5.12 names the older key, which is read when the new one is absent). It counts the agent's `ambient` messages since the UTC day began. A post past it is refused, and the refusal says the allowance is today's.

A mention gets its agent one short conversation session (added in 0.14). A mention is pending while it is newer than the latest message the agent's last conversation session was shown, which that session's `session.started` records as `in_reply_to`, so that a message posted while the session starts stays pending. A conversation that ends any way but at its provider's limit uses up the mentions it was shown; one stopped at the limit leaves them pending until its agent wakes. Mentions in a `reply`, a system line, or a `ceremony` message are never pending, so replies are one deep and a ceremony's words start no conversation (changed in 0.15). In `catervas run`, not `catervas plan`, after the budget rule and before the third rule, and when a tick is scoped to no task, the orchestrator takes the first agent in team order with a pending mention that is active and not asleep, while the daily budget has room. It starts one `conversation` session about no task, on Claude Sonnet 5.5 at `low` effort whatever the agent's own model. Its first message lists the pending messages with their authors and sequence numbers, then the channel summary, each in an `untrusted` block. Its closing instruction asks it to answer the mentions once with `catervas_post_message` and to file any work as a request with `catervas_create_task` without a parent. Its one post is a `reply` to the latest pending message, and a second is refused. `catervas run` prints it as `<agent>: <what>`. A mention of an agent that is paused, retired, or asleep waits.

The ceremonies (added in 0.15; changed in 0.116; ADR 0062). The review and the retro of a delivery are each one session of the ceremony runner: the active Scrum Master, else the active Product Manager, and with neither no ceremony runs. The session's purpose is `ceremony`, it is about no task, and it runs on Claude Sonnet 5.5 at `medium` effort whatever the runner's own model, with the read tier's built-in tools alone. Its `session.started` records its thread, `review` or `retro`, and each of its posts is a `ceremony` message in that thread, at most three per session: a fourth is refused with `channel_limit`. Its Catervas tools are the four reading tools, `catervas_post_message`, `catervas_write_memory`, and `catervas_read_decisions` (the last two added in 0.16); retro adds `catervas_append_retro`. Its first message gives it the ceremony's facts and then the channel summary, each in an `untrusted` block cut at 16 KiB, and its closing instruction says what to post, which tool ends it, and to mention no one, because the channel is read by all. No ceremony starts on a day whose budget is spent, and one whose runner sleeps at its provider's limit waits for it rather than passing to the other role.

A ceremony has run once a session in its thread started after its anchor and ended completed, aborted, or in error, or once three such sessions started, however they ended, so a ceremony stopped at a limit is tried again and none is tried forever; a retro has also run once it has appended, however its session ended, so no delivery gets two retros. The anchor is the delivery's `delivery.closed`. A task-less `plan` session with no thread, from a log recorded before 0.15, is no ceremony. The ceremonies run in a tick about no one task, before the rules of work and after the rule that closes a delivery, in the order review, retro:

- A delivery closes in the first rule of a tick scoped to no task after the chat rule and the interview (3): when one is due, the governor appends `delivery.closed { delivery_id: "D<n>", trigger, since_seq, task_ids }`, about no task and naming no actor, `n` one more than the deliveries closed before, `trigger` `epic_accepted`, `tasks_accepted` or `team_quiet`, `since_seq` where the delivery started (the previous close, or, for the first one, the last review of an older log), and `task_ids` the tasks it holds in the order they were accepted, each once and never a changelog task. In the same tick it files the Product Manager's changelog task (6.1).
- A delivery's review and retro run in `catervas run` and `catervas serve` for the latest closed delivery, once each; a delivery that holds no task gets neither. Their tasks are those `delivery.closed` lists, and their events those about them recorded after its `since_seq` and before its close. Review comes first: it is given each task's status, the first line of its last completion note, and what it cost in the delivery, what the delivery spent in all, and the digest (5.7): every open escalation and every daily budget spent since the delivery started, and it posts what the delivery delivered and what it did not. Retro follows once review has run: it is given the delivery's rejections with their failed criteria, escalations with their reason, blocks with their blocker, each task's iterations, and the last 16 KiB of `team/retro.md`, and it posts the retro and records what the team should remember with `catervas_append_retro` (5.8). A new delivery closes only once the previous one's retro is held, unless the team has no one to run it (3).

Folder documents at ceremonies (added in 0.94; ADR 0051; phase 8 step 03). The review and retro sessions are offered `catervas_write_folder_doc` (5.17) when their runner's role owns a folder: the Scrum Master's `delivery/`, or the Product Manager's `product/` on a team with no Scrum Master. No session that is not a ceremony is offered it. The review session's first message ends, after its facts, with the owner's words about its runner's proposals (5.7): a line for each decision of the owner's recorded since that runner's last review session began, oldest first, `The owner approved your changes to <paths>.` followed by ` The owner adds: <note>` when there is a note, or `The owner sent back your changes to <paths>: <reason>`; then a line for each proposal of the runner's that still waits, `Your change to <path> (proposal <n>) still waits for the owner; proposing it again replaces it.` The owner's words are not wrapped as untrusted text, being the human's own (ADR 0011).

`catervas run` prints a delivery's close and each ceremony as `D<n>: <what>` (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062); a close reads `closed it: an epic was accepted`, `closed it: 5 tasks were accepted` or `closed it: the team has no work left`, then `; filed CTV-<n> for its changelog` when it filed one.

The channel summary is derived with no model (changed in 0.14): the most recent messages that fit 2,000 tokens, counted as a quarter of their characters rounded up, oldest first, one line each as `<author> [<thread>]: <text>`. It is written to `.catervas/local/channel-summary.md` each time it is made, so the human can read what an agent was shown.

One-to-one chats (added in 0.34; ADR 0026) are not the channel. A chat message is a `chat_message.posted` event (8.5), never a `message.posted`, so no reader of the channel reads one: not `channel.messages`, the channel summary, `catervas channel`, the channel's pending mentions, nor `catervas metrics`' count of messages; an `@<id>` in a chat starts no conversation, and no session is shown a chat but its own agent's chat session. The user's message and the agent's reply are 1 to 4,000 characters, counted in code points, not blank, with their line breaks kept; a proposed request's title is 1 to 120 characters on one line and its text 20 to 4,000. A chat is pending when the sequence number of the user's newest message in it is above the `in_reply_to` of every `chat` session its agent has started, whoever wrote last, so a message sent while a session runs is answered next, with the reply in its history, and a session that ended without a reply is not tried again until the user writes again. In `catervas run` and `catervas serve`, not `catervas plan`, as the first rule of a tick scoped to no task, before the delivery rules, the orchestrator takes the oldest pending chat, by that message's sequence number, of an agent that is not retired (a paused agent among them), is not asleep, and whose day's budget has room, and starts one `chat` session for it (8.2), whose `in_reply_to` is that message; `catervas run` prints it as `<agent>: <what>`, as a conversation's. While the team is paused the tick runs this rule alone, and none while the pause is Catervas's for a key the provider refused (5.5). A command that sends a chat message wakes a waiting `catervas serve`. The privacy of chats rests on `.catervas/local/**` staying protected (5.6): the log, `.catervas/local/catervas.db`, lives there, and a chat session's `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` run in the project's root, so a user who takes that glob out of the protected list lets every session read every chat. A chat session is a fork (added in 0.118; ADR 0064): it starts at once, before any other work, beside the agent's work session, which it does not touch; an agent has at most one chat fork at a time, and messages written meanwhile are answered by the next one. It runs in the project's root with no worktree, sandbox, executor, connector or browser, on the read tier and the chat's tools, at low effort, within 100,000 input and 4,000 output tokens, 3 minutes and 12 tool calls, or the team's limits where smaller (the interview keeps the team's limits). Its first message says what the agent is doing now: the task of its running work session, else its oldest held task, with its title, status and the agent's last note on it.

The hard rule again: nothing said in the channel creates work. An agent that wants something done files a request, which is triaged and contracted like a request from the user (5.16). The tool for filing a request is available in the channel session precisely so that the conversational path leads into the governed path rather than around it.

The cadence at the retro (added in 0.101; ADR 0051; phase 8 step 07). The retro of a delivery that holds the Catervafication's epic, when its runner is a Scrum Master, ends its facts with the line "This delivery documented the project. Write the team's cadence to docs/catervas/delivery/cadence with catervas_write_folder_doc, as your skill catervafying-the-repository says."; a retro run by the Product Manager, on a team with no Scrum Master, is not told, the cadence being the Scrum Master's.

The delivery review's refreshes (added in 0.102; ADR 0051; phase 8 step 07b; changed in 0.116; ADR 0062). After the review of a closed delivery has run and before its retro, the Product Manager and the Architect each get one `ceremony` session in the `review` thread, read-only and offered the review's tools (`catervas_write_folder_doc` among them), once per delivery under the ceremonies' bound: a session counts for its agent once it ended completed, aborted or failed, or after three starts (the closed delivery's `reviewed_by`, each agent whose `review` session has run since its close). The Product Manager's runs only when `docs/catervas/product/spec` is on the integration branch, and its first message opens "The delivery <n> review is done. Keep the product plan true to what the delivery did." (<n> the delivery's id without its `D`), then asks it to write changes to `spec` and `roadmap` with `catervas_write_folder_doc`, with `agent_text`, only where the delivery changed what the product does or what comes next, and nothing otherwise, and to write the delivery report, for agents, to `docs/catervas/product/reports/D<n>` in the team's format; then the delivery's tasks, each with its status and its completion note as untrusted text; then, outside every untrusted block, the lines of 5.7 for its own proposals of an older log that the owner decided since its last `review` session began and, after them, those that still wait (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: nothing is proposed now). When the review's runner is the Product Manager (a team with no Scrum Master), its review session is its refresh: the review's message gains the same asks after its facts, and no second session runs. The Architect's runs only when `docs/catervas/architecture/structure` is on the integration branch and a task of the delivery has a `task.integrated` after the delivery's `since_seq`, read from the log (the delivery's events stop at its close, an integration may come after it); its first message opens "Bring docs/catervas/architecture/features, jobs and structure up to date with what delivery <n> added to the project." then "Change only what these tasks changed, each file with catervas_write_folder_doc." and each integrated task's id, title and completion note as untrusted text. The refreshes no longer wait for a task of the delivery to be integrated (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: under `auto_merge` they were passed over while a task of the delivery was `accepted` and awaiting its integration, so that rule 2 integrated it first; Catervas now merges nothing). Both are passed over on a spent day and while the agent sleeps, as the review is. "What moved" says "<name> sent the architecture notes as a pull request after the team's review" for each Architect `review` session with a `folder_doc.written` since the person last looked, at its latest write's time (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062; under every team file since 0.115; ADR 0061), since the change reaches the project only when it is merged.

### 5.10 What the harness does not solve

Two honest gaps. First, verification quality is only as good as the exit criteria the PM writes. A vague criterion passed by a sloppy reviewer is still a pass. The Scrum Master's judgment check and the human review of `high` risk contracts are the mitigations; they are not proofs. Second, the governor can prevent forbidden actions but cannot detect a semantically wrong change that stays within its allowed paths and passes its tests. Catervas makes that kind of error cheap to find (small tasks, diffs per task, a reviewer who reads them) rather than impossible.

### 5.11 Contract ownership (added in 0.2)

Every contract has an owner. A contract the Product Manager wrote is owned by the team until the human locks it. A contract with `locked: true` is owned by the human: agents may record criterion results and write their notes on it, and the governor refuses every other change by an agent, with the reason `contract_locked` when the change is to the contract's content and the reason for the field's owner when the field is one that agent never writes anyway. A lock holds the contract's content for the human; it does not stop the lifecycle, so the governor still writes `status`, `assignee`, `reviewer`, `iteration`, and `sprint` (a field of contracts made before 0.116, which is read and ignored) when it applies a transition, or a locked task could never leave `refining`. Neither locking nor unlocking is a content change: a human who locks a contract from `ready` onward does not send its task back to `refining`, or writing an epic by hand and locking it would undo the approval it was just given (5.16). Locking and unlocking are human commands, recorded as `contract.locked` and `contract.unlocked` events. This is how a user writes a contract themselves, or with the Product Manager's help (5.13), and has the team execute exactly that contract.

The contract's `summary` (added in 0.25) is a content field, the Product Manager's to write like the others, and so frozen with them once the task leaves `refining`. Every field of a contract has exactly one owner, and the governor refuses a write to a field the writer does not own (added in 0.3). The governor's own are `status`, `assignee`, `reviewer`, `iteration`, and `sprint`, at every status and whoever asks: 5.2 gives it the `status` field for its transitions, and every other row's trigger is an actor asking rather than writing, so a write of `status` by anyone else would move a task past every gate with no `task.transitioned` event behind it. Nothing writes `sprint` any more (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062): a contract made before keeps the field, which is read and ignored. `locked` is the human's alone. The store's are `id`, `created_by`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, and `branch` (added in 0.119; ADR 0066), which no actor writes through a contract tool; Catervas writes `branch` once, when the task's worktree is first made (5.14), a filing that sets it is refused, and the human's save leaves it as the file holds it, whatever the edited contract says. `kind` is fixed when the contract is created: the triage decides the kind (5.16) and its own tool changes it. `parent` is fixed when the contract is created too, with one exception (changed in 0.134; ADR 0079): the Product Manager may set it, and `dependencies` with it, on a task in `draft`, `refining` or `ready` that is not `locked`, to an existing epic, never to clear it; a task out of the epic its readiness was judged against is judged again by the next readiness check, and a `parent` that names no epic is refused. The Product Manager reaches a waiting child of an epic from the epic's own session with `task_id` (5.2). The notes are everyone's, at every status. Everything else is the contract's content, `change` among it (added in 0.11), written by the Product Manager and by the human on any contract, and by the Scrum Master on a task but never on an epic (6.2, 5.16 item 3); an assignee, a reviewer, and the governor never write content at all. A field name the governor does not recognise is refused as unknown rather than treated as content, so a field added to the schema is refused until somebody says who owns it. A contract whose task is `accepted` or `cancelled` takes no write but a note, the human's included: nothing leaves those two statuses, and a human's write of a frozen contract is defined by sending the task back to `refining`, which a terminal task has no way to do.

Independently of ownership, a contract is frozen once its task leaves `refining`: from `ready` onward, only `status`, `assignee`, `reviewer`, `iteration`, `sprint`, and `notes` change (`sprint` being the field of an older contract, read and ignored since 0.116, ADR 0062), and only through governed transitions and the note tools. An agent that wants a frozen contract changed asks the human (5.7). A human who edits a frozen contract moves the task back to `refining`, and the log says so. From the web UI that edit is saved on an escalated task, written while the task is still held, and only then does the escalation's resolve take it back, so that the session the move wakes reads the human's plan (changed in 0.26 by step 08's landing review); a save of a frozen contract the team is still working to is refused, and the user escalates the task first (added in 0.25's landing review). The human's save of a contract from the web UI never changes `locked`: a save whose `locked` differs from the file's is refused, because a lock is recorded as `contract.locked` or `contract.unlocked`, which a save does not write (added in 0.25's landing review).

A task's repository is fixed once set (added in 0.111; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 02). A write that would change a `repo` that was already set, to another name or to none, is refused with `repo_fixed`, "repo is fixed once set: this task stays in <repo>; cancel it and file another to change repositories", because the contract's expanded criteria come from its repository. Writing a `repo` where there was none, or the same name again, is allowed, and so is clearing it when the written contract is an epic or its assignee's role changes no code (readiness refuses a `repo` there, so the task could never be ready otherwise). It holds for both writers of a contract's content: the agents' `catervas_write_contract` and the human's `contract.save`, which refuse and leave the file and the log as they were. Locking or unlocking a contract changes neither.

### 5.12 Team rules (added in 0.2)

Team rules are constraints the human writes once, in `.catervas/team.yaml` under `rules`, that the governor applies to every contract and every tool call. Agents read them in every session and cannot change them. The owner sets every rule on Settings → Rules (`/settings/rules`, added in 0.136; ADR 0080) and, for one agent alone, on that agent's page; the rules live in `.catervas/team.yaml`, under `.catervas/`, which no agent writes (5.4), so only the owner's screens and the team file change them.

| Rule | Type | Enforced where |
|---|---|---|
| `protected_paths` | globs | every file tool call, read or write, is refused inside them (5.6) |
| `allowed_paths_ceiling` | globs | Definition of Ready refuses a contract whose `allowed_paths` reach outside them. A path lies within a directory glob such as `docs/**` only when its literal part, up to its first wildcard, reaches past the directory's `/` (`docs/adr/**`, `docs/*.md`), or it has no wildcard and is the directory or below it; `docs*/**` and `docs?/x` are outside, since the wildcard runs on into a sibling such as `docsrc/` (changed in 0.11); a path with a `..` segment anywhere, before or after a wildcard, is within no ceiling (changed in 0.17) |
| `required_criteria` | verification methods | Definition of Ready refuses a contract that has no criterion of each listed method |
| `require_new_tests` | boolean | Definition of Ready refuses a contract whose `test` criteria do not set `new_tests_required` |
| `max_task_budget_usd` | number | Definition of Ready refuses a task whose budget exceeds it, when it is set; an epic is not held to it |
| `document_paths` | globs | Definition of Ready refuses a task assigned to any role but the Software Developer and the UI/UX Designer whose `allowed_paths` reach outside them (5.3; added in 0.11; the Designer added in 0.31) |
| `ui_paths` | globs | a Software Developer's task whose branch changes a path inside them is a change to the interface, which the UI/UX Designer checks before the Architect reviews it (5.4; added in 0.33) |
| `forbidden_commands` | regular expressions | `catervas_exec` refuses a command that matches one: ECMAScript patterns, which have no inline flags such as `(?i)`, matched against the whole command and against each non-blank segment (split on `&&`, `||`, `;`, `\|`, and newlines), and a pattern that does not compile refuses every command |

Per-agent rules (added in 0.136; ADR 0080). Beside the team's `rules`, an agent's entry in `team.yaml` may carry `rules` with `protected_paths` and `read_only_paths` (added for this agent), `lifted_paths` (globs of the team's that do not apply to this agent, the shipped five among them, written exactly as the team writes them), `forbidden_commands` (added) and `git_subcommands` (added), and `session` (5.5). The agent's rules are the team's with these applied (`Team::rules_for`): start from the team's own, which are the shipped protected paths less `rules.lifted_paths`, then `rules.protected_paths`, deduplicated; add the agent's `protected_paths`, `read_only_paths`, `forbidden_commands` and `git_subcommands`; then remove from both the protected and the read-only paths every glob the agent's `lifted_paths` names, exactly as written. An id no agent has gets the team's rules. A `lifted_paths` entry that is not one of the five shipped globs, nor in the team's `protected_paths` or `read_only_paths`, would do nothing and is refused (`lifted_path_unknown`). Every check that reads the protected paths for a session or a task reads its agent's rules: the hook, the tools, `catervas_exec`, the folders' tools, the session's settings, the Team rules in the prompt and the Definition of Done; the project scan, `catervas doctor` and `catervas team` show the team's. The Team rules also name `read_only_paths`, `git_subcommands` and, to an agent that holds `git_remote`, `push_remotes`. Team-wide only, because they are the repository's and not an agent's: the remotes, the readiness attempts, the rejections before escalation, the hours blocked, the work per agent and the hours an escalation may wait. `team.schema.json` gains `rules.lifted_paths`, `rules.read_only_paths`, `rules.git_subcommands`, `policy.push_remotes`, `policy.readiness_attempts`, `agents[].rules` and `agents[].session`, each optional, so every team file stays valid. In the web app, Settings → Rules has six parts, each saved on its own: "Files agents may not touch" (the five shipped globs, each kept, lifted or read only, and the owner's own as off limits or read only, with the glob under "advanced"), "Commands agents may not run", "Git in agents' commands" (the eight read-only subcommands, always on, and the owner's), "Where agents may push", "When work stops and asks you" and "How long one session may run"; an agent's page has "Rules for <name>" with the team's file rules and a button to lift each for that agent, its own off-limits and read-only paths, commands and git, and its session limits, saved with the rest of the page.

Defaults: `protected_paths` as in 5.6, `max_task_budget_usd` unset, no cap (ADR 0015), `document_paths` `docs/**`, `**/*.md`, and `CHANGELOG.md` when the key is left out, `ui_paths` `**/*.tsx`, `**/*.jsx`, `**/*.vue`, `**/*.svelte`, `**/*.css`, `**/*.scss`, and `**/*.html` when the key is left out, where an explicit `[]` is kept and leaves only the contract's `ui_change` (added in 0.33), everything else empty or off. The web app edits `ui_paths` under Advanced, as "Which files are screens" (added in 0.33). An explicit `document_paths: []` is kept, not replaced by the default, and means that no task but a Software Developer's or a UI/UX Designer's can be ready (added in 0.11; the Designer added in 0.31). Rules never loosen a permission tier; they only narrow what a granted tier allows.

Protected paths in a read root (added in 0.114; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 03). In a read root (5.6) `.git/**` is protected as well as the team's `protected_paths`, since a member's `.git/config` can hold a token in a remote's address. Each root's protected globs are also Claude Code's own `Read` deny rules in its absolute form, except a glob whose literal folder holds the session's working folder: the project folder's `.catervas/local/**` would refuse a task its own worktree, which lies under it, so the hook alone guards `.catervas/local` and `.git` in that root.

Beside the rules, `team.yaml`'s `policy` holds the team's policies, flat keys such as `wip_limit_per_agent`, `escalation_age_hours` and `ambient_messages_per_day`. Two older keys are read and never written (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062): `ambient_messages_per_sprint`, which answers the policy of the day while that is absent (`Team::ambient_messages_per_day`: the day's key, else the older one, else 1), and `plan_in_sprints` (added in 0.36), a boolean that changes nothing now. A team file or a saved team that holds either loads without a refusal, and `Team::without_old_keys` moves the older ambient key to the new one and drops `plan_in_sprints` (and `judgment`) in `ProjectFiles::write_team` and in `team.get`; the defaults, `catervas init`, `catervas carry`, setup, `team.propose`, `team.updated` and a saved team write neither. A project made with `plan_in_sprints: true` assigns its work as any does (8.4).

Three policies are read differently since ADR 0061 (changed in 0.115). `integration` keeps its three values in the schema, `manual`, `auto_merge` and `pull_request`, so that every older file and template loads, and is read as `pull_request` whatever is written: `validate_team` and the template reader set it, a team written now carries `pull_request`, and setup and Settings offer no choice (5.14). `human_accepts_contracts` (`high_risk` or `all`) still loads and is ignored, since no contract waits for the human (5.16 item 2). `judgment` is accepted, ignored and dropped when Catervas writes the file or a saved team (5.3).

`merge_when_checks_pass` (added in 0.128; ADR 0073) lets Catervas merge its own pull requests (5.14). It is `policy.merge_when_checks_pass: true` in `team.yaml`, and absent means false. It is off by default, a team template does not carry it, `catervas carry` drops it, and a `team.save`, `team.start`, `agent.replace` or template application never changes it: `checked()` keeps the value already saved over whatever the incoming team says, and a team being set up has none. It is not enough alone: the team file travels with the repository and the log stays on one computer, so Catervas merges only when `catervas_store::merging::merging_allowed` is true, which is the key and the newest of `merge_permission.granted` and `merge_permission.withdrawn` in this project's log being the grant. A clone, a `catervas carry` or a hand edit that brings `true` merges nothing until its owner confirms the warning on that computer. One daemon method changes it, `merging.set { on, confirmed? }`, under the team's write lock. On: refused `merge_warning_unconfirmed` ("Turning merging on needs the warning confirmed.") unless `confirmed` is `true`, and refused `merging_offline` ("Catervas can merge only when your project is on GitHub.") when `online` is false, both at `/policy/merge_when_checks_pass`; a call that finds merging already allowed records nothing; otherwise it writes the key, records `team.updated`, then `merge_permission.granted { by: "human", into }` and wakes the orchestrator. Off: it removes the key, records `team.updated`, then `merge_permission.withdrawn { by: "human", into }`, and records nothing when the key was absent and merging was not allowed. It answers `{ merging_allowed }`, read after the write, and `team.get` answers `merging_allowed` too, so a clone whose file says `true` shows the switch off. Settings → How work runs, under the lead line of "How finished work is added", has a switch "Let Catervas merge finished work" with an information button of three bullets, disabled with "Needs your project on GitHub." when the project is not online. Switching it on opens a dialog, "Let Catervas merge?", with the bullets "Catervas will merge finished work into {branch} by itself." ({branch} the team's `integration_branch`, else "your main branch"), "It merges only when GitHub's checks pass. If your repository has no automatic checks, Catervas merges once its own checks pass." and "You won't see the work before it lands.", and, for one agent alone (`policy.solo`), "{name} works alone, so no other agent reviews its code."; its **Turn on** sends `merging.set { on: true, confirmed: true }` and **Cancel** sends nothing. Switching it off sends `{ on: false }` with no dialog. The effect line is "Catervas merges finished work once GitHub's checks pass." when the key turns on and "Finished work opens a pull request for you to merge." when it turns off.

`document_format` (added in 0.108; ADR 0058) is one of the policies: `html` or `markdown`, read as `html` when the key is left out, so every team, an existing one included, writes its new documents as HTML; team templates carry it, and `team.updated` does not, since only the next session's Team rules read it. Settings → Work has a group "Documents" with one switch, "Write documents as HTML" (on is `html`, off `markdown`), saved through `team.save`. The Team rules carry a documents line right after the folders line (5.17), built by `format_line`: in an HTML team ``- documents: write a new document under docs/catervas/ as HTML (`.html`, a human document's agent version `.agent.html`): one self-contained page with `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`, one `<h1>`, styles in one `<style>` block, widths that fit a phone (percentages, `max-width`), diagrams, flowcharts and charts as inline SVG with a `viewBox`, one block element per line, no scripts and nothing loaded from anywhere else. A document already in `.md` stays Markdown when you change it. The kit names documents without their extension.``; in a Markdown team ``- documents: write a new document under docs/catervas/ as Markdown (`.md`, a human document's agent version `.agent.md`), diagrams in Mermaid blocks. A document already in `.html` stays HTML when you change it. The kit names documents without their extension.``.

`documents_local` (added in 0.129; ADR 0074) is one of the policies: a boolean, read as false when the key is left out, whether the team's documents under `docs/catervas/` are kept on this computer, out of the repository and ignored through `info/exclude` (5.17). Only `documents.set_local` changes it (and setup's `team.start`, which runs the same command); `team.save` writes the saved value whatever it is sent, and a team template carries none, since it belongs to the project, as `integration_branch` does. Settings → How work runs → Documents has a switch under "Write documents as HTML", "Keep documents on this computer", off, with the info button's three bullets: "Your team's documents stay in docs/catervas in this folder.", "They are not added to your repository or pushed to GitHub.", "No history of changes is kept, and pull requests don't show them." Turning it on asks "Keep documents on this computer?" ("Documents already in your repository are taken out in one pull request.", "The files stay in your folder.", "Until you merge it, documents can't be changed.", "Keep them here", "Cancel"), turning it off "Put documents back in your repository?" ("Your documents go into one pull request.", "Until you merge it, documents can't be changed.", "Put them back", "Cancel"); then the switch is disabled and a line says "Taking your documents out of the repository. Merge the pull request to finish." or "Putting your documents back in the repository. Merge the pull request to finish." A project folder shows no switch.

`integration_branch` (changed in 0.122; ADR 0069) is set in Settings → How work runs, under "Where finished work goes", and left empty it is the repository's default branch. The daemon refuses a name git would not allow (`integration_branch_name`) and a name with no local branch of that name (`integration_branch_missing`) when the value changes, at `/policy/integration_branch`; the effect line reads "Finished work goes into <branch>." or "Finished work goes into the repository's main branch.". In a project folder each member keeps its own branch in `repos.yaml`, so `team.get` answers `members_present: true`, the page shows no field there and neither check is made.

**Autopilot (added in 0.138; ADR 0082).** The switch is "Autopilot: let the team run the product" in Settings, Allowed actions. It is kept in this computer's event log as the newest `autopilot.changed { on }`, set only by the daemon method `autopilot.set { on, confirmed }` and never written to `team.yaml`, so no agent, clone or hand edit turns it on; `team.get` says whether it is on. Turning it on is refused `autopilot_unconfirmed` without `confirmed: true`, which the web app sends on a second press after showing what the team will then do alone, and `daily_limit_required` while `budgets.daily_usd` is unset; while it is on, a team save that removes the daily limit is refused `daily_limit_required` too, and the owner turns autopilot off first. A call that changes nothing records nothing. The owner can turn it off at any time. The daily limit is the hard stop: when the day is spent (a UTC day) the team pauses until the next.

`policy.paid_calls_per_hour` (added in 0.138; ADR 0082) is a whole number from 1 to 1000, 30 when it is left out: how many paid or asking connector calls one agent may make in an hour while autopilot is on (8.6). It is set on Settings, Rules, as "Paid tool calls per agent per hour".

### 5.13 Contract authoring and the criterion library (added in 0.2)

A contract can be written three ways, and all three end in the same Definition of Ready check. The human writes it alone, in the editor or as a YAML file, and then the human's own triage sets whether it is an epic or a single task (5.16). The Product Manager writes it from a brief, an issue link, or the backlog, as in 6.1. An epic's task contracts come from the Architect's plan, written by the Product Manager: the plan task first, then one task per planned task once the plan is on the integration branch, or, with no Architect, from lanes the Product Manager plans itself (5.16 item 3; changed in 0.98). Or the two write it together: the Product Manager drafts, the human edits, the Definition of Ready results update as they type, and the human locks the result (5.11). The command line offers the same through `catervas contract new`, which files the request, runs its triage (or takes the user's), then runs a Product Manager drafting session over a brief or a link, answering its questions at the terminal, and prints the contract with its readiness results.

`catervas contract new --brief <text>` or `--from <issue>` (added in 0.8). The request's title is the brief's first line, cut at 120 characters, or the issue's title; its intent is the whole brief, or the issue's title, body, and address, and a brief under twenty characters, the schema's least intent, is refused before anything is filed. Every other field is a placeholder the Product Manager replaces while refining it: one item in scope and one out, a requirement, a `review` criterion, both roles Software Developer, risk `low`, the team's cap on a task's budget, and an allowed path no file matches. When no other process drives the project, this one starts driving it before anything is filed (8.2) and holds the run lock throughout, so that a start that refuses, for want of a credential or of a recent enough `claude`, files nothing. The request is then filed as the human's, sized when `--size` is given, and worked, in this process, with the triage and refining rules alone and for that request alone (8.2): each event about it is printed as `catervas task show` prints it, and each question the Product Manager asks is printed with an `answer>` prompt, whose reply is recorded as the answer. The end of the input or Ctrl-C at the prompt leaves the question open for `catervas answer`. Once nothing is left to do it prints the contract, its readiness (passed; failed with each failure; or not judged yet, and why), what waits on the user, and, with `--lock`, takes the contract, last, so that the Product Manager writes first; when the Product Manager has written none, it says so and takes nothing. While another process drives the project, the request is filed and sized and left to that process, and `--lock` is refused before anything is filed.

The criterion library, `.catervas/team/criteria.yaml`, holds named, reusable exit criteria: the project's own check and test commands found by the project scan, and any the human adds. When authoring, a criterion is referenced by name and expanded into the contract, so that contracts across a project verify the same way and the Product Manager is not asked to reinvent "the tests pass" every time.

A criterion can name its member (added in 0.112; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 02b). An entry may carry `repo`, a member's name in `repos.schema.json`'s pattern, which the criteria schema repeats and a test holds equal; left out, the entry suits any task, and an entry naming a member that `repos.yaml` no longer lists expands into no contract, since core cannot read that file. A contract's criteria come only from its own repository: expanding a reference to an entry that names a member other than the contract's `repo`, or one where the contract has none, is `criterion_of_another_repo`, answered as `criterion_not_expanded` like every refusal of an expansion, with "criterion <name> checks <member>, and this contract works in <repo, or the project's own folder>: set repo first, or use one of its own criteria". `catervas_write_contract` passes the `repo` the contract has once the call's `fields` are applied, so one call may set `repo` and name that member's criteria. `catervas_read_criteria` and `catervas criteria list --json` show each entry's `repo` (null when absent), and `catervas criteria list` a `repo` column.

A project folder's library is its members' (added in 0.112). Each check a member's scan finds is renamed `<repo>-<name>` (`app-the-tests-pass`), given `repo`, and keeps its text and verification; a name the library refuses once renamed, over 64 characters or against its pattern, is left out, not shortened, which could collide, and with member names of at most 32 characters no real scan reaches it. A reseed walks the library in order: an entry that is `source: project_scan` and whose `repo` is among the members being scanned is replaced in place by the check found under the same name, so that a re-found check keeps its place and a rescan with nothing new changes nothing, or is dropped if none is found; every other entry stays where it is; then each found check not already placed and whose name is not already kept is appended, a human's entry winning a clash as in a project of one repository, up to the schema's hundred entries; the names left out are written into `project.md` as "Left out, the library being full: <names>.", so that the owner and the agents see them. A member that is missing or whose scan fails keeps its entries. `criteria.updated` is recorded, by the human for `catervas init` and by `catervas` for a member joining, moving or leaving, when the library changed.

### 5.14 Integration of accepted work (added in 0.2)

Each task works on its own branch in its own git worktree under `.catervas/local/worktrees/CTV-<n>`, so that tasks running in parallel never share a working tree. The container for a task mounts that worktree. The branch says what the task changes (changed in 0.119; ADR 0066). A task's change has a type, from its contract alone: Docs when its assignee's role changes no code or every one of its `allowed_paths` starts with `docs/`; else Fix when its `change` is `fix`; else Feat. A bug a hunt files is filed with `change: fix`. Its branch is `<type in lower case>/<slug>`, the slug being the title in lower-case ASCII with each run of anything else turned into one `-`, trimmed of `-`, and cut to 40 characters at the last `-` within its first 41 (at 40 when there is none), or `change` when nothing is left. A name another branch of the repository has (locally or under a remote, or as the start of a name followed by `/`), or another contract or folder change records, takes `-2`, `-3`, and so on, the first free one kept. Catervas chooses the name when the task's worktree is first made and records it in the contract's `branch` before the worktree, under the same lock as every other write of a contract; it is never changed, so a start undone by a conflict makes the same branch on the next try, and every reader of a task's branch reads it. Nothing reads a task's id out of a branch made since 0.119. A task started before 0.119 has no `branch`; it keeps `feature/CTV-<n>`, `fix/CTV-<n>` or `docs/CTV-<n>` as 0.11 named them (a Software Developer's or a UI/UX Designer's task on `feature/` or, when its `change` is `fix`, `fix/`, every other role's on `docs/`). A branch `catervas/CTV-<n>` made before 0.11 is neither renamed nor read. A repository with a branch named exactly `feat`, `fix`, or `docs` (or, for an old task, `feature`) cannot hold a branch under that name, so git refuses the task's worktree at assignment and the refusal reaches the user as any git failure does; renaming that branch fixes it. The worktree folder `.catervas/local/worktrees/CTV-<n>` and the ref `refs/catervas/start/<id>` keep the id: both are local, and Catervas pushes `refs/heads/<branch>` alone. `task.diff` answers a task's branch as `branch` (absent for an epic and a task in a private folder), which the task page shows (added in 0.119).

A task in a member repository (added in 0.111; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 02). A task that names a `repo` (5.3) has its branch made in that member, from the member's integration branch, which is its `integration_branch` in `repos.yaml` or else the member's default branch; the team's `policy.integration_branch` names the project folder's own branch alone. Its worktree is still at `.catervas/local/worktrees/CTV-<n>` under the project folder, made by the member's git, so that the sandbox, the session's directory and the hooks are the same as any task's; the worktree's git directory is the member's. The task's resume, the commits, clean tree and changed paths its Definition of Done reads, `catervas_git_status`, `catervas_git_diff`, `catervas_git_commit` and `catervas_git_push`, the diff on its page (`task.diff`), `catervas task show --diff`, the reviewer's and the UI/UX Designer's prompts, and the designer's preview, which reads the task branch's tree, all act on the member. A task that names no `repo` works in the project folder on its usual branch, as does every task of a project of one repository. A task whose member is not where `repos.yaml` says it is waits, in every status: every rule of the orchestrator that resolves its repository (starting it from `assigned`, resuming it in `in_progress`, running its verification and its design review) passes it over for that tick, nothing is recorded, and the next tick tries again once the member is located, so one moved repository never ends a tick or `serve`; a preview that cannot open because its member is missing ends that session only, as a failed preview does, with "<repo> cannot be found"; a cancel, an escalation or a hold of it still goes through, and `verifying` is refused for the commits it cannot see. An accepted task in a member is integrated in that member (below).

Integration in a member (added in 0.113; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 02c). An accepted task that names a `repo` is integrated in that member, by pull request (ADR 0061; changed in 0.115: the policies `auto_merge` and `manual` are read as `pull_request`) and under the one integration lock, which stays the project folder's `.catervas/local/integration.lock`, so that integrations into different members are serialised too. Catervas pushes the branch to the member's `origin` and opens the pull request with `gh` run in the member, then reads its state there, the member's integration branch brought up to the forge's when it merges; a member with no `origin` waits for the human to merge the branch by hand, and the integration is recorded once the branch is in the member's integration branch (below).  `task.integrated { sha, into, integrated_by }` is unchanged: `into` is the member's integration branch and `sha` the member's merge commit (or, for a merge by hand, the integration branch's head when it was recorded); it carries no repository, since the contract names it, and `task.diff` reads them in the task's member. A task that names no `repo`, and every folder change, integrate in the project folder with its own git and `gh`, as they always did, and a project of one repository is unchanged. A task whose member is not where `repos.yaml` says it is waits to be integrated, as it waits in every status (above): a tick records nothing, and the task is integrated by itself on the first tick after `repo.locate`; the human's `catervas integrate` of it raises one integration escalation with the sentence "<repo> is not at <path>: locate it in Settings", so that the human hears why nothing happened, and a tick leaves it to the human from then on, as it does after any integration escalation. Any other repository that cannot be had, a name the project does not list, a `repos.yaml` or a contract that cannot be read, or git refusing the member's integration branch, is an integration escalation with its sentence. After an integration into a member the project scan (5.8) is refreshed for that member alone: when its checkout is on its integration branch, its checks are read again and its entries in the criterion library replaced, the other members' entries kept, `criteria.updated` by `governor` is recorded when the library changed, and `project.scanned`, about no task, is recorded on every such integration; a checkout on another branch skips the refresh and says "<repo>'s checkout is on <branch>, not <into>". The folder's own work still refreshes nothing. A task that depends on a task in another member is assigned once that task is accepted (5.2; changed in 0.115), and its worktree is made from its own member's integration branch; only an unmerged dependency in its own member, its plan, or an accepted unmerged documents task of its own member is carried into the worktree (below).

What happens to the branch after `accepted` is a pull request (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: Catervas never merges into the integration branch unless the owner allows it (changed in 0.128; ADR 0073), and the policies `auto_merge`, named `local_merge` until 0.8, and `manual` are read as `pull_request`).
