An accepted task is a board row of kind `task` in `accepted`; an epic is not one, and nor is a cancelled task, though what either cost and what the human did on it still count. Every rate is none, not zero, while no task is accepted. The first-pass acceptance rate is the accepted tasks that entered `verifying` exactly once and `rejected` never, whoever moved them, over the accepted tasks; a task the human accepted without a verification is not first pass. Human interventions per accepted task counts, on every row, each `escalation.raised` whose reason is neither `approval` nor `risk_gate` (the two the process asks the human for by design) and each move the human asked for that neither leaves nor enters `escalated` (unblocking, cancelling, resuming); questions, answers, approvals, acceptances, triage, locks, and a manual integration are not interventions. Cost per accepted task is every `cost.recorded` but a chat's, of any task or none, over the accepted tasks, split by every purpose (`triage`, `refine`, `plan`, `explore` for a UI/UX Designer's (added in 0.31), `implement`, `verify`, `ceremony`, `conversation`, `goal` for a goal session's planning and reading (added in 0.130; ADR 0075), and `finance` for a receipts sweep, added in 0.21, which is split out once the receipts sweep is built), which add up to the total; `catervas metrics` prints one line per purpose. A one-to-one chat's cost (purpose `chat`, 0.34) is no task's work and is left out of it, total and split alike, so `catervas metrics` prints no `chat` line and `--json` has no `chat` key (changed in 0.34's fix wave). The mechanically verified share is the exit criteria whose method is `command`, `test`, or `artifact`, over every exit criterion of the contracts of the accepted rows, epics included; an accepted row whose contract cannot be read fails the whole computation. Active weeks is the number of distinct ISO 8601 weeks (UTC) in which a session recorded a cost. `catervas metrics` prints them, and `--json` prints them as one object. The per-period option of 0.12 is gone (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062). Beside the five, `catervas metrics` counts the channel's messages by kind (added in 0.14), so the minimal register (5.9) can be judged against what conversation and ceremony sessions cost: `reaction`, `ambient`, `reply`, `ceremony`, `system`, and `human`, read from the log's `message.posted` events because messages are not projected. It prints them as one line, `messages: reaction <n>, ambient <n>, reply <n>, ceremony <n>, system <n>, human <n>`, and `--json` as a `messages` object with the six keys. The web app's Costs page (added in 0.28) says what the team has spent today against the daily limit, which it can set; a table gives each agent not retired what it spent today and what it is doing right now; and "How well the team works" gives the metrics in words, across the whole project, each rate reading "Not yet: no work has been accepted" while none is, and the cost split into the same words as the task page: "Planning", "Building", "Checking", "Meetings and talk" (ceremonies and the channel's `conversation` sessions), and "Conversations", which is the one-to-one chats alone and so never appears in the cost per accepted task, which leaves chats out (changed in 0.34's fix wave). The table's last row (added in 0.34; changed in 0.123), "Your chats with the team", with an info button saying they count toward the daily limit, gives `costs.summary`'s `conversations_today_usd`, today's spending of purpose `chat`, 0 with none; the channel's `conversation` sessions are not in it. Calls made on other services against their allowances are shown beside them (6.7; ADR 0037). `costs.summary` also gives `cancelled_today_usd` (added in 0.134; ADR 0079), today's spend on tasks that are now cancelled, left out when it is 0, and the Costs page says "$1.50 of it went to cancelled tasks." under its first line. The web app's Costs page (changed in 0.123) lists each agent's spend today, highest first, with the owner's chats as the last row, and shows the four rates as tiles, each note behind an info button, with active weeks and the message counts under "More numbers". Analytics across teams (added in 0.152) are a separate view over the owner's Claude Code history and each team's log: usage per team counted once per reply, the workflow and the blockers, in 4.4.

**F18 Goals (added in 0.130; ADR 0075).** The owner sets one goal on Today, with an optional number and unit and how it is counted; while the board is quiet the Product Manager (or the one agent alone) files the next one to five steps in a `goal` session; the agent that holds the goal's service reads it once a day; Today shows the progress and the owner pauses, edits, ends or marks the goal reached; the daily budget is the only spend limit (4.2, 5.5, 5.18, 6.1, 8.5). Out of scope: a goals page, several goals at once, deadlines, a goal budget, a `catervas goal` command, Catervas merging.

## 8. Architecture

### 8.1 Shape

A Rust backend and a TypeScript front end in one repository (decided 2026-09-15; ADR 0005). Local-first: the orchestrator and governor run on the user's machine, agents execute in a sandbox on that machine, and the project stays where it is. The hosted premium tier moves execution to the cloud; the local shell talks to it over the same event protocol.

```
crates/                       Rust, one Cargo workspace
  core/           catervas-core:     schemas, task state machine, governor, cost model  (no I/O)
  protocol/       catervas-protocol: event, command, and RPC types shared by daemon and front end
  store/          catervas-store:    SQLite event log and projections; file adapters for .catervas/; the git adapter
  runtime/        catervas-runtime:  Claude Code sessions, sandbox, Catervas tools, orchestrator, the daemon service
  roles/          catervas-roles:    shipped role definitions, skills and kits (6.7), and their loader
  cli/            catervas:          the binary: command line, `catervas serve`, `catervas hook`
xtask/                        the repository's own commands (check, generate, hooks)
packages/                     TypeScript
  brand/          @catervas/brand:   logo, app icons, design tokens (section 14)
  ui/             component library, scene renderer
apps/
  web/            React UI (board, channel, the whole working loop), served by the local daemon on 127.0.0.1, later by the hosted tier
  desktop/        Tauri shell (links the daemon in-process) wrapping the web UI, plus the pixel office
  site/           the public website on the project's domain, static; its build and hosting are planned separately in `catervas-ops` (ADR 0047)
  ios/            native iOS app, after the desktop app
  android/        native Android app, after the desktop app
```

The web app comes first (changed in 0.18, from a web app served for the hosted tier alone). The daemon serves it: `catervas serve` serves the built app on 127.0.0.1 beside its command route, so the user opens Catervas in a browser on their own machine. Only `catervas serve` answers the browser routes, `/connect` and `/rpc`; `catervas run`, `catervas plan`, and `catervas contract new` serve no page, and their daemons answer those routes with 404 (changed in 0.23). The page's socket at `/rpc` answers each request as soon as its answer is ready, so that a slow one holds up neither the page's other requests nor its events, and the answers come in the order they are ready, each under its request's id; `subscribe` and `unsubscribe` are answered in the order they came, before the next request is read, and a `subscribe`'s events follow its answer. A request read is carried out even when the page closes the socket before its answer is sent, and when the daemon closes, the answers under way are sent before the socket closes, so that the page has the answer to `project.open`, which closes setup mode's daemon (changed in 0.69). The app is embedded in the `catervas` binary: release builds embed `apps/web/dist`, and debug builds read it from disk (added in 0.23). `catervas serve` opens the link in the default browser unless `--no-open` is given, and says so on stderr if none opens (added in 0.23). A binary built without the app answers every page with one line saying the web app was not built into it (added in 0.23). `catervas run` and `catervas plan` ask Claude Code whether it is signed in (`claude auth status --json`) before they start, refusing with "Claude Code is not signed in: sign in on the AI account page of the web app, or run claude auth login, or set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY where you start Catervas", and `catervas run` prints "account: Claude Code, signed in with a subscription" (or "an Anthropic Console account", "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from your environment", "another sign-in"), its `--json` giving `account: { signed_in, kind }`, never a key, while `catervas serve` opens the first-run wizard on the account step instead of refusing (added in 0.141; ADR 0084). `catervas serve` listens on port 7420, else the first free port of 7421 to 7429, else any free port, and serves one project; before a project is chosen it serves the first-run wizard alone (added in 0.23). The hosted tier serves the same app later (phase 20). The launch is on the web alone (phase 16; changed in 0.20, ADR 0018, and renumbered in 0.22 and 0.24 and by ADRs 0025, 0048, 0049, 0051 and 0057). The desktop app wraps the same UI and runs the daemon in-process, so nothing is started in a terminal (phase 18); its work starts only after the web release has been tested with real users. The phone apps are native to each OS, each in the platform's own toolkit, not the web app on a phone; they come after the desktop app (phase 19), and how a phone reaches a running Catervas is open (section 12). Every client is built from `@catervas/brand` (section 14).

The hub and a daemon for each team (added in 0.144; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 05). The port `catervas serve` holds is never a team's own daemon: it serves the hub, which answers the wizard and the computer's own methods and routes the browser to the team's daemon. Each team's drive has a daemon of its own on a port the system picks, with its `daemon.json`, hooks, `/mcp`, `/command` and `/connector/*` as a single team has them. The hub serves `/t/<team>/rpc` and `/t/<team>/documents/raw` for the team its address names (404 for one it does not drive), `/hub/rpc` for the hub itself (the wizard's methods, `teams.*` and `computer.*`), and `/rpc` and `/documents/raw` for the current team while there is one, else the hub's, so that a page that knows one team works as before. A team's address is the slug of its team id, with `-2`, `-3` for a repeat, worked out when the team starts. The browser's sessions and connect codes are the hub's for every team, and each team's page names the hub's port as its own. The hub is served again, closing the sockets it holds, each time a project is chosen in the wizard or the last team leaves; a team's page ends with that team's daemon.

What Catervas hosts (added in 0.19; ADR 0017; changed in 0.73, ADR 0047). Catervas hosts its public website on the project's domain, Catervas Cloud from phase 11, before the web launch (6.7, 9; ADR 0048), and the hosted tier (phase 20). How and where each is hosted, and its infrastructure, are planned separately in `catervas-ops`, Catervas's private operations repository. The working web app is not served from the domain: the local daemon serves it on 127.0.0.1, because its token link and its origin check (8.6) hold only there. No user needs a cloud account of their own to run Catervas.

`catervas-core` has no I/O and is where every rule in section 5 lives. It is tested exhaustively, in isolation. This is the piece that must be right and is the piece most worth reading for anyone evaluating the project.

### 8.2 Agent runtime

The first runtime adapter drives the Claude Code program (the engine underneath the Claude Agent SDK) as a child process in its non-interactive mode (ADR 0005). The choice is pragmatic rather than ideological: it ships the file and search tools a developer agent needs, it speaks MCP natively, it supports the Agent Skills folder format, it has subagents, and its hooks fire before and after every tool call, which is exactly where the governor needs to sit. Building a coding agent from scratch would cost the first two milestones and produce something worse.

Concretely, one agent session is one `claude -p` process with `--output-format stream-json` and `--input-format stream-json`, given: the agent's system prompt assembled from role, persona, memory, and contract (`--append-system-prompt-file`); only the built-in tools the agent's permission tiers grant (`--tools`, an allowlist, with `--disallowedTools Bash` as a second refusal of the one tool ADR 0004 names, followed by every `denied` tool of the session's connectors, added in 0.33, a user's servers' among them from 0.38); the agent's MCP servers and Catervas's own tool server (`--mcp-config`, `--strict-mcp-config`); a `PreToolUse` hook command, `catervas hook pre-tool-use`, that asks the daemon, which runs the governor and answers allow or deny with a reason; a `PostToolUse` hook that records the event and the running cost; a permission-prompt tool that denies anything the hook did not decide; a turn limit; and a stop on any budget. The program's shell tool is never enabled: commands run through the `catervas_exec` tool (8.3), git through `catervas_git_status`, `catervas_git_diff`, and `catervas_git_commit` under the `git_local` tier and `catervas_git_push` under `git_remote` (corrected in 0.8 from one `catervas_git`), and the program's web tools are enabled only under `network` (ADR 0004; added in 0.2). The runtime pins the oldest Claude Code version it was tested against and refuses to start on an older one.

The daemon's `PreToolUse` answer (added in 0.8). A call is denied, with a reason that starts with its kind, when its session is not one the daemon registered (`unknown_session`), when the agent is not active (`agent_not_active`; a paused agent's `chat` session excepted, in the hook and in Catervas's tool server alike, changed in 0.34), when the session has made its `max_tool_calls` (`tool_call_limit`, counted by the daemon, one per allowed call), when the tool is neither one of Catervas's nor a built-in with a tier (`tool_not_allowed`; `Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`, `LS`, and `ToolSearch` need `read`, `Edit`, `Write`, `MultiEdit`, and `NotebookEdit` `write_workspace`, `WebFetch` and `WebSearch` `network`, and no other built-in has one; Claude Code 2.1.280 no longer has `LS` or `MultiEdit`, which are kept only for an older version and are never put in a session's `--tools`), when a Catervas tool is not one of the session's own (`tool_not_in_session`: each session is registered with the Catervas tools it was given, a triage session with `catervas_triage_request` alone (a judgment session with `catervas_record_judgment` alone, added in 0.10, is gone, 0.115), a UI/UX Designer's `explore` session (6.8) with `catervas_read_task`, `catervas_read_board`, `catervas_read_rules`, `catervas_read_criteria`, `catervas_read_decisions`, and `catervas_propose_design_plan`, and `catervas_check_page` with the browser (added in 0.33), and the read tier's built-ins whatever its agent's tiers, the Designer's design review (5.4), a `verify` session, with `catervas_read_task`, `catervas_read_board`, `catervas_read_rules`, `catervas_read_criteria`, `catervas_read_decisions`, `catervas_check_page`, and `catervas_record_design_review` (added in 0.33), a conversation session (5.9) with `catervas_read_task`, `catervas_read_board`, `catervas_read_rules`, `catervas_read_criteria`, `catervas_post_message`, `catervas_create_task`, `catervas_write_memory`, and `catervas_read_decisions` (the last two added in 0.16), those of them its agent's tiers allow, and the read tier's built-ins alone, run in the project's root rather than a worktree (added in 0.14), a one-to-one chat's `chat` session with `catervas_read_task`, `catervas_read_board`, `catervas_read_rules`, `catervas_read_criteria`, `catervas_read_decisions`, and `catervas_chat_reply`, registered with the read tier alone whatever its agent's tiers, the read tier's built-ins, no connector and no `network`, run in the project's root (added in 0.34), and any other with those its agent's tiers allow, and Catervas's MCP server neither lists nor calls another to it), when a built-in's path is outside the session's worktree (`path_outside_workspace`), and otherwise by the check of 5.6, which for a kit connector's tool reads the tool's tag (6.7; added in 0.22), and for any connector's tool, `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, checks its server, its tag, and, for the built-in connector, every `url` in its input, and asks no tier (5.6; added in 0.33, changed in 0.38 from the built-in's alone and a tier after), and, for an `external_effect` tool, the Designer's plan gate, the input's size and the human's grant, asking the human when there is none (changed in 0.39), and, for a tool that changes the project (5.6), a session that is not an implement session about a task (`no_task_no_write`, after the Designer's plan gate; added in 0.92). Until 0.115 a session held to read paths was also refused a read outside them (`read_not_allowed`, last of all; added in 0.93; 5.6; ADR 0061 removed it). A session is no longer registered with `web` or `reads` (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: from 0.71 and 0.93 a role held to approved sites or to read paths was judged on the sites and the paths it named, 5.6): every session's web tools and reads are open to every role, and only the tiers, the protected paths and the working folder hold them. A path is resolved against the worktree and through its symlinks, so a committed link that points out of the worktree is judged by where it points; a read outside it is denied as a write is, because a session's files are its worktree's and nothing else on the machine (8.6); a finance session's are its finance folder's (6.6; added in 0.21). A `Glob` whose pattern is absolute or climbs with `..` is denied the same way. So is a path or a `Glob` pattern with a part that starts with `~` (`~`, `~/x`, `~user/x`, `src/~x`), because Claude Code expands a leading `~` to a home directory before the tool runs, and the hook would otherwise judge a path under the worktree that the tool never touches. A decision the log cannot record is a deny (`record_failed`), because a tool call the log cannot vouch for is one the governor cannot either. A decision whose team file or contract cannot be read is a deny (`team_unreadable`, `contract_unreadable`), for the same reason. The hooks fail closed: `catervas hook pre-tool-use --daemon <path>` prints a deny, with a reason that starts `hook_failed`, whenever it cannot get an answer (no daemon file, no daemon, a daemon that does not answer within ten seconds, an answer that is not a decision), and exits 2 with the reason on standard error if it fails itself, since exit 2 is the other answer Claude Code treats as blocking; the command Catervas gives Claude Code ends `|| exit 2`, so a hook that cannot be run at all (a missing or unrunnable `catervas`, which the shell reports as 127 or 126) or fails in any other way blocks the call too; the ten seconds are well under Claude Code's own hook timeout, after which it would let the call through. `catervas hook post-tool-use` prints nothing and never blocks, because the call it reports is over.

The session's process (added in 0.8). It is run in the task's worktree, or, for a task of a role with a private folder (6.6), in that folder, made for its owner alone when it is not there and with no sandbox (changed in 0.62), with `--session-id <id>`, so that every hook names the session Catervas registered; its system prompt is written to `.catervas/local/sessions/<id>/system-prompt.md` and kept after the session, as the exact text the session was told; and its MCP config is a file beside it, `mcp.json`, readable by its owner alone, because it holds the daemon's token and a process's arguments are readable by every user of the machine. The user's own settings are not loaded (`--setting-sources ""`), so neither the user's nor the repository's hooks, permissions, or `CLAUDE.md` reach a Catervas session; its settings are Catervas's alone, passed with `--settings` and built at each session start from the team file as it is then: the two hooks, and a `Read(<glob>)` deny rule for each protected path, which Claude Code also holds `Grep` and `Glob` to. A protected path that holds a parenthesis, a backslash, or a control character cannot be said in such a rule as it is, and Claude Code in `-p` mode ignores settings it cannot read without a word, so a session is not started while the team has one; the refusal names the path. The session pays with the account Claude Code is signed in to, which Claude Code finds for itself, or with a key the user set in their own environment (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`), which passes through as it was found and is never read (changed in 0.141; ADR 0084), and its environment is `PATH`, `HOME`, `USER`, `LANG`, `TERM`, `TMPDIR` and, each only when set, `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, nothing else inherited, with `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1` and `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` set so that the program neither updates itself nor keeps a memory of its own beside the agent's, so a base URL, a provider switch, or another secret in the user's shell cannot change which account pays or reach the session. `--max-turns` is the session's tool-call limit plus one, a backstop to the daemon's count. The session takes one message; a later one is a `resume` of it, once its process is gone. The oldest-version check gives `claude --version` ten seconds to answer. It ends at its `result` line, and is killed with all its process group when its caller aborts it or at its wall-clock limit, ending `aborted` or `limit`, whether or not its caller is still reading its events; a connector call that asks the human (5.6) stops the session as an agent's pause does, the hook denying every later call `session_stopped`, and it ends `aborted` with the detail `approval_needed: approval <seq>`, `tool_approval.requested` being the record of why, so `session.ended` gains no reason (added in 0.39); a process that exits without a result ends `error` with the tail of its standard error. A result that is an error ends the session `error`, one whose subtype says `success` while its `is_error` is set among them, or `provider_limit` when it shows the model provider's usage limit (5.5): to tell, the stream parser keeps the last `rate_limit_event`'s status and reset time and reads the result's `is_error` and `api_error_status` (added in 0.13). Whatever way it ends, its process group is killed once it is over, so nothing it started outlives it, and so it is if the daemon's runtime shuts down under it. The log records `session.started` with the purpose, model, and effort, and for a conversation the sequence number of the latest message it was shown (added in 0.14), and `session.ended` with the reason and what the program said. Catervas's tool server speaks the MCP revision the program asks for; to one on `2026-07-28`, as Claude Code 2.1.280 is, a list of tools says it is fresh for no time (`ttlMs` 0) and may be cached by that session's client alone (`cacheScope` `private`), because the list is the session's own and the program drops every tool of a list that says neither (added in 0.8). The oldest Claude Code Catervas runs on is 2.1.272.

Driving the team (added in 0.8). One process drives a project at a time: `catervas run`, `catervas serve`, `catervas plan`, and `catervas contract new` hold an exclusive lock on `.catervas/local/run.lock` for as long as they run, and a second refuses, naming the first's pid from `daemon.json`. A driving process starts in this order, and a step that fails leaves nothing running: the lock; the Ctrl-C listener; the settings; the credential, of which it prints the variable's name and never its value; `claude` on `PATH`; the daemon; the adapter, whose version check refuses an old `claude`; and recovery (5.15). It then ticks until nothing needs doing, printing what each tick did. A tick takes the process's turn and holds it while it reads the board, asks the governor, runs Catervas's own criteria, integrates, and prepares a session; it gives the turn back while its session runs and takes it again when the session ends. So every agent may have one session running beside other agents' sessions, while everything else is done one at a time; an agent never runs two work sessions at once, and a rule passes over an agent whose session runs as it passes over a sleeping one, and over a task whose session runs; an agent's chat is the one session beside its work session, a fork (5.9). There is no other limit than the team's active agents. A session's start prints `<task>: <agent> started its <purpose> session` (`<agent>: started its <purpose> session` about no task; JSON `{"started", "agent_id", "task_id"}`), and its tick's line follows when it ends. While sessions run and the next tick finds nothing, the process waits for a session to end, a command, a filed request, or the minute's recheck, and ticks again; it says it is idle, or that it waits for a sleeping agent, only when nothing runs (added in 0.118; ADR 0064). A tick that has nothing to do but wait for a sleeping agent (5.5) prints that it is waiting, for which agent and until when, and the process waits for that time, re-checking the board at least once a minute so that work filed straight into the store rather than through a command the lock-holder handles (`catervas task create` while the lock is held, among others) is not left until the agent wakes, and ticks again, the first Ctrl-C or `catervas stop` ending the wait at once, and a command of the user's that records something (an answer, a resolved escalation, a move, a paused agent) ending it too, so that the next tick gives what the command made to an agent that is awake, for `catervas run`, `catervas plan`, and `catervas contract new` alike; the waiting line prints again only when the agent or the time it names changes (added in 0.13). Once nothing needs doing, it says what waits on the user (5.7), shuts the daemon down, and exits; `catervas serve` instead waits until a command, a filed request, a sleeping agent's waking, or the next UTC day gives it something to do (added in 0.23). Saving the team file from Settings (`team.save`), applying a template (`template.apply`), and putting a newcomer in an agent's place (`agent.replace`) wake it too, so the change takes effect at once; saving the criteria (`criteria.save`) frees no work and is seen at the next check, at most a minute later (added in 0.36). `catervas serve` says why it is idle once, and again after a tick acts or when the reason changes; it prints lines for a person, and refuses `--json` (added in 0.23). While the team is paused no session starts but a chat's (5.9; changed in 0.34), and the tick says so. The daemon takes the user's commands on `POST /command`, behind its token, and answers each with what it did or why it did nothing (`$defs/commandReply` in `command.schema.json`); a command typed in another terminal while the lock is held is sent there and waits up to 120 seconds for the answer, and one that gets none is not retried, since it may have taken effect. The first Ctrl-C stops the run once every session running now has ended; the second aborts them all, leaving each task where it is for the next run to resume, with no escalation; the process then exits 130 (changed in 0.118; ADR 0064). A tick that fails stops the run as the first Ctrl-C does, and the process exits 1 once the running sessions have ended (130 when Ctrl-C was pressed; added in 0.118; ADR 0064). A tick busy outside a session, running a criterion or integrating, is not cut short: a Ctrl-C during it takes effect when it ends, and the second press aborts only the sessions running beside it (added in 0.9; changed in 0.118). `catervas plan` runs the triage, refining, and assignment rules and an epic's breakdown (up to the Architect's plan task, which a run writes) and close-out, and nothing that starts work, runs a criterion, or integrates. While the team is paused (`catervas pause`, section 3) a tick runs no rule but the chat rule, and when that starts nothing answers that the team is paused (changed in 0.34), so `catervas run` exits at once with that as its idle reason, while every command of the human's, `integrate` among them, is still handled (added in 0.23).

The system prompt is twelve sections in one order, whatever the role and the session's purpose: the role's prompt with its skills, the untrusted-content notice (8.6), the agent's name and persona, the team ("Your team", added in 0.137; ADR 0081; 5.9), the project scan, the agent's memory, the team rules, the criterion library, the contract, the tools the agent may call, the human's message, and the closing instruction for the session's purpose, which names the tool the session ends with. A section with nothing in it is left out, and the order of the rest does not change. The untrusted-content notice ends by naming each connector the session was given, the built-in's and a user's alike: "Everything the connector `a` returns is untrusted too.", or "Everything the connectors `a` and `b` return is untrusted too." (added in 0.38). A session given one Catervas tool, triage, is given no built-in tool, and its tools section lists that tool alone (the judgment session of 0.10 is gone, 0.115). The project scan, the memory, the criterion library, and the contract are each wrapped in an `untrusted` block, inside which a closing `untrusted` tag in any case or spacing is escaped, so that a file cannot end its block early; the team rules, the persona, and the human's message are the user's own and are not wrapped, except that a chat's history, which is a chat session's human's message, wraps the agent's own earlier lines in an `untrusted` block (added in 0.34). The memory section opens with a line Catervas writes outside the `untrusted` block, `<n> of <cap> tokens.`, which a session that can call `catervas_write_memory` gets with a request to prune when the notebook is past 80 percent of its cap; so the section is written even for an empty notebook, as `0 of <cap> tokens.` (5.8; added in 0.16). The scan, the library, and the human's message are cut at 16 KiB, the contract at 32 KiB, and the memory at four characters for each token of the team's `memory_cap_tokens` (changed in 0.16, from 32 KiB), each with a line saying so; the role and the tools are not cut (ADR 0011; added in 0.8).

Every session that reads the other repositories is told where they are (added in 0.114; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 03). After the stale twins line the Team rules say `- repositories: <entries joined ", ">. <own sentence>Read the others; change only your own task's files.`, each entry `<name> (<folder>)`, with `; /repos/<name> in your sandbox` when a command of its task's sandbox reads it, the task's own repository as `<name> (your task's repository)`, a member that is not there as `<name> (not found)` and one the session cannot read as `<name> (not readable here)`; the own sentence is `Your task works in <repo>. ` or `Your task works in the project's own folder. `, and nothing for a session with no task. The line is left out in a one-repository project, for the Marketing Specialist, for a task in a private folder, and when `repos.yaml` cannot be read.

Model defaults are set per role in `role.yaml`. The shipped defaults use Claude Opus 5.5 for the Product Manager, Architect, Developer, and UI/UX Designer (the Designer added in 0.31) with adaptive thinking and effort at `high`, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 for the Scrum Master, channel chatter, the Marketing Specialist's drafting, and the Finance Specialist (added in 0.54). Channel chatter is the conversation session, on Claude Sonnet 5.5 at `low` effort whatever the agent's model; a reaction is posted from the session that made the move, on that session's model (changed in 0.14; 5.9). A one-to-one chat's session runs on the agent's own model at `low` effort, so the agent answers in its own voice and knowledge (added in 0.34). Effort is the first knob a cost-conscious user should turn; setup's agent sheet and the Team page show it per agent as one of five, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`, the levels Claude Code takes, and name the model as Anthropic names it ("Opus 5.5"; changed in 0.125). Temperature is not a setting: Claude Code takes none and every model Catervas offers refuses one other than its own, so the sheet shows "Set by the model" (added in 0.125; ADR 0071). An agent's `model` in the team file may name an effort without a model id, and the role's model stands; changing an agent's effort never changes the model it runs on (added in 0.26).

The Designer's two tools (added in 0.33). `catervas_check_page { path, width, theme }`, the width `phone` or `desktop` and the theme `light` or `dark`, needs `read` and is offered only to a UI/UX Designer's session about a task that has the browser (5.6); anywhere else, and for a path that does not start with `/`, it is refused with `check_page_refused`. Catervas runs the check itself (8.3) and records `page.checked`. The answer holds the width, the theme, the path, the screenshot's file name, and the number and list of the problems found, the list in an `untrusted` block (8.6), followed by the screenshot as an image. `catervas_record_design_review { pass, reasons }` is offered to the design review alone (5.4).

The chat session (added in 0.34; ADR 0026). A `chat` session is about no task, run in the project's root, on its role's session limits, and is registered with the read tier alone, so the hook denies its edits, commands, web tools, connectors and every other Catervas write (`tool_not_allowed`, `tool_not_in_session`), and the protected `.catervas/local/**` keeps the log unread. Its first message is "<Name>, the user wrote to you in your one-to-one chat. Answer the newest message." followed by that message; its human's message is the chat's last 16 KiB, oldest first, the user's lines as "The user:" and the agent's as "You:" inside an `untrusted` block, a proposed request's title and text with its reply; and its closing instruction asks for one answer with `catervas_chat_reply`, in the persona's voice, with a request in it when work is needed. No other session is shown any chat. `catervas_chat_reply { text, request?: { title, text }, heard? }`, tier `read`, is offered in a chat session alone and records one `chat_message.posted` by the agent, in reply to the session's `in_reply_to`, answering `{ seq, said: "Sent. Your turn is over." }`; the model's turn then ends the session. It is refused with `chat_reply_refused` outside a chat session, for a second reply in one session, even one sent at the same moment as the first (the check and the record are one step; changed in 0.34's fix wave), and for a reply outside its limits (5.9), and a reply refused for its limits does not use up the one. While an agent is in a chat session, paused or not, `team.activity` says "Answering your chat", with no word of the chat.

A user's connectors in a session (added in 0.38; ADR 0030). A session about a task, `refine`, `plan`, `explore`, `implement` or `verify`, the Designer's design review among them, is given its agent's own servers (6.7); a session given one Catervas tool (triage) gets none, and nor do `ceremony`, `conversation` and `chat`, which are about no task. The built-in connector keeps its own rule (5.6). Only a confirmed server is given: one whose definition kept beside its keys hashes as the team file's entry does now, with every key the entry names kept. Any other is left out of `mcp.json`, out of the session's registration and out of the untrusted-content notice, so the hook denies its tools `connector_not_in_session`, and the agent page says "Connect again" (F9). What the store answered at session setup is remembered, so a keychain or private file that could not be read leaves the server out and the page says why (`store_unavailable`). A user's server adds no tier to the session, so it never lets `WebFetch` or `WebSearch` through for an agent without `network`. No key is written to `mcp.json`. A `stdio` server's entry is the launcher, `catervas connector run --daemon <daemon.json> --session <id> --server <name>`, with no environment of its own. It asks the daemon for the server's command, arguments and keys, clears its environment, keeps its own `PATH`, `HOME`, `LANG` and `TMPDIR`, adds the server's keys, and execs the server, so the model credential in Claude Code's environment never reaches a connector. An `http` server's entry is its `url` and a `headersHelper`, `catervas connector headers` with the same arguments, each word single-quoted for `sh`, a `'` written `'\''`, because Claude Code runs the helper through a shell; it prints the server's headers with the keys filled in, as one JSON object. Both ask the daemon's `POST /connector/launch { session, server }`, which takes the daemon's token, answers 503 in setup mode as the hook's route does, and is never logged. It refuses a session the daemon did not register (404 `unknown_session`); a server the session was not given, or that is no longer a custom server of the session's agent (403 `connector_not_in_session`); a server whose kept definition is missing, hashes differently, or lacks a key the entry names (403 `connector_not_confirmed`), the second check after session setup's; and, when the keychain or the private file fails, or does not answer within five seconds, less than the helper's eight, as a keychain waiting to be unlocked may not, answers 503 `secret_store_unavailable` (the deadline added in 0.38 after review). Otherwise it answers `{ command, args, env, cwd }` for `stdio`, `cwd` the server's own folder (6.7), which the launcher changes to before it execs and refuses an answer without, and `{ headers }` for `http`. On any refusal the launcher writes the reason on standard error and the helper prints nothing, and both exit 1. A `stdio` server then does not start. An `http` server does not fail with its helper: Claude Code (probed on 2.1.287) connects it without the headers and offers its tools. So the route takes any server it refuses from the session's registration, and the hook denies its calls `connector_not_in_session`; the server, at its confirmed address, is sent no key. Claude Code gives a headers helper ten seconds, which a computer's keychain asking the user can outlast; the helper then fails as any other refusal does, and the Advanced copy says to allow Catervas "Always".

The goal rules (added in 0.130; ADR 0075). The planning and the measuring rule of 5.18 come last in a tick, after rule 10 and before the tick says it is idle, so they act only when no other rule did; both run only under every rule in a tick about no one task, and neither runs while the team is paused. A `goal` session is a work session of its agent (an agent has one at a time), is about no task, and is given its agent's connectors as a task session is (the paragraph above, changed in 0.130: `refine`, `plan`, `explore`, `implement`, `verify` and `goal`); the exact text it was told is kept like any session's. A tick that ran one says `<goal>: ran <agent>'s goal planning session, which <how it ended>: <its last words>` (`goal reading` for a measuring session), and `catervas run` prints it as `goal-<n>: <what>`.
A signed-in connector in a session (added in 0.41; ADR 0033). The headers helper sends `Authorization: Bearer <access token>` for a server whose entry holds a grant, and Claude Code, given an `Authorization` header, does not try to sign in itself. Session setup first refreshes a token that would expire within the session's wall clock and five minutes; a server the service ended is left out (`sign_in_again`), and one whose refresh failed while its token has expired is left out of that session alone. The launch route refreshes a token that would expire within a minute, waiting three seconds for the service and the whole answer within five (`KEY_STORE_DEADLINE`), and the refresh and its save run on a task that finishes when the wait does not, so a rotated token is always kept; a lapsed grant answers 403 `sign_in_again` and a refresh that did not finish with an expired token 503 `sign_in_failed`, each taking the server from the session as any refusal does. Two launches of one expired grant make one request to the service.

A user's skills in a session (added in 0.40; ADR 0034). Every session not given one Catervas tool alone, that is a task session, a `conversation`, a `ceremony` and a `chat`, loads its agent's `in_use` team and agent skills (6.7) on demand, through Claude Code's own skills mechanism. The adapter writes a plugin folder for the session outside the project, `<state>/skills/<local project id>/<session id>/` in the user's Catervas state folder, `<local project id>` as 6.7 keeps a connector's keys. The folder is 0700 and its files 0600; it is written fresh at each start and resume, removed when the Claude Code process exits whatever the outcome, and the project's whole `<state>/skills/<local project id>/` is removed when the daemon starts. It holds `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, `{"name":"catervas"}`, and `skills/<name>/` with a copy of each skill whose `SKILL.md` frontmatter is rewritten to `name` and `description` alone, the body left byte for byte. It is outside the project because `.catervas/local/**` is a `Read` deny rule that Claude Code applies to a session run in the project's root (`conversation`, `ceremony`, `chat`), which a hook's `allow` cannot lift, and a skills folder in the worktree could be committed by an agent. The adapter passes `--plugin-dir <that folder>` and adds `Skill` to `--tools` only when the session has at least one skill, and every session's `--settings` sets `"disableSkillShellExecution": true`, which stops a skill's `!` commands whatever is allowed. Claude Code names each skill `catervas:<name>` and lists its name and description itself, so the prompt gains nothing; it loads a skill's body when the skill is used and a referenced file when the agent reads it. The `role.yaml` skills stay in the prompt (ADR 0011), unless a confirmed skill of the same name replaces one, which then leaves the prompt of the sessions that load skills.

Kits in a session (added in 0.44; ADR 0036). A session's skills include its role's kit's, after the agent's and the team's and with no pin or confirmation, and its `stdio` and `http` connectors include each kit entry in the agent's file that is exactly what the role's kit says now and is confirmed on this computer, as a custom one is; an entry the kit has changed since is left out of the session's `mcp.json`, registration and launch, and the agent's page says `connect_again`, or `not_in_kit` when the kit has no service of the name. The kit changes only with the binary, which ends every session, so the launch route needs no kit check of its own. Two checks of the hook belong to skills. A `Skill` call is allowed only when its input is exactly `{ "skill": "catervas:<name>" }`, or that with `"args": <string>` holding no `@`, with `<name>` one of the session's skills; anything else, a bare name, which would load Claude Code's own skill of that name, one of Claude Code's own skills, another field, a non-string or an `args` with an `@`, is denied `skill_not_in_session`. It is judged after the `tool_call_limit` check and before the connector check, asks no tier, meets no plan gate, and an allowed call counts towards `max_tool_calls`. A `Read`, `Glob` or `Grep` whose `file_path` or `path`, resolved through links, lies under the session's skills folder is allowed at tier `read` with no paths, so the contract's `allowed_paths` and the protected paths are not asked about, whatever the session's worktree; a `Glob` pattern stays relative; every other tool's path there, and any write, is `path_outside_workspace`.

The `runtime` crate defines an adapter trait (`start_session`, `resume`, `abort`, with an event stream on the session handle) so that a second provider can be added. The web UI (phase 6) runs on the Claude Code program alone. Other providers and engines come in phase 13 (added in 0.24, ADR 0023; renumbered by ADR 0029, ADR 0048, ADR 0049, ADR 0051 and ADR 0057): the user connects any AI account, Claude, OpenAI and more, and chooses an engine, open-source ones such as Hermes and OpenClaw included, and Catervas's tools, the skills (Agent Skills format) and the connectors (MCP servers) work on every engine. The governor's enforcement holds on each: an engine without an equivalent of the `PreToolUse` hook is limited to Catervas's own MCP tools, so the governor still sees every action. Claude Code holds the account (ADR 0084), so the provider is whatever Claude Code is signed in to. The trait is not promised stable until a second adapter exists (changed in 0.24, from "there is no second provider in the first release").

### 8.3 Sandbox

Agents with `execute` run commands inside a container per task, with the task's git worktree (5.14) mounted at `/workspace` and network disabled unless the agent holds `network`, which every role does by default (changed in 0.115; ADR 0061: a role held to approved sites got a sandbox with no network from 0.71, and now every sandbox has the network; the user can take `network` from an agent, and its sandbox is then made with none). Docker is the first backend because it is what target users already have. The container is discarded when the task is accepted or cancelled. The image's tag is `catervas/sandbox:<crate version>-<digest>`, the digest the first 6 bytes of the sha256 of its Dockerfile as 12 lowercase hex digits, so a changed Dockerfile is a new tag, the old image counts as missing, and the computer check in Setup offers to prepare the new one (added in 0.110). The image carries the shared libraries a headless browser needs (libnss3, libnspr4 and the rest of Chrome's, added in 0.135), because a project's own browser binary (Remotion, Playwright, Puppeteer) fails to start without them and an agent cannot install system packages there; the browser itself is not in the image. The owner's system packages (added in 0.137; ADR 0081). `team.yaml`'s `sandbox { packages }` lists Debian packages, each matching `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9+.-]*$`, unique, at most 40. When the list is not empty, task and preview containers run the image `catervas/sandbox:<version>-<digest>-p<12 hex>`, the 12 hex digits the first 6 bytes of the sha256 of the sorted list, built once when missing from the shipped image with `apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends`, before the container starts; a build that fails is `SandboxError::Unavailable`, which carries the last lines of the build output. A held sandbox made with another list is recreated (the daemon's sandbox recreator). Settings, How work runs, under Show advanced settings, has "System tools in the sandbox", one package name per line. The agent tool `catervas_install_system_packages { packages, why }`, tier `execute`, held by the Software Developer, the UI/UX Designer and the Architect, takes 1 to 10 names (checked the same way, at most 40 in the team) and a `why` of 1 to 300 characters; it builds the image first, so a name that cannot be installed is never left in the team file, then makes the task's sandbox again (the worktree is mounted, so no file is lost), writes the names into `sandbox.packages`, records `team.updated` with the agent as `updated_by`, and posts "<name> added <packages> to the sandbox: <why>" in the channel. Agents still never run as root; the owner sees and removes the packages in Settings.

The image's `/tmp` holds nothing, the Dockerfile's last step emptying it, so npm, pnpm and cargo write their caches there as the user's own uid, which every container runs as, rather than finding root's (added in 0.110). A missing sandbox image, in a task's sandbox or a preview, says to open the computer check in Setup and choose Prepare it, as the Designer's browser does (added in 0.110). Git operations run on the host through `catervas_git_status`, `catervas_git_diff`, `catervas_git_commit`, and `catervas_git_push`, on the task's branch in its worktree, not inside the container (ADR 0004; corrected in 0.8); the governor's diff check for `allowed_paths` and the protected paths runs against that branch before acceptance. The no-sandbox choice made in setup is written to the project's `.catervas/local/settings.json` as `sandbox: none` when the project is taken on (added in 0.23).

The other repositories (added in 0.114; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 03). In a project folder the container also mounts every other present member of its task's read roots (5.6) read-only at `/repos/<name>`, after the worktree, so that a command can read a sibling; a task in the project's own folder mounts every member. A path with a comma is refused as the worktree's is. The base container mounts none, and the no-sandbox mode ignores them. A member added while the container runs is mounted when the container is next made.

**Git in the checks (added in 0.122; ADR 0069).** The `command` and `test` criteria Catervas runs execute in a container made for them, which mounts the worktree's git store (`git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, the task's member's for a task in a member) read-only at its own absolute path, so that the worktree's `.git` file resolves and git can read refs, the index and objects; it can write no hook, config, ref or lock that the host's git would run or read next. The container is dropped after the checks; an agent's container is a different one, the held container remembering which it is. Since 0.137 (ADR 0081) an agent's container mounts the same store read-only too, under the same secret rule, so its read-only git commands (`git log`, `git diff`, `git status`) work in it; writes still go through `catervas_git_*` (ADR 0004). Because every sandbox has the network (ADR 0061), a repository whose settings hold a secret (a remote URL with a user part, or any `http.*.extraheader`) is not mounted, and its checks run without git, as before. The base container of a `new tests` criterion is unchanged.

Users who will not run Docker can opt into a no-sandbox mode with a loud warning. The governor still enforces paths and permissions, but process isolation is gone. Commands then run on the host as the user, with `HOME` set, so a command can read the user's credential files (`~/.git-credentials`, `~/.ssh`, `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, the `gh` configuration), can push through a git wrapped in a script, which `catervas_exec`'s first-word check does not see, and can read `.catervas/local/daemon.json`, whose token lets it give the daemon the user's own commands (8.2); the warning names all three, not only the loss of isolation (added in 0.8; the third in 0.9). Every start of a driving process in no-sandbox mode prints it on standard error: "warning: no-sandbox mode (.catervas/local/settings.json says sandbox: none). Agents' commands run on this machine as you, with your HOME: they can read your credential files (~/.git-credentials, ~/.ssh, ~/.claude/.credentials.json, the gh configuration), push with a git hidden in a script, which catervas_exec's check does not see, and read .catervas/local/daemon.json, whose token lets them act as you through catervas: approve, accept, answer, add skills, mark orders placed and received, and integrate, and get the keys you gave a connector, which they can also read from a running connector's /proc/<pid>/environ. The governor still checks every path and permission it is asked about." The clause on connector keys was added in 0.38, and "add skills" in 0.40: a command that reads that token can send `skill_save`, whose `skill.added` counts as the person's confirmation (6.7, 8.6). "Mark orders placed and received" was added in 0.74 after review: the same command can send `purchase_order_place` and `purchase_order_receive`, which an order's fold counts as the owner's own marking of it placed and received (6.10, 8.6). The choice is this machine's, not the project's, so it lives in `.catervas/local/settings.json`, which is never committed (added in 0.6); a machine that has never been asked runs the sandbox.

The preview (added in 0.33; ADR 0026, the founder's decisions of 2026-09-30). `team.yaml`'s top-level `preview { prepare?, start, port?, path }` says how to open the project's app: `prepare` and `start` are commands of 1 to 500 characters, `port` is optional (changed in 0.106) and, when given, 1024 to 65535, and `path` starts with `/`, `/` by default. Every project command runs in the sandbox (ADR 0004), so the preview needs Docker. `prepare` installs and builds: it runs in a container `catervas-prepare-<project>-<task>` of the sandbox image, with the worktree mounted and the network on (`bridge`) and the owner's computer named `host.docker.internal` (`--add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway`; changed in 0.120; ADR 0067), for at most 15 minutes, and only its output's last 40 lines are kept. Left out, it is skipped. It is reused while its key holds, the sha256 of the task branch's tree and the `prepare` text, kept in `.catervas/local/previews/<task>.json`; uncommitted edits are not in the key, and `start` reads the worktree as it is, so a development server shows them and a prebuilt program only after a commit. `start` runs in `catervas-preview-<project>-<task>`, with the worktree mounted, on the network (`bridge`) with the same `--add-host`, so the app reaches the internet and the services on the owner's computer at `host.docker.internal` (changed in 0.120; ADR 0067; on Linux that is the Docker bridge's address, so such a service must listen on every address, not `127.0.0.1` alone). The owner's environment file (added in 0.120; ADR 0067): when `.catervas/local/preview.env` is a file, `prepare` and `start` get it with `--env-file <its absolute path>`, read by Docker itself in Docker's env-file format (one `NAME=value` per line, `#` comments, no quotes, a line without `=` passing Catervas's own variable of that name), and no other container, session or process gets it. It is read each time a preview opens; editing it does not prepare again. Catervas waits up to 120 seconds for `http://localhost:<port><path>` to answer, asking once a second from inside the container (`curl`, else `wget`), since the host cannot reach that network namespace. With no `port` it finds the port (added in 0.106; ADR 0054): each second it reads `/proc/net/tcp` and `/proc/net/tcp6` in the container, either of which may be missing, takes the ports in the listening state at 1024 or above, in ascending order, and probes each with `<path>` until one answers; that port is the one `preview.started` records and the session is told. `preview.prepared { tree, seconds }`, whose seconds count the preparing and the starting together, `preview.started { port }`, and, once the session ends, `preview.stopped { reason }` record it (8.5). Each preview has its own network namespace, so two previews on one port never collide (changed in 0.120). Catervas opens a preview for each session given the built-in connector (5.6) and tells every browsing session the preview's address (`http://localhost:<port><path>`) at the end of its first message, the Designer's design review included (added in 0.106), and one it cannot open escalates the task with `preview` (5.7), except that a Designer's explore or implement session whose `prepare` failed or whose `start` never answered, while its task branch has no commit of its own, merges from the integration branch not counting (`git rev-list --count --no-merges --first-parent base..branch` is 0), runs without the preview instead (added in 0.134): its first message says "The preview did not start (<the error's first line>); this task has no commits yet, so build without it and run the app yourself when its entry point exists.", nothing is escalated, and every later failure escalates as above. Whether Docker can be reached is asked of `docker info` at most once a minute, and `docker info` is given 10 seconds: a Docker that has not answered by then counts as not reachable until the next ask (changed in 0.63); only an answer that needs it asks, a design review that waits on the Designer's browser and an assignment that names a Designer, so no other request of a page waits for it (changed in 0.63). Those that ask do not wait either: the driver asks `docker info` for its first answer before its daemon listens, which takes at most those 10 seconds, and from then on a page's request and the governor's door are given the last answer at once, while `docker info` is asked again on a thread of its own once that answer is a minute old (changed in 0.69). In no-sandbox mode it cannot be.

The browser (added in 0.33). The connector runs as a container `catervas-browser-<project>-<task>` of the pinned Playwright image (6.7), labelled as the sandbox is, as the user's uid and gid, in the preview's network namespace (`--network container:catervas-preview-<project>-<task>`), so it shares the preview's network and its `/etc/hosts`, `host.docker.internal` included (Docker refuses `--add-host` beside `--network container:`). Chromium runs with `--proxy-server http://127.0.0.1:9`, a dead port, bypassed for `localhost` and `host.docker.internal` (`localhost,host.docker.internal`; Playwright turns Chromium's own loopback bypass off once a proxy is set), and with `--allowed-origins http://localhost:<port>;http://host.docker.internal:*;https://host.docker.internal:*`, and the governor checks every `url` (5.6). The page check (`catervas_check_page`) takes the same bypass. These are three barriers, the preview's network being on the bridge (changed in 0.120; ADR 0067). A test in Docker proves the proxy and the origins each on its own, and that with every flag on the browser reaches a page on the owner's computer and nothing else, and the governor's is proved by its own test; `--allowed-origins` alone does not stop a redirect, which is why the proxy is there. Stopping a preview, and the task's cleanup, remove its preview, browser and prepare containers by name, so a killed session leaves none behind.

The page check (added in 0.33). `catervas_check_page` (8.2) runs Catervas's own script, which the agent never gets, in the same image, as the same user, in the same namespace and behind the same proxy. It opens the page 360 or 1280 pixels wide and 800 high, in the light or the dark colour scheme, fails on a status that is not `2xx`, takes a screenshot of what is in view, and runs axe-core 4.13.0, the version the web app's tests pin, shipped with its licence, with the tags `wcag2a`, `wcag2aa`, `wcag21a`, `wcag21aa`, and `wcag22aa`, reporting one problem per element. The script ends itself after 90 seconds, and Catervas ends the check on its own clock after 150, so a docker that hangs cannot hold the tool call. Each check's container is named `catervas-check-<preview container>-<random>`, and a check Catervas ends on its clock has its container removed by that name at once, rather than left running (changed in 0.37). The check and the browser run with `--pull never`: an image that is not on the machine fails them at once, rather than being pulled unseen (both changed in the step's fix wave). So the preview does not start without the browser's image: the session escalates its task at once with reason `preview`, and the detail tells the human to open the computer check in Setup and fetch it, rather than the Designer failing every check until its sessions run out. Screenshots are kept at `.catervas/local/screenshots/<task>/<session>-<width>-<theme>.png`. Only the check writes there: the browser saves what it saves, and its own files, in a folder of its session's own, `.catervas/local/browser/<task>/<session>/`, so an agent cannot replace a check's screenshot (changed in the step's fix wave). That folder is removed with the task's worktree once the task is accepted or cancelled (5.14).

The release build (added in 0.33). The web server's admission of a browser at `localhost:<port>` without a code (8.6) is compiled only with the `e2e` feature, into `catervas-e2e-serve`; the release build is never built with `--all-features`, which would compile it in, and `cargo xtask check` fails when an xtask command or a CI workflow names that flag.

### 8.4 Storage

SQLite through `rusqlite` with the bundled engine for the event log and the projections the UI reads (board, costs; the channel is read from the log until phase 6 needs a view; changed in 0.18 from phase 5). The one-to-one chats are kept in the log alone, as `chat_message.posted` events, and read from it with no projection (added in 0.34). Files under `.catervas/` for anything the user should be able to read, diff, and edit: contracts, decisions, memories, role overrides. The event log is the source of truth for what happened; the files are the source of truth for what the team knows. The log is machine-local, under `.catervas/local/`, and is never committed; the files are what travels with the repository (decided 2026-09-15). On startup, Catervas reconciles the two and reports any drift rather than silently picking one, and recovers interrupted sessions (5.15). Task ids come from a counter in the log, so they are unique across processes and unbroken across restarts, and the counter is moved past the highest id a contract file under `.catervas/contracts/` already holds and past the highest number any `feature/CTV-<n>`, `fix/CTV-<n>` or `docs/CTV-<n>` branch holds, local or remote (branches made before 0.119, since a branch made since names no task, so a fresh clone's counter does not see those tasks and an id it hands out again clashes with nothing on the forge, where no id is; changed in 0.119, ADR 0066), a repository whose branches cannot be listed counting as having none (changed in 0.83, ADR 0053), and in a project folder past the task branches of every member that is present as well, a member that is missing or whose branches cannot be listed counting as having none (changed in 0.111, ADR 0057), so that a task's id is unique across the project's repositories, so a new task's number is past every committed contract and every old task branch, and an id is never one a contract in the repository already has — a fresh clone, whose log starts empty, does not hand out CTV-1 again — and a new contract is refused rather than written over a file that is already there (added in 0.8); a project has 999,999 of them, which is where `CTV-<n>` stops being an id the contract schema accepts, and Catervas refuses to create a task past that rather than hand back something that is not one. Older projects (changed in 0.116; ADR 0062). A project made before 0.116 may hold what sprints left, and Catervas keeps reading it and never writes it again: `.catervas/sprints/S<n>.yaml`, left as it is and read by nothing (`sprint.schema.json` is gone); the events `sprint.started`, `sprint.planned` and `sprint.ended` and sessions in the `planning` and `standup` threads in its log, which the store folds into its tables and columns so that the log replays (8.5); `team.yaml`'s `plan_in_sprints` and `ambient_messages_per_sprint`, read and not written (5.12); and a contract's `sprint` field, read and ignored (5.11). Its Backlog and any sprint left open hold nothing: a task there is assigned like any other ready task on the first tick, and the allowances and the channel's ambient allowance count per UTC day whatever sprint is open. Past events are never rewritten or deleted. The Finance Specialist's books, receipts, statement imports, receipts-mailbox settings with its approved senders, and ledger of filed messages live under `.catervas/local/finance/`, machine-local like the event log and never committed (6.6; added in 0.21). The ready-made teams (3) are not kept there: they live in the binary, not in `templates/` (added in 0.103). Team templates (3) are kept outside every project, in the user's Catervas state folder: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/catervas`, else `$HOME/.config/catervas`, else `%APPDATA%\catervas`, the first of the three that is set, as `templates/<slug>.yaml` (added in 0.35). A save makes the folders it needs 0700, the state folder too when it is the first thing to make it, and writes each file 0600, beside the file and then renamed over it, so a reader never sees half of one. Only a slug names a file, so no name or slug reaches outside the folder; a file whose name is not a slug is not listed, and one that is not a template is listed as unreadable. Saving, renaming and deleting a template record no event, since no project's log owns the file; using one records events in the project (4.4). With none of the three variables set there is no state folder, and saving, renaming and deleting a template, and previewing or using a saved one, are refused with `no_state_folder`, while the list answers with no saved team (`folder` null) and a ready-made team can still be previewed and used (changed in 0.103). The Procurement Specialist's `mail/` (added in 0.77), under its private folder, holds `mailbox.json` (the settings, never the password), `ledger.json`, `out/<n>.txt` and `out/<n>.sent.txt`, and `in/<yyyy-mm>/<n>/`; it is left out of a task's copy of the folder and of the baseline its changes are read against, since a reply is a seller's words and not the agent's work.

A project folder's members (added in 0.110; ADR 0057; phase 9 step 01). `.catervas/repos.yaml`, held to `docs/schemas/repos.schema.json`, is `{ repos: [{ name, path, integration_branch? }] }`, one to sixteen entries, and has no `version` field; unknown keys are refused. `name` is kebab-case starting with a letter, at most 32 characters, so that `<name>-<criterion>` is always a valid criterion name; `path` is the absolute path of the member's top folder on this computer; `integration_branch` is 1 to 255 characters with no whitespace, and when it is left out the member's default branch is read when it is needed. Names are unique, paths are unique and none is inside another, which the schema cannot say and `validate_repos` does. A file with one entry is what removing members leaves; `project.create_folder` takes two. The file is written before the event that records its change, as a contract's is, by `repo.add`, `repo.remove` and `repo.locate` under the integration lock, one writer at a time. The project folder is a git repository with no remote, and it is a repository root, so everything that treats a project's root as a repository's works on it unchanged. Its scan is its members' (4.1, 5.13): the folder itself is never scanned, and its criterion library holds the members' checks, named for their member.

The machine-level index (added in 0.139; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 02). `machine.db` in the state folder (`~/.config/catervas/`), apart from every project's log, SQLite's default rollback journal with a 30 second busy timeout, every table `STRICT`, with a `schema_migrations` and migrations of its own under `migrations/machine/`, run by the runner the event log uses. Four tables: `transcript_files` (`path`, `read_to`, the byte offset read up to, `turns`, `unreadable_lines`, `read_at`), so a second scan reads only what was appended, and a file shorter than its offset is read again from 0 (`unreadable_lines` counts every line it could not read, a blank line included, and `catervas discover` says "skipped <n> lines it couldn't read"); `sessions` (`session_id`, `cwd`, `git_branch`, `version`, `entrypoint`, `title`, `first_at`, `last_at`, `place` one of `owner`, `catervas`, `gone`, `not_a_project`, and `project_root`), one row per session whose folder, branch, version and entrypoint are those of its earliest turn; `replies` (`reply_key`, `session_id`, `model`, `at` and the four token counters), one row per reply keyed by its message id, else its request id, each counter the largest seen because Claude Code writes one line per content block and a resumed session repeats earlier replies, and its session the one that started earliest; and `projects` (`root`, `is_git`, `ownership` `yours` or `explored`, `present`, `first_seen_at`, `checked_at`), whose rows are never deleted. Times are RFC 3339 UTC with milliseconds. Placement is recomputed over every session each scan.

The finding tables (added in 0.146; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 06). Migration 7 of `machine.db` makes `choices` (`key` primary key, `choice` one of `team`, `watch`, `ignore`, `at`), `separations` (`a`, `b`, the two real paths the owner said are different, `a < b`, primary key on both), `moved` (`old` primary key, `new`: a gone folder located, applied when sessions are placed, so the sessions that worked under `old` and below it are placed under `new`), `declared_services` (`service_id` primary key, the catalog's id or `other:<name>`, `name`, `at`) and `hand_routines` (`id`, `name`, `project_key`, `schedule` free text, `at`), all `STRICT`. `catervas_core::claude_history::fold_by_remote` takes the separations: two roots with one normalised repository address are one project unless the owner separated them. `state.json` also holds `finding_paused: true` while the owner paused finding and `export_card: "dismissed"` once the owner dismissed the card that offers the export; neither is written otherwise, and Forget everything clears `export_card` and leaves finding paused. A declared bookkeeping service forms the project "Bookkeeping (<service>)", sourced `declared`, when no session formed one; a name with no catalog id is kept and forms nothing.
The GitHub tables (added in 0.148; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 06d). Migration 8 of `machine.db` makes `github_repos` (`full_name` primary key, `remote_key` the repository's normalised remote as a found folder's is, `pushed_at`, `private`, `default_branch`, `seen_at`, the time of the read that last listed it) and `github_claude_work` (`full_name`, `kind` one of `branch`, `pull`, `name` the branch or the pull request's title, `number`, `draft`, `updated_at`, primary key on the first three), both `STRICT`. A read replaces the rows of the repositories it listed; a repository it did not list keeps its rows and shows as not seen lately.

The links tables and the files proofs are read from (added in 0.149; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 06b). Migration 9 of `machine.db` makes `links` (`a`, `b`, `answer` one of `yes`, `no`, `proof` the JSON of the proofs shown with the answer, none for a Yes chosen from the Maybe list, `at`; primary key `(a, b)`, project keys, `a < b`) and `session_roots_written` (`session_id`, `root`; primary key on both), both `STRICT`, and reads every transcript again once. A `Write`, `Edit` or `MultiEdit` call's file path is looked at when the transcript is read, decided as the root of the project it is under (a root the index holds, else the nearest folder above it with a `.git` folder), and dropped: only the root is kept, never the path or any text. Proofs are read from the committed files of a project's repository at `HEAD`, through `git show`, never from the working tree: `package.json`, `Cargo.toml`, `go.mod`, `vercel.json`, `netlify.toml`, `CNAME`, compose files (`docker-compose*.y*ml`, `compose*.y*ml`) and Terraform `*.tf` files in a folder at most three deep, `.gitmodules` at the root, `.github/workflows/*.y*ml`, and `k8s/**` and `deploy/**` YAML at most four deep. A file over 256 KiB is skipped, at most 300 files are read for a project, the shallowest first, nothing under `node_modules`, `vendor`, `target` or `.git` is walked, and a folder with no git repository or no commit gives none. Nothing is written to a repository.

The proposal tables (added in 0.150; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 06e). Migration 10 of `machine.db` makes `proposal_edits` (`card_id` primary key, `name`, `template`, `purpose`, each null until edited, and `from_claude` 0 or 1, 1 while the name, purpose or template is Claude's suggestion and the owner has not changed it), `moved_out` (`card_id`, `project_key`, primary key of both: a project the owner moved out of a card) and `made_teams` (`slug` primary key, `root`, `made` the JSON of what Catervas created, `{ created: [paths], projects: [keys] }`, and `at`). Nothing in them is read from a conversation. A team made from the proposal is undone from `made_teams`, and a card's id is a hash of the sorted keys of its group, so an edit follows the card across calls.

The jobs table (added in 0.140; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 03). Migration 2 of `machine.db` makes `jobs` (`origin`, `file`, `name`, `kind` one of the 13 wire values, `display_name`, `schedules` a JSON array of strings as written, `folder`, `project_root`, `expires_at`, `state`, `state_at`, `last_seen`), keyed by `(origin, file, name)` with an index on `project_root`, and sets every `transcript_files` row's `read_to`, `turns` and `unreadable_lines` to 0, so each transcript is read again once and the tool calls in lines read before are found; the upserts of migration 1 give the same result when repeated, so nothing counts twice. A job source's rows are replaced only when the source answered, in one transaction, and every row written or confirmed gets `last_seen` set to the scan's time; a source that did not answer keeps its rows and their `last_seen`. Session crons (`origin` `claude_session`, from `CronCreate` calls in transcripts) are kept as they are read and never replaced, and their `project_root` is set again from `sessions` on each scan. The key stands in for a repository's identity: the root.

The services tables (added in 0.142; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 03b). Migration 3 of `machine.db` makes `tool_calls` (`tool_use_id` primary key, `reply_key`, `tool_name` as written, `touches_spreadsheet`, `at`, with an index on `reply_key`; a row only for a tool use with a server or on a spreadsheet file, the first row of an id staying) and `configured_servers` (`source` one of `claude_code`, `claude_ai`, `claude_desktop`, `found_in`, `name`, `kind` one of `stdio`, `http`, `sse`, `host`, `program`, keyed by `(source, found_in, name)`), and sets every `transcript_files` row's `read_to`, `turns` and `unreadable_lines` to 0, so each transcript is read again once and the tool calls are found; the inserts are idempotent, so nothing counts twice. `configured_servers` is a snapshot, all of it replaced on each scan; `tool_calls` is the history. Services are not stored: they are derived on each read from the two tables and the catalog, so a catalog update applies to old rows.

The claude.ai and copies tables (added in 0.143; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 04). Migration 4 of `machine.db` makes `claude_exports` (`account`, `content_at`, `imported_at`; one row per export by the latest time its content holds, an export already imported ignored), `claude_conversations` (`uuid` primary key, `account`, `title`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, `messages`, `seen_in_export_at`, `first_imported_at`) and `claude_projects` (`uuid` primary key, `account`, `name`, `description`, `doc_names` a JSON array, `created_at`, `updated_at`, `seen_in_export_at`, `first_imported_at`). A re-import replaces an item's fields when the incoming `updated_at` is at least the stored one or the stored one is none and keeps the latest export time that held it; whether an item is in its account's latest export is worked out when read, so import order never matters. Migration 5 makes `session_links` (`session_id`, `other_id`, `kind` `copy_of` or `maybe_same`) and `reply_copies` (`reply_key` primary key, `same_as`), both rebuilt in one transaction by every scan, so a third copy turns a merge into a maybe; a reply in `reply_copies`, and every reply of a `copy_of` session, is not counted. Migration 6 adds `projects.remote` and makes `hand_projects` (`key` primary key, the root else the remote; `name`, `root`, `remote`, `added_at`). Every table is `STRICT` and every time RFC 3339 UTC.

The computer's state file (added in 0.144; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 05). `state.json` in Catervas's folder in the user's configuration folder (mode 0600, the folder 0700) is `{ last_project?, projects: [<root>...], agents_at_once?: 1..16, daily_cap_usd?: number }`: every team's project in the order they were taken on, the one remembered last, and the limits of 5.5. A file written by an earlier version, with only `last_project`, reads as that one project. `catervas serve` adds a project to `projects` when it first drives it, and a team removed or left is taken out; a file that cannot be read reads as empty.

Hosted tier (phase 20): the same file layout inside the cloud workspace; how it is stored is planned with its hosting, separately in `catervas-ops` (changed in 0.73, ADR 0047).

### 8.5 Event protocol

A single event type with a discriminated `kind`, stamped with time, team, project, task, agent, session, and a monotonically increasing sequence. Kinds are named `<entity>.<past_tense_verb>` (see `docs/standards/code.md`) and include `task.transitioned`, `tool.called`, `tool.returned`, `tool.denied`, `message.posted`, `cost.recorded`, `budget.exhausted`, `escalation.raised`, `escalation.resolved`, `session.started`, `session.ended`, `review.recorded`, `human.accepted`, and, added in 0.2, `question.asked`, `question.answered`, `contract.locked`, `contract.unlocked`, `task.integrated`, `memory.written`, and, added in 0.3, `product_doc.written` (no longer written since 0.91, when `catervas_write_product_doc` went; kept so older logs read), `request.triaged`, and, added in 0.4, `task.created`, `contract.written`, `drift.detected`, `project.scanned`, `team.updated`, `criteria.updated`, and, added in 0.8, `transition.refused`, `contract.evaluated`, `criterion.recorded`, `note.written`, and `pull_request.opened`, which records the pull request Catervas opened for an accepted task under the `pull_request` policy: its address, its number, and its branch (5.14). `task.integrated` records where an accepted task's branch landed: the commit, the integration branch, and whether Catervas (`governor`) or the human (`human`, their `catervas integrate` or a pull request they merged on the forge) integrated it. A `task.transitioned`'s `effects` are `increment_iteration`, `raise_escalation`, `reset_blocker`, `stamp_blocked_at` and, added in 0.62, `nothing_to_integrate`, which the move of a task in a private folder into `accepted` carries (5.14); the board then leaves the task awaiting no integration.
