It opens only `~/.claude.json` (under `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` when that is set), `<claude dir>/settings.json` and `plugins/installed_plugins.json`; for each enabled plugin with a user-scope install, `.mcp.json` and `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` in its install folder, only when the canonical install folder is inside the canonical `plugins/` folder; each present project root's `.mcp.json`; and for each Claude Desktop folder `claude_desktop_config.json` and `Claude Extensions/<dir>/manifest.json`. A project's `.mcp.json`, the desktop config and each manifest are opened only when they are regular files whose canonical path is exactly that file inside its canonical folder, so a link pointing elsewhere is not followed. It never opens `.credentials.json`, `Claude Extensions Settings/`, `mcp-needs-auth-cache.json` (the daily reminder reads its names alone, 0.151) or anything else. Of a server it keeps its name, its kind (`stdio`, `http` or `sse`), the lower-case host of its address (no user, password, port, path or query) and the file name of its program (none when the command holds whitespace or `=`); it never reads `env`, `headers`, `args`, `oauth` or any other field, so no key reaches the index, the printout or `--json`. Of a transcript's tool use only its id, name and, for a file tool, whether the file had a spreadsheet extension is kept. On WSL (`WSL_DISTRO_NAME` set) Claude Desktop's folders under `/mnt/c/Users/<user>/AppData` (Roaming, and the Microsoft Store install's `Local/Packages/Claude_*/LocalCache/Roaming`) are read only when exactly one Windows user has any; with several, none is read and `--json` says `desktop: "several_windows_users"`.

The claude.ai export reader (added in 0.143; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 04). It opens only the `.zip` the owner names, never a folder or a lone JSON file, and reads only `conversations.json`, `projects.json` and `users.json` from it. An entry is matched by its enclosed name, at the root or under exactly one top-level folder; a directory, a link, an absolute name and a name that leaves the folder never match, and two matches are refused. An entry is streamed into the JSON reader through a counting reader and is never extracted: nothing is written to disk but `machine.db`, and the reader names only the fields it keeps, so no message text and no document content is read even into memory, and from `users.json` only the account's id. The zip is limited to 2 GiB and each entry to 1 GiB unpacked, checked on its declared size and on the bytes read. A file that is not a zip, not the export, damaged (a checksum that does not match), encrypted, of a kind the reader cannot unpack, too large or with nothing dated is refused in a sentence, with nothing written; one transaction writes an import. A remote's user, password and port are dropped before it is kept, and every name it prints goes through the terminal-safe printer.

What finding writes and keeps outside the index (added in 0.146; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 06). The only write Catervas ever makes into Claude Code's own settings is `cleanupPeriodDays` in `<claude folder>/settings.json`, when the owner presses "Keep my history longer" (`finding.keep_longer`, 4.4): it sets that key to 90, 365 or 3650 days, keeps every other key and the file's mode, replaces the file whole by renaming a finished copy, and leaves a file it cannot read as JSON as it is. An export dropped onto the page (`POST /hub/export`) is written to a file in the state folder with mode 0600, read by the reader above, and deleted whatever the result, a failed or refused one included; the route answers only the page's own origin with a live session cookie, as the socket does (8.1), takes no more than the reader's size limit and answers 413 `export_too_large` past it. Nothing the scan reads leaves the computer.
The reminder tables (added in 0.151; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 07). Migration 11 of `machine.db` adds `open_todos` to `tool_calls` (the count of not completed items of a `TodoWrite` call, null for every other tool; no to-do text is kept) and reads every transcript again once, and makes `github_runs` (`full_name`, `workflow`, `state`, `last_conclusion`, `last_run_at`, primary key of the first two), `github_deploys` (`full_name` primary key, `environment`, `state`, `created_at`) and `reminder_marks` (`key` primary key, `kind` `snooze` or `dismiss`, `until`, `fingerprint`, `at`), all `STRICT`. `state.json` gains `reminder_time` (`HH:MM`, 09:00 when absent), `reminder_browser` and `reminder_system` (both on when absent).

What GitHub's token reaches (added in 0.148; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 06d). The computer's GitHub token is sent to GitHub's API and to `git clone` and nowhere else. The clone gets it through the process environment (`GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0`), so it is on no command line; git's last line of complaint is shown with the token cut out. The only writes are the key store's, `machine.db`, and the clone's new folder; nothing is written to GitHub.

What the daily reminder runs and reads (added in 0.151; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 07). When a digest is due and no Catervas tab is open, `crates/runtime/src/notify.rs` runs one program with fixed arguments, never a shell, and the title and the body reach it as arguments: on Linux `notify-send --app-name=Catervas <title> <body>`; on macOS `osascript -e 'on run argv' -e 'display notification (item 1 of argv) with title (item 2 of argv)' -e 'end run' <body> <title>`; on Windows `powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command <a fixed script>`, and under WSL (`WSL_DISTRO_NAME` set) the same by `/mnt/c/Windows/System32/WindowsPowerShell/v1.0/powershell.exe`, the fixed script showing a toast from `Windows.UI.Notifications` that opens `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/needs-you`, with the title and the body its arguments after the letter `x` and in base64, and the port, so that PowerShell never parses a word of them. The title is "Catervas · <time>", the body "<count> things need you" and the headline. A missing or failing program is `NotSent`; a test records the program and its arguments and runs none. Git is read in a session's folder only for `git status --porcelain` (with no optional lock) and `git rev-list @{u}..HEAD --count`, only when the folder is a git repository present inside the owner's home, and never writes anything.

What Claude is shown when it names the teams (added in 0.150; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 06e). `proposal.names` runs the owner's `claude` once, as `claude -p` with the prompt on standard input, `--model haiku`, one turn, no tools, no settings and no servers, as the connection check runs it (ADR 0084), and only after the owner pressed the button whose label gave the estimate. The prompt holds, for each card, the names of its folders, the first 40 lines of each README at `HEAD`, the titles of its last 20 sessions and its jobs' names, and all of it goes through `catervas_core::scrub::scrub` first, which replaces `sk-` keys, `ghp_` and `github_pat_` tokens, `AKIA` keys and `xox` tokens, any `NAME=value` line whose name names a key (the rule of an argument that holds a secret, 6.7) and the name, password, query and fragment of an address with `[removed]` or nothing. Claude is asked for a JSON list of `{ id, name, purpose, template }`: a name over 40 characters or a purpose over 120 is cut, a template that is not a ready-made or saved team is ignored, a card id that is not a card's is ignored, and every other key is dropped, so Claude never makes or changes a link. The cost reported as `total_cost_usd` is shown once as "Names from Claude · cost $0.02". A run that fails is refused `names_failed` with Claude Code's words, and the cards keep their names.

The jobs scan (added in 0.140; ADR 0059; phase 10 step 03). It runs only read-only programs, each looked up on `PATH`, with a cleared environment, no input and a ten second limit: `crontab -l`, `systemctl [--user] list-timers` and `systemctl [--user] cat`, `plutil -convert json -o -` on a plist in `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, and `schtasks.exe /query /fo CSV /v`. It keeps a job's schedules, its name and its project, and never a command line or its arguments, an environment line or value, other unit keys, a prompt, a key, a Task Scheduler column but the few named, or any other field of a background job's `state.json`; a crontab line is keyed by a hash and never kept. No tool input is read but `CronCreate`'s schedule fields. A file is opened only by its canonical path: a repository's inside its canonical root, regular and at most 1 MiB; a saved cron file only when its canonical path is the folder's own `.claude/scheduled_tasks.json`; a background job's `state.json` only inside the canonical `jobs/`; a link pointing out is refused and nothing else in a job's folder is opened.

**Autopilot and connector calls (added in 0.138; ADR 0082).** While autopilot is on, a `paid` or `ask` connector call runs with no grant and no allowance, from a session about a task or about none, and is recorded `tool.approved { by: autopilot }` with its whole input before `tool.called`. A `denied` tool and a tool the active plan marks are unchanged; so are credentials, which never enter an agent's context, and Catervas's own state, which no tool writes. Such calls are rate limited per agent, counted from `tool.approved` in this computer's log over the past hour, so the count survives a restart. A call is refused `rate_limited` when the agent has made `policy.paid_calls_per_hour` calls of any tool, when it has made a third of that (at least 1) of this tool, or when it has made 3 calls of this tool with the same input (its `input_sha256`), a loop and not work; the refusal says which, and when the hour frees a place. The third `rate_limited` refusal in one session ends the session and flags its task in Catervas's name (`task.flagged { flagged_by: catervas }`, needs "<agent> kept calling <tool>"), and a flagged task gets no session while autopilot is on. A session about no task only ends. The daily limit stays the hard stop above all of it; off, nothing is rate limited and the call asks.

## 9. Open source and premium

The repository is one codebase under Apache 2.0, with premium code in an `ee/` directory under a separate commercial license, following the GitLab and PostHog pattern. Everything in section 5 is Apache 2.0 without exception; a governance layer that people cannot audit is not one they will trust with their repositories.

Free, forever: the full harness, all six roles and their kits (6.7), the pixel office, local execution with the user's own API key, MCP and skills, the audit log.

Premium, in rough priority order: hosted execution with included model credits so the user does not need a key; cloud sync so a team can be opened from more than one machine; cost analytics and history beyond thirty days; additional office themes and avatar packs; priority support; and, later, multi-user teams and SSO.

Catervas Cloud, from phase 11, before the web launch (ADR 0048), has a free tier that signs users in and does nothing else: it holds Catervas's own sign-in apps, a GitHub App and a Google app, and their secrets, server side, and a user signs in to it with a Catervas account, once per computer (6.7, 8.6; ADR 0044; changed in 0.61 from 0.60's "until the premium phase, every login is the user's", ADR 0043). No build carries a credential of Catervas's. The premium phase is Catervas Cloud's paid tier: hosted execution and the rest of the list above, with the same apps.

Nothing that makes the agents safer or more controllable is ever premium.

## 10. Non-functional requirements

- The governor evaluates a tool call in under five milliseconds; it is on the hot path of every action.
- The UI stays responsive with ten thousand events in a project. Projections, not raw log scans, back every view.
- The shipped models are chosen so that a first day of the suggested team of six doing a delivery's work and its two ceremonies costs, by estimate, about twenty-five dollars on the user's key at current list prices; this is a property of the defaults, not a cap (ADR 0015). This number must be re-derived when prices change and is stated, as an estimate, in the setup screen and on the Team page, as the suggested six's with "A smaller team costs less." after it, since a team started from a saved one or from scratch is often smaller (added in the 0.35 fix wave). (Changed in 0.31: the earlier figure, under twenty dollars for a team of five, dates from revision 0.1 and the repository records no derivation of it, so the six's figure is that one scaled by six agents to five, twenty-four dollars, rounded up; the UI/UX Designer runs on the Developer's model and adds an `explore` and a decision session to each of its tasks, so the scaling may understate it, and a measured first day should replace it. Since a scaled figure bounds nothing, the setup screen says "about", with "(an estimate)", not "under".)
- Everything works offline except model calls and MCP servers that need the network.
- All user-facing text is in English for the first release, with strings externalized.
- Configuring the harness is user-friendly and foolproof (added in 0.10). Every setting has a safe default and a one-line explanation in plain language. A change that would leave the team unable to work, such as a team without an active Product Manager (F1; changed in 0.103), is refused before it is saved, in words that say what to change; the daemon names each refusal by a code that the page words for a person, so a schema's own text never reaches the screen (changed in 0.26). Every refusal the web app shows is a plain sentence of its own, worded from the refusal's code, or, for a setup refusal that carries none, from the daemon's sentence it knows, with one plain sentence for any other; the daemon's or a parser's own text never shows (changed in 0.37). Each change shows its effect before it is saved, and every setting can be put back to its default: the defaults are the values `catervas init` writes, which the daemon answers to the page, and each page that changes a setting offers "Put back the default" beside it (changed in 0.26). Setup's questions stay changeable after setup, from Settings, the same controls saved the same way (added in 0.27). The web UI does this by asking the daemon to validate the change and name its effects, in plain sentences such as "Ari may now run commands", "Finished work waits for you to merge it" or "The team may spend up to $10 a day", which the page lists before Save (added in 0.26). The page works out none of the team's rules itself: the daemon answers, for the team as it is and for a change before it is saved, each agent's model and effort as its sessions run them, in words (a model older than its family's newest is marked older), the tiers it holds and those its role and the team's permission answers give it; the page shows what each agent may do from those tiers.
- Every screen meets WCAG 2.2 AA (added in 0.18).
- The web app is responsive from 360 px wide (added in 0.18). It is not a phone app: the phone apps are native (8.1).
- Every client is built from the brand's design tokens in `@catervas/brand` (section 14), so no colour, type size, or spacing is written into a client by hand (added in 0.18).
- The pixel scene renders at 60 frames per second on a 2020 laptop with integrated graphics, and can be disabled entirely for users who want only the board.

## 11. Milestones

Milestone 0, the harness. Four to five weeks. `core`, `store`, `runtime` with one adapter, a command-line interface, and two roles: Product Manager and Developer, the latter instantiated twice so that one Developer reviews the other (5.1). Exit criterion: on Catervas's own repository (private until the open-source launch; decided 2026-09-15, and moot since the repository was found public on 2026-09-27), the PM writes contracts for three real issues, one Developer implements them, the other verifies, the PM accepts, and a human reviews the diffs and the event log and agrees each task was done as contracted. No UI. This milestone exists to find out whether the governance loop works before anyone draws a pixel. Its live run was not held at the command line: the founder decided on 2026-09-24 that all live testing is done in the web UI once the product side is built, so Milestone 0's exit is run in the browser together with Milestone 1's run of the team's work, which shows a delivery's review and retro (changed in 0.18; changed in 0.116).

Milestone 1, the team. Five to six weeks. All five roles, the channel, ceremonies, and then, once the brand is recorded (section 14), the web UI covering the whole working loop, the one-to-one chats among it (moved from Milestone 2 in 0.34; ADR 0026) (changed in 0.18; the desktop shell moved to Milestone 3 in 0.20). Exit criterion: a new user with no help can go from nothing to an accepted task on their own repository inside thirty minutes, measured with five test users, at least three of them non-technical. The test is run in the browser (changed in 0.18 and 0.20).

Milestone 2, the ecosystem and launch. Six to eight weeks (four to five until 0.22). Other providers and agent engines, with every engine under the same governor (phase 13; added in 0.24, ADR 0023; renumbered by ADR 0029, ADR 0048, ADR 0049, ADR 0051 and ADR 0057); per-agent MCP and skills UI, the Finance Specialist (added in 0.21), the role kits that equip every role with its skills and connectors (6.7; added in 0.22), memory (the one-on-one conversations moved to Milestone 1 in 0.34), the audit viewer, notifications. Public open-source launch at the end of this milestone, on the web alone (changed in 0.18 and 0.20), once a pre-registered, blind benchmark shows a Catervas team at least as good as one fully equipped agent on quality and clearly better on failure rates and cost control (phase 15; added by ADR 0025).

Milestone 3, desktop (added in 0.20). Starts only when the web release is complete and tested: the founder and at least three non-technical testers run the released feature set in the browser, and the founder signs off the record. Then the Finance Specialist's receipts intake, as the first release after that check (added in 0.21); then the Tauri shell with the daemon in-process, the office scene, native notifications, and a desktop release. Exit criterion: the Milestone 1 loop repeated in the desktop app.

Milestone 4, mobile (added in 0.18; Milestone 3 until 0.20). Native iOS and Android apps, each in the platform's own toolkit, after the desktop app has shipped. How a phone reaches a running Catervas is open (section 12, question 8), and the answer may make this milestone follow premium rather than precede it.

Milestone 5, premium (Milestone 3 until 0.18, Milestone 4 until 0.20). Hosted execution on the same event protocol, license and billing, cloud sync. Timing depends on what the open-source launch teaches.

## 12. Open questions

Recorded here so they are decided on purpose.

1. Resolved 2026-09-15: human acceptance of contracts is a team policy, `human_accepts_contracts`, with values `high_risk` (the default) and `all` (superseded 2026-10-16 by ADR 0061: the policy loads and is ignored, and no contract waits for the human). A "training wheels" period is the user switching it to `all` for a while.
2. Resolved 2026-09-15, superseded 2026-10-16 by ADR 0062: there are no sprints; a delivery closes on an accepted epic, five accepted tasks or a team with no work left (section 3).
3. Resolved 2026-09-15: the board and task detail show cost; the scene does not.
4. Resolved 2026-09-15: no-sandbox mode ships, with a warning on every run and in the setup screen.
5. Resolved 2026-09-15: the register is kept minimal (5.9), and the channel is instrumented so the choice can be revisited with data.
6. A second model provider. Not before someone asks, but the adapter interface is there.
7. The brand (added in 0.18): the logo, the palette, the type, the slogans, the voice, and whether the office scene's pixel-art look extends beyond the scene. It is the founder's to supply, and phase 5 records it (section 14). No implementation after phase 4 starts until it is recorded.
8. How a phone app reaches a running Catervas (added in 0.18), since a phone does not run agents: the user's own desktop Catervas over a secure link, or the hosted tier. The mobile phase decides (phase 19).

## 13. Glossary

Epic: the contract that translates one request from the user, approved by the user before it is broken into tasks (5.16). Contract: the document that makes an epic or a task ready. Locked contract: a contract the human owns and agents cannot change (5.11). Team rule: a constraint the human sets once and the governor applies to every contract and tool call (5.12). Criterion library: named, reusable exit criteria (5.13). Worktree: a task's own checkout of the repository (5.14). Exit criterion: a check that must pass for a task to be accepted. Governor: the deterministic enforcement layer. Ceremony: a structured team conversation, a delivery's review or retro (changed in 0.116). Delivery: the work accepted since the last one, closed by an accepted epic, five accepted standalone tasks or a team with no work left, and reviewed once (3; added in 0.116). Tier: a permission capability. ADR: architecture decision record. MCP: Model Context Protocol, the open standard for connecting tools to models. Skill: a folder of instructions an agent can load, following the Agent Skills format. Human gate: a point where the work waits for the human, a contract's approval or a result's acceptance, shown with a plain-language summary, the diff, and Catervas's check results (5.4; added in 0.18). Design token: a named value of the brand, a colour, a type size, a spacing, that every client reads from `@catervas/brand` (section 14; added in 0.18).

## 14. Brand (added in 0.18)

The brand is recorded in `docs/brand/brand.md` (founder, 2026-09-26; palette changed 2026-09-28). This section says where it goes and what it governs.

The name is Catervas.

The logo, the colour palette, the type, the slogans, and the voice are the founder's to supply. They are recorded in `docs/brand/` as the guidelines people read: logo usage and clear space, the palette and each colour's role, type, voice and tone, the slogans, and what not to do.

The assets and the design tokens live in `packages/brand` (`@catervas/brand`): the logo, the app icons each client needs, and the tokens (colour, type scale, spacing, radius) in a light and a dark theme. Every client uses them, the web app, the desktop app, and later the iOS and Android apps, so that one brand holds from the first screen (section 10). Every colour pair the tokens use for text meets WCAG 2.2 AA contrast, and no two jobs share a colour.

The office scene (F10) is pixel art. Whether that look extends beyond the scene, to the rest of the web and desktop apps, is the brand's decision.

The provisional design system the project plan held (D13) is superseded by the brand (ADR 0016).
